dams. Watercare Services would also very much rather that no one messed around with
the potential safety of Auckland’s water supply. It is very professional, and it is very
worried.
Maybe the people of Auckland need to be worried as well, because have they been
told? Has anyone actually taken the time to explain properly to Aucklanders what is
going to be done in their water catchment next month, and what might happen if
something goes wrong? The Auckland Council website says very reassuringly that
“Each hectare will receive around 2-3kg of cereal pellets, containing 0.15 per cent of the
active 1080 ingredient. That’s about one teaspoon of 1080 per hectare.” Well, just to put
that into perspective. A lethal dose of 1080 for an adult is about 200 milligrams, which
is about a twentieth of a teaspoon. So that is enough poison to kill 20 people per hectare,
which over 17,000 hectares is enough poison to kill 340,000 people. No one believes it
is going to go anywhere near that wrong, but it does show us just how dangerous this
stuff can be. There are sub-lethal effects that can be very nasty as well.
But all that aside, it is a very great concern that this operation wi ll require half of
Auckland’s Hunua dams to be taken out of commission, two at a time, for an
unspecified period, until the poison drop is over and the tests have all come back clear.
That is if nothing goes wrong. Never mind the cost to the Auckland ratep ayer—
$500,000 roughly, and that is on top of the cost of the drop itself. It might all be based
on faulty, inaccurate, or massively overstated data, just like with TB. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak in this general
debate. The other day I was chatting to some constituents and they said to me that it is
phenomenal what National has been polling, because of a couple of things. Firstly,
leadership. Andrew Little is at 9 percent, and I will tell you why. There are a couple of
reasons. Firstly, ultimately, politics is a contest of ideas. That means it is about not only
putting up good policy for our country but also supporting when the other side has
really good policy. What have we seen from Labour members in the area of social
innovation? They oppose the ACC cuts, they oppose mental health bonds, they oppose
everything, but they do not have good policy for New Zealand. Under our Government,
we have embar ked on a very significant programme of both economic and social
reform. That is why New Zealanders are voting for us. It is because they can see the
results. They can see that 170,000 jobs have been created. They can see that we are on
track for another 2.8 percent growth. They can see another 150,000 jobs on track to be
created. They can see that we are making real results in areas like vulnerable children —
whether it is the $790 million package or whether it is the thousands of houses that have
been insulated in this country. How about the policy of free GP visits for the under -13s?
This Government has done a significant amount, not just in the economic area, but also
in the social area.
4266  General Debate 3 Jun 2015
What do we have from Opposition members? They just say no. We saw tha t this
week with mental health bonds. It is significant because, ultimately, people ask the
basic question: is the Opposition focused on the issues that matter? This week, what
have we heard from the Opposition? We have heard about Saudi farms. Actually, t here
are a whole lot of people in New Zealand who care about our most vulnerable children.
They care about the issues of housing. They care about tax reform. They care about
ACC levy reductions. These are the issues that matter to New Zealanders. We have an
Opposition that is not focused on the issues that matter to New Zealand. Compare that
with a Government that is absolutely achieving the results.
Let us look at some of those results. We have seen a 38 percent reduction in youth
crime. In terms of the n umber of teenage sole parents, they have dropped by 40 percent
since 2011. This Government’s social reforms have been phenomenal, and the reason
the left is in trouble is they know they are bereft of ideas. They cannot compete at the
social level. National  Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) results are
improving, and they are improving across some of our most disadvantaged groups. The
NCEA results for Māori and Pasifika students are up. Why are we able to do so well in
terms of targeting those students? It is because of national standards. It is actually
saying that to be able to help those children we need to know where they are, and that
means knowing those schools in Northland—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Been up to Northland College lately?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: That is right, Mr Peters. It means knowing the schools in
Northland, where those kids are, actually targeting them, and ensuring they have got the
teaching support to be able to raise achievements and, ultim ately, give those kids a
passport to a better future. That is what this Government is focused on. That is what this
Government has policy for. This Government has leadership.
Compare that with the Opposition, which is not focused on the things that matter .
That is why Andrew Little is at 9 percent. I saw it better than anyone. At the end of the
day, when you look at ACC what were Opposition members’ comments? What were Mr
Little’s comments? Firstly, he started to talk about pay as you go. In a situation wh ere
we have finally got a social investment approach, we are finally able to help some of
our most vulnerable in terms of the seriously injured, Labour wants to unravel ACC, it
wants to gut the assets, and it wants to go back to a situation where we cannot  have
long-term meaningful injury prevention. It is very clear that we have got a party on this
side that has good ideas, and new ideas in terms of social innovation, like mental health
bonds. We are doing things right across education reform. We are doing a huge amount
in terms of ACC reform, to make sure the scheme is more transparent for our most
vulnerable New Zealanders. Compare that with an Opposition, particularly the Labour
Party, that will oppose everything and propose nothing. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: At question time today, just a moment ago, I
asked the Acting Attorney -General whether the terms of reference of our intelligence
review would be amended to reflect the views of other legislatures that are moving to
protect civil liberties. This included the US Congress, which yesterday passed the USA
Freedom Act to end the mass collection of metadata. Minister Adams was not especially
forthcoming in her reply. She stressed the  adequacy of the terms of reference and then
confessed that she basically lacked the ministerial competence to comment further on
the question, the question having been passed on to her by the Prime Minister. So let us
analyse the issues that were passed o ver so lightly by the Acting Attorney -General. The
terms of reference contained two general tasks. The first is to determine whether the
legislative frameworks of the intelligence agencies are well placed to protect New
Zealand’s national security arrangem ents while protecting human rights. The second is
3 Jun 2015  General Debate 4267
around whether there are sufficient safeguards to ensure the agencies act lawfully and
maintain public confidence.
Well, if we are talking about public confidence, it is time that New Zealand emulated
the United States in restoring the principles of civil liberties laid down by Jefferson and
cherished in the United States and, presumably, here as well. There is a distinction
between the general review requirement that is in the statute and the precise terms  of
reference that the Attorney -General has crafted. The statute foresees a review of any
matter relevant to the functions of effectiveness and efficiency of the agencies in their
contribution to national security. But the terms of reference are more focus ed. They are
on whether the legislative frameworks are well placed to protect national security while
protecting human rights. It may be a coincidence, and it is good to have human rights
included, but what we have here is national security as the primary value and central
framework, with human rights as a secondary value, something to be protected from the
onslaught.
A specific task identified in the terms of reference is whether the recent foreign
terrorist fighters legislation should be extended or modified beyond March 2017. This is
an issue of some moment. Just last Friday the Security Council adopted its latest
presidential statement on foreign terrorist fighters. The overriding concern is that
foreign terrorist fighters have increased in numbers to 25,000 from 100 countries.
Receiving one back into one’s own country is proving too dyspeptic for Australia, but
New Zealand, at least, is maintaining for the moment a level head on the matter. The
Attorney-General’s statement to the council had many good elements—in particular, the
stress he placed on countering violent extremism through supporting individuals in
communities in having a positive stake in society. The key, he said, is to be inclusive,
not exclusive—to integrate, not marginalise. We agree and  commend him for this. But
that approach needs to be buttressed with legislative reform on mass surveillance. It
needs to lead with the principle of human rights and make national security compatible
with the inalienable rights of the individual.
That Jeffersonian principle has just been rediscovered in the United States in the past
few days, following the loss of its constitutional compass 14 years ago. Sanity at last is
being restored. The USA Freedom Act, replacing the notorious Patriot Act, limits the
Federal Government’s ability to collect phone data. It requires the FBI to formally
declare a statement of facts showing reasonable grounds to believe that the information
sought is relevant to a particular investigation, and that the facts give rise to a
reasonable, articulable suspicion of activities associated with a foreign power or its
agent. Under the terms of reference here in New Zealand, the review will also have
regard to any additional matters that arise during the review as agreed by the Attorne y-
General. We therefore recommend that the Attorney -General notify now in writing in
the New Zealand Gazette  that the modification of intrusive surveillance powers and
restoration of civil liberties, as legislated in the United States, be taken up as a matter
that has arisen and that New Zealand consider emulating the US initiative.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: It is a pleasure to speak
here in this general debate in the first week of June. As we have already heard, the polls
were quite clear in the last week. National continues with our ability to stay in the high -
40s. The Labour Party, of course, is wallowing in the early -30s. We have got Winston
and his crew hovering around 5, 6, or 7 percent. And you have got members opposite
who complain and whine and moan and say that the sky is falling. Well, clearly,
according to New Zealanders across this nation, the sky  is not falling. You have got to
ask yourself why. I was at the Warriors match on Sunday night and a few Australians
were asking me why this Government is so popular. They asked what we were doing
that leads us to have these types of polls in our third ter m. I said to them that it is
4268  General Debate 3 Jun 2015
because we have got leadership —clearly. We have got John Key, an extraordinary
politician, an extraordinary man, and a man who is leading this country admirably.
Clearly, we have got a caucus that is capable, that is competent,  and that is doing its job
of leading this country. But the other thing we are doing is focusing on the things that
matter to all New Zealanders.
On top of that list is jobs —on top of that list is jobs. When I survey my electorate of
Maungakiekie and I ge t 2,500 responses from the 46,000 people who live there, they
say the No. 1 issue that they want me to focus on, that they want John Key and our
caucus to focus on, in this Parliament is jobs. Today, this morning, in New Zealand 2.36
million people —2.36 mi llion people —got up and went to work, and that is the most
New Zealanders who have got up and gone to work than at any time in our history. We
have got unemployment falling steadily to 5.8 percent and we know that that is heading
towards 4.5 percent in 3 y ears’ time. We know that we have created over 194,000 jobs
in the last 4 years, and in the next 4 years we estimate that we will create another
Jobs are important. Why? Well, let us just give members opposite a little bit of a
lesson as to why jobs are important. They help families. They help families feed, clothe,
and raise their kids as well as look after their elderly, as well as look after their
communities. That is why jobs are important and that is why our focus, our primary
focus of this Government, has been on jobs. Jobs also release people from the
dependency of welfare. I know that the Hon Anne Tolley, as the Minister for Social
Development, will know this. It gets people off welfare and into jobs and away from the
dependency on welfare that you get. It also helps with the reoffending rates, because we
know that if people are working —people are in employment, people are occupied and
earning money, looking after their families, looking after their communities, building up
this nation—they are less likely to reoffend. That is why it is important that we focus on
jobs, and this Government’s track record on jobs is unsurpassed.
But it is not just about jobs. We know that there are families, there are kids, suffering
out there, and that is  why at the heart of Budget 2015—at the heart of this Budget —we
are focused on a support package: $790 million. Yes, that is right. If you did not hear
that right: $790 million will be spent on helping children in our poorest households.
That is $25 a week for the beneficiaries out there who are struggling. I went to my local
budgeting agency just after the election. I spent 5 hours there listening to people who
were suffering, listening to people in hardship, and they told me that they needed a hand
up, not a handout. The $25- a-week increase in benefits for families with children is the
first time in 43 years that any Government has raised them above inflation. It is the first
time and it is a National Government. I am proud of this package. I am proud of t his
Government for focusing on jobs, for focusing on those who are impoverished, and for
putting together a Budget —the seventh Budget in a row —that is actually committed to
the welfare and the well-being of all New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: For me, the member who just resumed
his seat, the Hon Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, personified the arrogance that has taken over the
National Party going into this third term of Government . He modestly said: “People ask
me all the time: ‘Why do you do so well? Why are you so popular? Why are you so
well-liked?’ ”. How modest can he be? The Government has stopped connecting with
what ordinary New Zealanders really feel. One of the examples t hat I am increasingly
hearing frustration about from members of this House is the Ministers’ arrogance and
dismissal of select committee procedures, where members of select committees —
including National Party members who are the chairs of the committees —hear about
determinations of bills that are the property of the committees through a ministerial
statement. How arrogant and disrespectful of the process and of members of the select
3 Jun 2015  General Debate 4269
committee—including members of their own party —is that? It really is just o ne of
many indications of the increasing arrogance and dislocation of this Government, that
its members must be a little bit despondent. They all went into the last election —and,
actually, the election before—with their No. 1 promise being to deliver a Government
Budget surplus in the 2015 Budget. And what did we see? Yet again, Bill English—
failed leader, now failed Minister of Finance —after seven Budgets, each failing to
deliver a surplus. It was not just an expectation or a hope; it was the No. 1 election
promise in the 2011 campaign and the 2014 campaign—another broken promise.
Judith Collins seems to be the only one who is reasonably excited about the future of
the National Party. She recently led the caucus revolt. I have heard a number of people
saying about the National caucus being revolting—but she led the revolt in relation to
the health and safety reforms that Michael Woodhouse had promised. She ruined his
speech to a very large workplace safety conference. Michael Woodhouse had said “I
will be there, and I will be giving a speech with great promises and detail.”, and he had
to turn up and say “It has all been put on hold.”, because of the revolt that Judith Collins
had led. Then there was her less -than-subtle attack on Gerry Brownlee, where she
launched an attack about the doors that he has required to have put in. I am not sure
whether he thinks the doors will keep Judith Collins out of their caucus room, or just out
of our corridor, but it certainly was Gerry Brownlee’s idea.
That pales into in significance, though—pales into insignificance —beside what
Murray McCully has done. An $11 million bribe —there can be no other word to
describe it—paid to a private Saudi farm. I disagree with the politics of a number of
members of the National Party, than k goodness, but I do not challenge the integrity of
every single member, and I know that some of them will be squirming because they,
like many other New Zealanders, deeply value the integrity of our country, of our
representatives, and of people who travel overseas to represent us. And our international
reputation has been tarnished by Murray McCully’s bribe. He is off on overseas leave
now; he is having a bit of a rest.
Meanwhile, we have got Steven Joyce causing bother for the National Party. He said
he did not know much about the sign that cost—what?

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: $43,000 for a sign.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: $43,000 for a sign saying “MBIE” —“MoBIE”. It seems like
quite a lot of money to pay for a sign.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: It’s a whale of a time.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: It certainly is. I will leave that to your contribution, Mr
Cunliffe, because that was a very good interjection. But Steven Joyce today, during
question time, was exposed as not only knowing details about the sign but having
personally chosen the colour. This Minister for Economic Development is right into the
details of his portfolio. It is just another example of the disconnect between Ministers,
their departments, and ordinar y New Zealanders. We have had poor old Maurice
Williamson. How he sits in the House every day, watching hapless Ministers struggle
through questions, when he is still consigned to the backbench. And now he has been
publicly rejected by the ACT Party —publicly rejected. There were the Northland by -
election bribes with the bridges, and now we have got the Prime Minister distracting,
once again, with boat people coming to New Zealand. It is a really Tony Abbott trick.
Can I conclude on an Australian point, a serious point, that I want to make. The first-
ever—and only, actually—woman Premier of Victoria passed away this week. I want to
conclude with a tribute to the memory of Joan Kirner and all she did for women
internationally and for education. Thank you.
4270  General Debate 3 Jun 2015

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Just following on from that point
about the death of Joan Kirner, the first woman Premier of Victoria, National members
pay our tribute as well.
In this House today we had a question from the New Zealand First Party around the
SuperGold card access that they were supposed to deliver for the punters who voted for
them. I will just read from an article that quotes the words of the member for Northland:
“I’ll get you a Gold Card across there. But it goes like this: you’ve got to vote for us
first.” Well, they did that. They voted for them. They voted for them. And have they
been delivered the SuperGold card access? No, not at all. What I am going to say next—
there will be points of order from the New Zealand First Party, because they will not
like this, but this is the truth of what happened. There was an email on 27 May from
Winston Peters to the Minister for Senior Citizens. That is only because he knew that
the media was on to the story first. He did that email only after the media was on to the
story to cover himself. That is the old Winston Peters, New Zealand First -  approach to
politics. What they did is they came into this House today and said “Oh, we sent you an
email on 27 May.” —only a week ago, not even that —and “We are looking after our
constituents.” What a load of rubbish. The people of Northland will never get anything
out of the New Zealand First Party, and they know it. That is the real ity of that political
party.
Denis O’Rourke: Why did they vote for us then?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Oh, why did they vote for you? They voted for you for some
unknown reason that nobody can find out, but they will not do it again, I  know that
much.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: 70 years.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Seventy years. OK —43 years it took for this Parliament to
deliver for the people of New Zealand who were on welfare, 43 years. Labour could not
lift a finger and deliver for thos e people, and National did it. Labour never did it. It
cannot even get a decent leader who can do a decent speech. Labour members sit there
now, ignoring the reality of what is going on.
Bill English did a great speech yesterday He talked about the realit y of left -wing
politics. In the left wing it is about control of people. That is all it is about. It is not
about empowering people, it is not about giving people education and the ability to
make their own futures. It is about control by having a group of  academics on that side
of the House who think that they are holier -than-thou, and can come in and tell other
people what they should do with their lives. We have seen the newest of the holier-than-
thou come in as the leader of the Green Party. I say to the Labour Party you should be
worried about that man. You should be worried about him, because he is putting across
a rational image for the Green Party —which is unusual, I know, but he is doing that.
And he is actually talking about the environment, which is something they never talked
about and was one of their big failings. But he is doing those two things, and in doing
that he is eroding the left -wing vote from the Labour Party. He will be eroding the left -
wing vote from the New Zealand First Party.
But I tell you, the public of New Zealand, you cannot trust anyone on that side. Even
if they come into this House saying what you want to hear, they do not believe it. There
is no way a leader of the Green Party can actually have a rational thought. That is not
possible, because that party is the party of extremes. They do not vote in people like
that. People who will have rational thoughts will not be in that party, and you can do all
the messages you like, but your party is in exactly the same boat—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume his seat. I have a point of order —
well, I hope I have a point of order.
3 Jun 2015  General Debate 4271

items.speaker: Denise Roche
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I find what he is saying
personally offensive, and I would ask that he withdraw it—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No—this is a robust debate. If that offends the member, she
is, frankly, in the wrong game.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Look, I just want to back that up with a bit of proof, if
anything. Richard Prosser spoke, and his line of the day was that possums live in the
bush and eat the bush. So let us talk about rational thoughts coming out of that side of
the House. That is your best speaker and he talks about possums living in the bush and
eating the bush. Are  we not lucky to have a bush at the end of the day? That was
Richard Prosser. Well, the Green Party —do not trust them. Do not trust that man. That
man is coming into this House professing to be some kind of neutral leader of a political
party. The Green Party will always be the extreme in this Parliament. It will hurt the
Labour Party at the next election, because it will go out there and try to take those
rational left-wing votes. So the Labour Party will have to take out the Green Party at
some stage, and , well, the New Zealand First Party is just a protest party. It is just a
party where, if nobody can find anything else to vote for, they vote for them. It is a
shame that its members actually believe that they stand for something and that they are
of any worth in this Parliament, because they are not. It will be a good thing when they
go, because then this Parliament will actually be a much better place. It has been a great
Budget, it has been a great time to have these speeches, and we look forward to it
following through the House.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: The member who has just
resumed his seat, David Bennett, personifies this National Government. Instead of
making a  logical argument, he just gives us abuse. Whether you allow it or not, Mr
Speaker, it is just abuse. This is a Government that is mired in distractions, in scandal,
and in corruption—which is not too strong a word—while New Zealand lacks a plan
that will put more money in the pockets of hard- working Kiwi families, relieve the
housing crisis, and get New Zealand back to work.
Let me tell you about the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment—what a
multi-headed hydra. It was created by the Prime Min ister to give Steven Joyce a sandpit
almost as big as Bill English’s. It was divide and rule at work, balancing the lieutenants
to give Mr Joyce an empire. It has been a miserable, singular failure. Steven Joyce can
micro-manage the portrait and landscape on his slide pack but he cannot oversee cost
control on a $43,000 street sign. What an embarrassment, what a failure of ministerial
responsibility, and what a failure of cost management in his department.
It is no surprise, because this is the same depart ment that spent $360,000 on luxury
couches for its staff. It is the same department that screwed up the negotiations with
Skycity, which was not helped by the Prime Minister giving the casino a lucky break or
two or three or four. It screwed up the discuss ions with MediaWorks and gave it a $43
million suspensory loan. Oh, and what did happen to John Campbell recently when he
got a bit uppity with the Prime Minister? I wonder. The Government folded for Rio
Tinto—a $15 million, roughly, bribe to stay in offic e. That reminds me somewhat of
Murray McCully’s exploits building sheep farms in the desert.
This is a Government mired in scandal, mired in distraction, and without a decent
idea about how to effect change in our economy. We face a choice, ladies and
gentlemen. The choice is between muddling through, banking on milk powder,
earthquake rebuilds, and bits and pieces, or being a country that undertakes a proper
change programme for the future. To do that it has got to be high value. It has got to be
driven by innovation, science, and technology.
Today in the Education and Science Committee, Minister Joyce showed what a
complete waste of space the Government’s science and technology programme is. The
4272  General Debate 3 Jun 2015
chief executive officer of the MacDiarmid Institute no less  says that the Marsden Fund
is a shambles. Only 7 percent of project bids get through, and the Minister admitted they
have no idea of the overhead costs of the 93 percent that do not.
The Prime Minister’s Chief Science Advisor, Sir Peter Gluckman, whom th e
Government just made a member of the Order of New Zealand, said the system is beset
by “short-termism” and that the Government has no strategy. Shaun Hendy, an eminent
professor of physics and co- author of a book with no less than Sir Paul Callaghan, sai d
that is because they have to go cap in hand for co- funding to the dairy industry, because
it is the only one that has any money. The science system reinforces the old economy
instead of building the economy of the future. That is why we have had a Budget  of
broken promises and seven deficits out of seven, instead of Labour’s nine surpluses out
of nine.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: Also not true. $4 billion deficit in 2008—$4 billion.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: There is a growing internation al deficit as exports go
backwards, Mr Bishop, from 32 percent of GDP, not to the Government’s target of 40
percent, but in this Budget, by its own admission, down to 26 percent from 32 percent.
That is an amazing snatching of defeat from the jaws of the v ictory of the post global
financial crisis rebound. It is a spectacular failure, and we have hundreds of billions of
dollars of external debt and savings debt.
What is the Government’s solution? Knacker KiwiSaver and take away the kick- start
to fund some public relations for beneficiaries that it never believed in in the first place.

items.speaker: That is the game of this Budget
items.text: spin above substance, fiddling while Rome burns. This
is a Government without a plan, a Government beset by distractions, and a New
Zealand that deserves better.

items.speaker: BARBARA KURIGER
items.text: In the words of
Minister Anne Tolley this afternoon, this is a Government that really cares. As you have
heard from other speakers, National is the party that is investing another $790 million
over the next 4 years —money that is going to go into families on benefits and low
incomes and help those children. A $25 weekly increase in benefits for families is going
to be immensely helpful.
Also, this Government is the Government that is interested in what works. To help us
make the right decisions and investments for taxpayers’ money in the future, we are
actually using data to get a better understanding o f the people who use our services and
have the need for that support. Just as an example, right now if you take the most
vulnerable 1 percent of all 5 -year-olds, which is around 600 children in any one year
and we know who these kids are, and actually help them get on to a wonderful track as
5-year-olds—at the moment the trajectory says that three -quarters of those children will
not get National Certificate of Educational Achievement without help. It also says that
40 percent will have been on a benefit for  2 years by the time they are 21 years old and,
probably, it is likely a quarter of those children will be in prison by the age of 35.
We know that actually taking these children now, investing in them, and changing
services in order to intervene will hel p these people lead more fulfilling lives. Imagine
the self-esteem of being able to be on the straight and narrow, as opposed to the other
options that are currently the tracks where they might head.
The other impressive thing about this Government is it is actually putting a lot more
money into education and health. I was very, very impressed in the last adjournment
week, about 3 weeks ago, when I had a day out around Te Awamutu and Ōtorohanga
with the Hon Hekia Parata and we looked at some of the money that was going into
special education, particularly around literacy. It was really worthwhile to hear from a
young girl standing up with an iPad, who had been really struggling with literacy about
8 months prior, and through having a wonderful school principal who cares, sharing
3 Jun 2015  General Debate 4273
their knowledge and information with young people —she was so proud of herself, this
young girl. That very same principal is actually working with other schools in the
community to share those programmes and share those skills.
The other thing is that this Government also is a caring Government. Mental health
funding has increased by over $200 million since 2008- 09, and today was a classic
example. I have just been out for a coupl e of hours at a function at lunchtime where a
programme was released called Farmstrong. It is there to help connect rural
communities, help well- being, and help farmers get through this stage in their life
where, actually, the payout is not brilliant. It w ill come right and we all know it will
come right; we just do not know when it will come right. There are going to be a lot of
farming families out there who are going to be struggling in the meantime until it does
come right.
How do the Green Party membe rs show they care about that? They stand up in the
House this afternoon and they talk about carbon taxes —more targets on farmers who
have already got enough on their plate. We are doing so much work at the moment
trying to hold them all together and trying  to solve as many issues and save potential
suicides as we possibly can. The money that the Greens are targeting in terms of
wanting to put carbon taxes on these people might just be the money that helps those
people to feed their families and take part in  their family activities over the next little
while.
So I actually applaud what this Government is doing. I applaud the money that is
actually being put into exploring these social bond programmes, particularly around
programmes that will expand on pilots  that are delivering employment services to New
Zealanders who have mental health conditions. I have been witness to those people in
my own community and some of the organisations in Te Awamutu that are helping
those people get into work. They are doing a fantastic job, and we will help
communities to help themselves. Thank you.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : Transport is one of the most vital functions for
any Government, but in New Zealand, regional transport is being shunted aside. New
Zealand First is the party for the regions because we would put that right. We deplore it
that only $97 million has been set aside in the Budget for regional roads and only $210
million has been set aside for rail. The se are drops in the bucket and show no real
commitment to regional transport issues by this Government. Northland has suffered
transport neglect for far too long. An improved highway from Pūhoi to Wellsford is a
high priority. Everybody agrees with that, but only the link as far as Warkworth has
been actually planned and budgeted for.
Rail is also seriously neglected there. You can have a look for yourself, as I did on
the weekend, at the rail link from Auckland to Whangarei, which is in a shocking state
and needs significant improvement and maintenance to service the deep -water port at
Whangarei, which is the main alternative to the struggling Ports of Auckland. Passenger
rail for far too long has been neglected in north- west Auckland, and it is being run
down. There is a special housing area of 2,500 homes planned for Huapai, Kūmeu, bu t
the Waitakere Station is to be closed in July and the station at Huapai has been closed
for some time, yet it is a modern, fully functional station built only in 2009. North- west
Auckland has got the railway line, it has got the stations, it has got the rolling stock, and
it has got the population growth. What it needs is that rail link upgraded and not for
stations to be closed.
Let us look at Hawke’s Bay. We have the dumb decision by KiwiRail and this
Government not to reopen the Napier -Gisborne rail link. Currently, there is 1.6 million
tonnes of logging per year there and 390 trucks on the road, projected to go to 2.2
million tonnes and 430 trucks by 2022.
4274  General Debate 3 Jun 2015

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: Logs have never used that railway line—never.
DENIS O’ROURKE: The cost is only $4 million, and local MP Anne Tolley once
supported the reopening of that line at home, but not when she is in Wellington. She is a
lion in public at home, but a lamb in Cabinet. That is her record on regional transport;
that is her record in the Hawke’s Bay—not one to be proud of.
In Wellington, the Capital Connection service is planned to close. It is the only
commuter service for up to 700 people per week between Palmerston North and
Wellington, but poor management by  KiwiRail and a lack of maintenance and
development of the route are the problem there. Incompetent KiwiRail management
actually wants to de -electrify the main trunk line from Hamilton to Palmerston North.
Ditching a core, existing, electrified rail route is nothing short of vandalism. New
Zealand First would instead electrify the entire Auckland to Wellington route.
In Canterbury the earthquakes caused a huge outflow of people north to Rangiora,
Kaiapoi, and Pegasus, and south to Rolleston. Road traffic, to the north especially, is
now chronic. Surplus carriages and locomotives are available, and so for just the cost of
a few temporary, low -cost railway stations, we could have an effective passenger rail
system from those places to the centre of Christchur ch. It could easily be done, but
nothing, of course, is being done by this Government.
In Auckland the completion of the Auckland City Rail Link is urgent, but this
Government dithers. There is also a need for a passenger rail link to the airport in
Auckland via Onehunga, and there are many opportunities for new light rail networks in
Auckland City.
Rail should have a great future, but it needs a better development strategy, and I am
not confident that this 30- year strategy talked about by Simon Bridges today would be
what we need. I would have very little confidence in that because, as a consequence of
the National Government’s underfunding and downgrading of the rail network,
KiwiRail has degraded and undermined the entire rail network, and has ignored a ny
opportunity to enhance and expand it.
Finally, other countries develop and electrify rail networks; in this country, the
opposite happens.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

sections.heading: Arts Centre Of Christchurch Trust Bill

items.text: Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: It is with great
pleasure and delight that I bring this Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill for its third
reading. As we have heard in the House over the last few weeks—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Minister must move the
third reading—not the preamble—just move the bill’s third reading and then you can go
into the substantive matter of what you want to say.

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. I move, That the  Arts
Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill be now read a third time . This bill is very important
for Christchurch and for the Arts Centre, so it is my delight to be here at its third
reading.
As we have heard in this House over the last few weeks, the Arts Centre is beloved
by the people of Christchurch, and actually also by the visitors and tourists who come to
our city. It is a magnificent site. It is the site of 23 neo -Gothic buildings, it is something
that every Christchurch person has spent time in, and it is part of our everyday life. The
Arts Centre has been a centre of activity, full of arts events. It has a weekend market
that I think most tourists visit, it has craft stalls, it has the  Dux de Lux —and we have
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4275
heard about lots of events there over past years. It also has Le Café, which was also
frequented by many of us, often.
Of course, the site suffered dreadfully in the earthquakes. In fact, it was damaged in
both the September and Fe bruary earthquakes, and 23 of the 24 heritage buildings were
badly damaged. The first of these buildings was built in 1876, and the rest were built
over a period of time, until the last one was built in 1923. They have been such an
important part of our ci ty as they were used for different purposes, and so it has been
enormously difficult for the people of Christchurch, and also very sad for us to see them
damaged.
It is fortunate that the buildings were well insured. What the trust board is now
facing is about a 7- year restoration and rebuild period and nearly $300 million worth of
restoration. Actually, the work is well under way. It is going very well. We have already
seen the Registry Building on the corner of Montreal Street and Worcester Street
completed, and now that is tenanted. The gym has also been completed. That is now
used as a performance space, and people are able to go in there and enjoy that art.
The grand hall is the next one to be completed. This is a magnificent building. It had
a turret, which has been put back up there. It also had immensely special stained glass
windows, which, fortunately, survived the earthquake and will be put back into that
building. The trust board is also expecting that the work on this restoration will be
finished earlier than in 7 years, and so I think it is really a feather in the cap of the
people working on that to see that this work is being done beautifully. It is really
restoring these buildings, and also it is going to be on time and on budget.
This Arts  Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill is a really important element in the
protection and the preservation of the Arts Centre for the future. It sets out to modernise
the governance arrangements of the trust and sets out the charitable objects of that trust
in legislation. This is to give greater certainty around the original intention of the trust
deed and to formally recognise the heritage and cultural significance of the Arts Centre.
The modernising of the governance arrangements brings the trust in line w ith
currently accepted best practice, and this is absolutely vital. It is really important that
the trust board maintains a strong set of skills not only during this restoration phase but
also into the future, as the Arts Centre is repopulated and again be comes a central,
important part for the people of Christchurch and those who visit our city.
I really want to commend the work of the Arts Centre board—commend it for the
way it developed this bill. As we know, people are very fond of the Arts Centre and
they also want to have their say on the Arts Centre, so there have been quite a lot of
controversial debates over the years. The way that the board discussed, talked to
stakeholders, consulted widely, and explained its rationale to the people of Christchur ch
was very well done indeed. I would like, in particular, to recognise the Hon Margaret
Austin, who has talked about the Arts Centre, I have to say, to all and sundry probably
for decades, but she was particularly active in this area, explaining what was going on
and putting people’s minds at rest, knowing that this was a good thing for the Arts
Centre.
I also want to acknowledge the work of Jen Crawford, the chair of the board, and
André Lovatt, the chief executive officer. Both of them have led this process, and while
they have been leading this process, it was on top of managing this huge restoration but
also future planning for the site. So it has been a huge job—a lot of energy, a lot of
effort, a lot of enthusiasm, and a lot of hard work by a lot of people to get it to this
stage.
I just want to recap on the bill. What it will do is, first, modernise the trust
governance arrangement; second, set out the objects of the trust in legislation to reflect
the cultural and heritage significance of the Arts Centre; third, provide legal foundations
4276 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3 Jun 2015
for the trust board to continue to recover from the earthquakes; fourth, provide for a
skills-based board appointed by an appointment committee; and, fifth, ensure that there
is a safe pair of hands in the short ter m if the circumstance ever arose that the board
could not perform. I think that is really important. It gives us much greater certainty
than there was in the past. Finally, the bill sets out in legislation the trust’s current
objectives—again, giving that certainty.
I would like to thank the Local Government and Environment Committee for its hard
work on this bill. Committee members took it very seriously. They even visited the Arts
Centre, and I think that was really important because it gave them an opportunity to see
why it is important to the people of Christchurch. I would like to commend the work of
Scott Simpson as the chair.
The committee made some very helpful amendments. In particular, it introduced a
new subclause 5(2) for clarification, which requires all income to be used to advance the
charitable purposes of the trust. It also deleted clause 8, which provided for the transfer
of the trust property to the Crown on an interim basis. That is what clause 8 was going
to do. Instead the committee in serted clause 9 and that states that the Charitable Trusts
Act 1957 applies. So that is standard right across the country and I think it is a better
solution. Basically, I think the work the committee did improved the bill and made it a
much more certain and more acceptable bill to the public of Christchurch and, actually,
to the board itself.
I just want to make a comment about the importance of the references to the historic
stone buildings. The buildings were central to the intentions of the original tr ust deed,
so it is particularly important that the stone buildings are referenced in the preamble and
in clause 4 of the bill.
Finally, it is my great pleasure to be here at the third reading. The Arts Centre is a
magnificent cultural and heritage site fo r New Zealand. It is beloved by the people of
Christchurch and beyond, by our visitors and our tourists. It is a hub of activity. It is
something that we all go to for arts, for crafts, for the market, for entertainment, to the
pub—something that all Christchurch people can enjoy. The passing of this bill gives it
a fantastic footing for the future and it will be there for many, many generations to
enjoy. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: It is my great pleasure to speak in this
third reading of this bill. I think that this bill is an incredibly important and symbolic
piece of legislation in terms of the recovery of Christchurch, and part of that recovery
needs to be our cultural recovery.
I too want to pay tribute to the work of a number of people. The member who has
just taken her seat, the member for Christchurch Central, the Hon Nicky Wagner, has
worked hard on this bill and I would like to commend her for that work. I would also
like to pay tribute to the chairwoman of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Board,
Jen Crawford, and to the chief executive officer, André Lovatt, who are here, for the
work that they have put in, and to other members of that board who have done the work.
Also I pay tribute to my fellow members of the Local Government and Environment
Committee, one of the most productive committees in this Parliament, who work very
well together to find good solutions. The Minister who has just taken her seat has talked
of some of the changes that we were able to achieve at that select committee, which I
think has led to the strengthened piece of legislation that we are now seeing here today
for its final reading.
I think what this bill has done besides modernising the governance arrangements and
setting in place the future of our Arts Centre in Christchurch, which are incredibly
important, is that it has given many members of this House also the opportunity to
reminisce about the site of the Arts Centre, throu gh the course of its readings, and what
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4277
it meant to them. I think it is clear from all stages of the bill what an important cultural,
symbolic, and emotional heart of Christchurch the Arts Centre has become since —well,
it was the university—it was transferred from the university to the city in 1973. I think a
reading and consulting of Hansard  will be a very important record of just how
important this set of buildings has been.
I think it is incredibly important that we do have the proper provisions to ensure that
we can preserve these buildings, because heritage and the heritage fabric of our city
have been one of the victims of the Christchurch earthquakes. We have lost far too
much of our built heritage and I think that is something that we in Christchurc h all feel
strongly. As of February 2015 there have been 1,240 demolitions within the four
avenues. That is compared with 292 building consents, by the by. But 20 percent of
those 1,240 buildings have been heritage buildings that have been demolished. I think it
is with great sadness that all Cantabrians look on at the loss of this built history of their
city. It was in the aftermath of the quakes, of course, when the Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery Authority through section 38 of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act was
given the power to demolish damaged heritage buildings without consultation. I think it
is an important time to put on record, while we are talking about the way in which we
are going to preserve an incredibly important set of heritage buil dings in Christchurch,
that we on this side of the House believe that the time for that has passed. We believe
that we do need to return to a proper discussion about our heritage in our city.
At previous readings of this bill I have spoken about the part that one of my
predecessors, the Rt Hon Norman Kirk, the member for Sydenham —a very fine seat —
played in the preservation. [ Interruption] Yes, the Hon Ruth Dyson is also claiming the
Rt Hon Norman Kirk—quite rightly so —and the Hon Clayton Cosgrove can claim  him
as a Mayor of Kaiapoi as well. It was the Rt Hon Norman Kirk who had a dream about
the Arts Centre buildings becoming the cultural and educational centre for Christchurch.
It was he, in 1973 at the university centennial convocation, who made the
announcement that these buildings were to be gifted to the city. When Norman Kirk
made this announcement about the buildings being gifted to the city, he made the point
that it was about drawing together the various strands of culture in New Zealand to
produce something that was uniquely New Zealand. I think these are the words that we
need to hold dear to, because Norman Kirk did have a very firm grasp of the importance
of culture and our history in the place of the making of a modern identity in 1970s New
Zealand.
In 1973, that same year, the Rt Hon Norman Kirk said that “Politics is the conscious
projection of a country’s identity … and not something removed or remote from
everyday life.” I think they are important words for me to leave the final passage of t his
bill on, because I think the passing of this legislation and the preservation of these
buildings are not something removed or remote from the everyday life of Cantabrians.
Thank you.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: As the first non-Cantabrian to speak
in this third reading debate, and as chairman of the Local Government and Environment
Committee, it actually gives me enormous pleasure to support my colleague the Hon
Nicky Wagner, the MP for Christchurch Central, who has been sponsoring this bill
through the House. This is a very good and momentous piece of legislation, and it is a
good and momentous day for Canterbury and for the Arts Centre of Christchurch.
Seldom in this House do we get unanimity, and I am hopeful that we will get it today on
this piece of legislation.
It is an opportunity for this House to actually put in place a piece of legislation that
will provide for a modernised governance structure for the Arts Centre of C hristchurch,
one that will help it cope with the massive rebuild that is under way at present, and also
4278 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3 Jun 2015
one that will set it up for the future, for years to come, for the children, grandchildren,
and great-grandchildren yet to be born of Canterbury to enjo y and learn to love the Arts
Centre as much as Cantabrians clearly and obviously do already.
As other speakers have already indicated, I want to also acknowledge the leadership
and contribution of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Board chair, Jen Cra wford,
and chief executive officer, André Lovatt, who came and presented to the select
committee when it met in Christchurch. We took the trouble, as the sponsor indicated,
to travel to Christchurch to have a look at the site, to have a look at the restora tion, and
to have a look at the work that is being done with such care and skill by the many able
craftspeople who are using skills that probably have not been used on a building site in
this country for many, many years. These are craftspeople from around the world who
are bringing their stonemasonry skills to the Arts Centre for what is believed to be the
largest heritage restoration project of its type in the world currently under way.
As a non- Cantabrian, there is absolutely no doubt in my mind that there is a very
special place in the hearts and minds of all Canterbury people for their Arts Centre. It is
a place that holds fond memories for many Cantabrians. As this bill has been making its
progress through the House we have heard some of those stories.
The purpose of this bill is actually quite simple: it is to enshrine the trust’s objects
into statute to ensure that the Arts Centre continues as a cultural centre for the people of
Christchurch and Canterbury and for people from other parts of New Zeal and and,
indeed, international visitors as well who care to visit the site. The bill consolidates the
terms of the trust’s structure and it modernises the governance arrangements. Both the
consolidation and the modernisation are required for the trust to a dapt to its changed
circumstances, which are largely as a result of the Canterbury earthquakes.
Modern governance best practice calls for the establishment of skills -based boards.
This piece of legislation seeks to put in place a board that will be able to draw from the
broader, wider community, skills that will assist with the restoration project as it
continues over the next 7 years or so and that will indeed set the governance trust up for
the future. It will mean that there is a strong set of skills on  the board during the major
phase of the restoration that is currently under way. A truly skills -based board will
create an enduring governance structure for the future, and it is the future that I think is
most important, even though this is a very signif icant heritage project. The current deed
that the trust is operating under does not actually provide sufficient certainty or
robustness to protect the site as most of us would want it to be protected. If the trust was
ever to be wound up, the current trust  deed does not provide sufficient robustness to
ensure that safe hands would be able to manage and secure the future of this nationally
important heritage site. This bill actually fixes that process.
I want to spend just a minute talking, as others have done, about the history of the
site. It is true to say it is not just one building; it is an amalgam of a number of buildings
built over a number of years, some dating back more than 100 years, of which there are
24 buildings in total. All but one —23 of the 24 buildings —were damaged in the
Canterbury earthquakes. It was very fortunate that the trust had the good sense and
wisdom to be well insured. This has meant the $290 million restoration project can be
funded adequately and appropriately. I think that is going to be enormously important
for the future of the site. The site was, of course, originally occupied by the University
of Canterbury, plus it was the site of two of Christchurch’s original second ary schools.
It is an absolute cultural icon for Canterbury and its people, housing these days —or, in
fact, before the earthquakes —a variety of arts -focused facilities, not the least of which
was the regular market. The current Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Board was
established way back in 1978—over 40 years ago. It is fair to say a lot has changed in
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4279
the 40 years subsequent, not only on the site but also in terms of what is now considered
to be best governance practice for trusts of this sort.
The earthquakes of 2010 and 2011 resulted in very significant damage to the site. We
were able to see that firsthand during our visit. We were also able to see that, bizarrely,
as a result of the earthquakes, some quite unique original work has been rediscovered
because some of the fascia work done in the period between the original construction of
the stone buildings through to modern times had actually covered up some of the really
intricate and lovely, beautiful fretwork and other stonework over the years.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Is it now on display?

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is now on display, Mr Whip, and it is good to see it. I
commend to people who want to visit Christchurch that it would be a good thing to do.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: “Professor Whip”.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: He is “Professor Whip”, to most of us. “Sir Whip”,
sometimes—“Mr Whippy”. He is a very fine and highly regarded member of this team.
It is $290 million that is being spent on this site and it is a 7 -year project. I am
delighted to hear from Nicky Wagner that there is a likelihood that the project will be
concluded earlier than the 7 years, and that it will likely come in under budget as well.
A revitalised Christchurch Arts Centre is actually symbolic  and goes to the heart of the
whole Christchurch rebuild. For many Cantabrians it is a visible, tangible sign and
manifestation of what the future holds for a new, rebuilt Christchurch, while at the same
time protecting the heritage and the history of a si te that is so important to so many
people. This legislation provides an opportunity for much greater certainty around the
intentions of the trust and for the preservation of the architecture and heritage values of
the site. The rebuilt centre will, in my v iew, be an outstanding icon of Canterbury and,
indeed, of national significance.
One of the things the bill does is codify the charitable objects of the trust into statute.
What that means is that a couple of things have been achieved. One of them is that  the
objects of the trust have been separated from the powers of the trust. That separation—
dealing with the trust’s powers —means that if there is ever to be any future change, it
will require a further passing of legislation in this Parliament. I think th at kind of
protection is very useful and very powerful. The new governance structure follows a
comprehensive review that was initiated by the trust itself. That review included the
commissioning of an independent report by the Ministry for Culture and Heri tage. It
also involved, as part of that process, a very extensive consultation with key
stakeholders. So this has been a very good process all round.
In my concluding comments I want to again just thank the leadership team —the
chair and the chief executiv e—for their guidance and steady hand through this process.
There is absolutely no doubt in my mind that the result of this legislation will provide
an enduring governance structure for the trust and for the people of Canterbury and,
indeed, of New Zealand. I have great pleasure in commending it to the House.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Can I begin my contribution in support
of this bill by acknowledging the member who has just resumed his seat, Scott Simpson,
and thank him for the manner in which he chaired the select committee that considered
this bill, the Local Government and Environment Committee, and particularly for taking
the trouble —and it is quite a lot of trouble —to pack e verything up and come to
Christchurch. It is a local bill but it means a lot to us, Mr Simpson, that you took that
effort and that leadership, so I acknowledge that. I want to also acknowledge the Hon
Nicky Wagner, member of Parliament for Christchurch Cen tral, for her role in
shepherding this bill through to this stage. I guess for the National Government that this
is a bit of a bright light in a sea of disasters post -Budget, so it is nice to be part of the
4280 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3 Jun 2015
good feeling around what I think is going to be unanimous support of this legislation.
That is a pretty unusual thing for this Parliament, so we should celebrate that.
As Scott Simpson noted in his speech, it is not just Cantabrians who are proud of this
beautiful collection of buildings but also people  who have been part of the life of the
Arts Centre in one way or another over its long life, so having the opportunity, which
this legislation accords, to ensure that the passion we all have for the Arts Centre is
translated into a very robust governance s tructure that will ensure the continuance and
protection of this building is a very good thing for us all. It is a sharp juxtaposition
when we look at the loss of so many beautiful heritage and historic buildings in
Canterbury over the last 4½ years, many of which could have been restored, could have
been repaired, and could have remained part of our landscape if it was the desire of the
Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery to offer some leadership in that area, or
indeed if the property owners thems elves had had full insurance. Some buildings were
demolished, despite their having very good insurance, because the owners decided it
just was not worth the bother and that they would rather put their money somewhere
else. I think that is a tragic lack of support for the beauty and the part in our culture and
our understanding of ourselves that heritage and historic buildings play.
Other buildings, of course, have been demolished by what I strongly consider is
inappropriate use of the extraordinary powers of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
Authority and the Minister. A beautiful theatre was demolished because Manchester
Street was not wide enough to meet the Minister’s desire for a new part of the city and a
different landscape there, and that was a big loss. But in this bill we are celebrating, not
a loss, but a restoration and a preservation and our Parliament’s desire to make sure that
the governance structure is robust and supports that.
A lot has been said through the various stages of this legislat ion and I do not think
there is much more to add. There were some parts of the bill originally that were not
clear enough. I think the select committee has done an excellent job in ensuring that we
are clear about the mandate of the legislation and what it  covers so that the concerns of
people who were registered right in the very early stages have been put to rest, and I
certainly hope that is the case. I think it has been a jolly good job done by the select
committee and it is great to see the bill progressing in its final stage through the House.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: I rise to spend just a few minutes
here in the third reading debate, obviously speaking very much in favour of the Arts
Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill. It is has been quite a journey, actually, to follow this
bill through as a new backbencher. It has b een, of course, great to be on the Local
Government and Environment Committee with our chairperson and our colleagues from
across the House.
This is one of the first bills that were, essentially, put in front of us as a new
committee to progress. Can I ad d my voice to those who have spoken already and
acknowledge the Hon Nicky Wagner and the leadership she has brought to this issue. I
acknowledge also our chairperson, Scott Simpson. I think it is worth taking a moment to
reflect—during what, at times, have been a pretty rancorous last few weeks, particularly
on one side of the House —on hearing the collegial comments, mostly, from the other
side of the House, on the approach we took as we walked our way through this bill and
provided opportunities for people  who are interested in this to make their submissions
felt and heard. As noted —and I will talk about this shortly —we had the opportunity to
visit the site.
As we know, this bill is all about establishing in perpetuity the purpose of the trust
and giving t he appropriate governance arrangements for the Christchurch community
and for this world- class precinct. As we have heard, the 23 buildings are made of
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4281
stone—various durations, as we have heard, going back to 1878—and all but one
building was impacted on severely by the earthquake of February 2011.
One of the highlights for me, as we have gone through this bill, has been the
opportunity to go and visit the site and see firsthand what we are trying to put in stone,
in a legislative context, down in Christch urch. To be able to see the wide array of
stonemasons working on their craft and to see the pallets of stone ready to be put into
the new buildings, I found quite an enjoyable experience. As Mr Simpson mentioned in
his comments, it was quite extraordinary seeing parts of the buildings that have had
their old fascia removed and they have suddenly revealed something of even more
moment standing behind. We were able to see that and know that through this tragedy
there will be something that is more enduring an d more powerful for the community of
Christchurch and indeed the country.
We saw the rooms where Lord Rutherford was a young student. An area that was an
old swimming pool is now being turned into an outside promenade, and even though it
was a very cold s ummer’s day, we could picture what it will look like when the
community of Christchurch fully engages with the site in the next few years, once the
building project has been completed.
What a building project this is—7 years and $300 million—and it is absolutely worth
adding my voice to acknowledge those who are very close to this: Jen Crawford, the
chair, and André Lovatt, the chief executive officer. I think it is a very well -made point
that not only have they had a business -as-usual requirement in their  jobs but they have
been able to oversee what has been declared to be the largest heritage rebuild going on
in the world at the moment. That, I think, is a testament to them and the skills they bring
to the table, and the team they have around them. So the y should be acknowledged for
that.
One of the key deliveries of this bill, discussed here already, is setting out the
charitable objects of the trust and enshrining them in law so there is absolute clarity for
the community around the purpose of the trust and what it is there for. I think the moves
and the changes in respect of the governance structure are very well -thought-through,
and the community of Christchurch and the stakeholders of Christchurch should be
acknowledged and recognised. The University of Canterbury, the Christchurch City
Council, Heritage New Zealand, the Christchurch Civic Trust, and Papatipu Rūnanga
are the key stakeholders that historically have had a very direct linkage into the
governance of this organisation, and it was a representative governance model, which so
often is the case in organisations like this.
But it takes some courage to be able to look at the scale of the rebuild that is
occurring in Christchurch in this precinct and realise that if you genuinely wish to be
world class in terms of protecting and enhancing a series of buildings that are in place in
that precinct, then it is appropriate to have world- class, best -practice governance
arrangements as well. It is not easy to move from a representative model to a skills -
based model, particularly in a tight community such as Christchurch, which has always
had such direct representative governance around the Arts Centre. So they should be
acknowledged. I think that is a very strong step forward, and obviously a key
component of this bill.
I do hold the view, though, that once we have had the third reading and the bill
becomes law, there is an opportunity for those who are going to participate in this new
governance structure to ensure that they take off their parochial lense s. It is very easy
for communities to think that they are the sole harbinger of what is good and best
practice when it comes to precincts like this. But as we have heard earlier from Megan
Woods when she reflected on the comments of former Prime Minister N orman Kirk
around the importance of bringing a wide strand of perspective and engagement around
4282 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3 Jun 2015
this precinct, so too does it fit, in my view, that a wide strand in diverse governance
skills should be brought around this board.
So now there is an opportunity for those stakeholders to be able to put forward
people. I would ask them to consider not necessarily putting forward people just from
their own organisations or from whence they have come; they should look externally,
not only externally to Christchur ch but externally, potentially, to New Zealand, to
ensure that the mix of skills that sits around that board are genuinely world class.
Ultimately, for this legislation to endure in time, these phenomenal stone buildings
need to engage with people and with communities, and, as we have noted through this
process, the community of Christchurch is very different from the one that built these
buildings all those years ago. The community of Christchurch in the next 10, 15, 20, or
30 years and beyond will, equally, change and become more diverse.
Buildings are ultimately just stone buildings, however beautiful they may be, if they
do not have people connected with them and inside them. If they are not evocative to
people then they are simply that —just stone buildings. This precinct is far more than
that. It has got an incredibly evocative power for the people of Christchurch, and for
that to be maintained, enhanced, and to grow, they must ensure that that precinct
continues to engage in a way that is quite profound and that moves with the evolving
nature of the community.
The other key change that we reflected on —and that I think is a good one from a
good-practice perspective–is the removal of the requirement for the Minister to be
informed of vacancies. I thi nk that was a minor change but one that I think was an
appropriate amendment if you are looking at it through a belt-and-braces lens, which we
did.
Also, we had quite a lot of debate about the requirement to have the conservation
plan available at the ann ual meeting. Again, I think it is a very sensible amendment to
this bill and one that, by the sound of it, we will have cross -party support for. It ensures
that those who have a strong connection with this Arts Centre precinct can have
visibility at a time  every year as to the vision around conservation that the board has,
and it will give them comfort that the institution is heading in the right direction.
Can I conclude by adding, finally, my congratulations to the Hon Nicky Wagner.
This is something that she has championed well as a local MP. She is a great MP for the
people of Christchurch. That is why they have voted her back with the strength that she
has, and I can see why, because she is a great advocate for Christchurch. She knows
what is important for Christchurch and she has, through her leadership, facilitated a bill
that is going to benefit the community of Christchurch for many decades to come.
Thank you very much.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: I am pleased to take a call on the Arts Centre of
Christchurch Trust Bill and to help it on its way to becoming law. I, like other speakers,
congratulate the Hon Nicky Wagner on her work on the bill, and also Scott Simpson on
running a very collegial process ar ound the Local Government and Environment
Committee’s consideration of the bill. Certainly, this bill is an example of how parties
can cooperate. It is really disappointing that there has not been a similar cross -party
agreement on one of the most important issues of our time —our climate. It is really
disappointing that the Prime Minister has dismissed the Green Party’s invitation to build
a broad, cross -party consensus around the emissions reduction target that we take to
Paris and the changes that our cou ntry needs to make to its economy to ensure, just as
Scott Simpson talked about, present and future generations enjoying the heritage of the
Arts Centre. We need to have that cross-party agreement around reducing our emissions
so that we get a stable climate for future generations.
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4283
The Arts Centre, as others have noted, is one of Christchurch’s major heritage assets.
MPs at the select committee talked with submitters and each other on this bill in a very
constructive way to make some changes in response to some of the issues that
submitters raised. All of the parties have been able to agree on how the objects of the
Arts Centre trust should be translated into the legislation, and how the trust should be
governed in future to ensure that it guides the manage ment of this wonderful heritage
precinct at the heart of the central city.
We should also be able to do that on our climate, because the issues—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is not about climate
change; this is about Christchurch—

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Well, the issues, in terms of—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, this is a narrow debate,
specifically as mentioned by previous speake rs, and I will ask the member to come
back.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. Well, in terms of the bill and
the heritage restoration project, $290 million is being spent on that. When MPs visited
the Arts Centre on our field tr ip, a lot of us were excited about what we saw in terms of
the traditional craftsmanship that was evident there, with the stonemasonry work that
was being undertaken, the huge scale of the challenge of repairing the buildings after
the earthquakes, the ded ication and commitment of all of the contractors, staff, and
consultants engaged in that very ambitious project, and the leadership and vision, of the
trust board, chaired by Jen Crawford, and the chief executive officer, André Lovatt, in
ensuring that the work was happening across the complex. It is quite a complex project
and I think everybody was very proud of the work that was being done there.
I would also like to acknowledge the foresight of the former trust board and the
former chief executive officers in ensuring that the Arts Centre was very well insured.
This meant that post -earthquakes it was able to get a good settlement and had the
financial wherewithal to begin the restoration work. So it has been that combination of a
lot of dedication, compe tence, craftsmanship, and expertise that I think is contributing
to the rapid progress that the Hon Nicky Wagner alluded to in getting the project
potentially completed ahead of target. We still need that same commitment on the
climate, but I will finish talking about the climate there.
Everybody agrees that the Arts Centre is worth saving and restoring—

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: The climate of the House.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: And so is the climate —thank you, Mr Mark. In fact, it is worth
saving even more. The purpose of this bill in terms of setting out the objects and powers
of the Arts Centre trust in legislation is updating, revising, and consolidating the trust’s
governance arrangements, and revising its winding up arrangements. Of course, we
hope that those provisions will never be called upon.
Others have certainly canvassed the scope of the bill, and I would just like to talk a
wee bit about the changes to the appointment process. The original Arts Centre trust
deed provided for a mix of trustees a ppointed by both the board and by nominating
bodies. As Historic Places Canterbury noted in its submission, over the years this split
model had become quite a source of contention because successive boards altered the
bodies that could appoint members, and those changes tended to reduce the community
appointees. That led to a perception that the board had become quite unresponsive to the
beneficiaries of the trust —the public —and, also, that it did not result in the most
appropriately skilled trustees being appointed. So this bill actually changes that to
provide for the appointment of a skills-based trust board of no more than nine members,
and the board invites nominees for consideration.
4284 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3 Jun 2015
It was reassuring that organisations such as Historic Places Canterb ury said that the
appointment process strikes a good balance between the desires of interested groups to
put forward potential trustees and the need of the board to obtain trustees with a range
of skills. The fact that the bill also provides for trustees to serve a term of no more than
6 years instead of the previous 9 years means that the board will be regularly refreshed.
One of the other changes that the select committee made was to ensure that the
conservation plan was presented at the annual meetings of the trust in the same way that
the strategic plan is also required to be presented at those meetings. That helps promote
accountability and engagement with stakeholders.
In this final reading I would like to repeat a call that I made earlier for the Chu rch
Property Trustees, who are responsible for the Christchurch Cathedral, to visit the Arts
Centre to see what can be achieved in terms of restoration. The Church Property
Trustees, in the way that they are treating the cathedral, leaving it open to the e lements
and to continue to decay —really, refusing to engage with any of the many initiatives
that the Great Christchurch Buildings Trust has put forward to restore the cathedral —
are really lacking in vision. The cathedral has become a huge source of contention and
opposition in Christchurch because of the Church Property Trustees’ reluctance to
progress its restoration.
The Arts Centre, in contrast, shows what can be achieved with a commitment to
restoration and with dedication and energy. That is particularly important because of the
huge loss of heritage in Christchurch thanks to the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
Authority’s overzealous approach to the demolition of heritage buildings. We have seen
235 significant listed heritage buildings be demolished.  If anyone has visited shop 7 in
Cathedral Junction, they will have seen where those interested in heritage have got a roll
of honour in terms of the 235 buildings that have gone, showing us what we have lost.
That is why the Arts Centre is so important, b ecause of what it represents in terms of
Christchurch’s Mountfort buildings, and the heritage of his architectural legacy and
Hurst-Seager’s legacy —all of the basalt stone, the limestone, the Oamaru stone, the
woodwork in those buildings, which represent huge craftsmanship and the ability to
restore those. That could also happen at the cathedral, but it is not.
I commend this bill and the Green Party is very pleased to support it.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Good afternoon, Mr Assistant Speaker. I rise on behalf of
