the New Zealand First to take this call on the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill. I
am very pleased to do so. It is an interesting thing when you stand up and talk to a bill
that enjoys such a  high degree of support across the House —well, actually, unanimous
support across the House. When one listens to the speeches that have been made it is
sometimes a bit of a challenge to find what contribution you might make that is a little
different from all the other contributions that have been made.
In fact, looking back over the course of the progress of this bill through the House in
the time that I have been back here with the 51 st Parliament, I think we have all pretty
much recognised the same reasons as to why this legislation needs to proceed, and the
importance of it. We have talked somewhat affectionately, particularly those who were
university students who over their time spent a little time socialising and conversing in
places like Dux de Lux, which is one of the places within the precinct that is affected.
I am going to start by doing something a little different, I guess. The reason we are
able to stand and support this pie ce of legislation is, one, because the Minister Nicky
Wagner has quite rightly brought it before us and brought it before the Local
Government and Environment Committee in good form, and, two, because of, I think,
the tone and flavour of the select committ ee. I am very aware that this piece of
legislation came in in the 50 th Parliament and in that time I think there were other
people on the committee —and you might have to help me out over that side. I
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4285
remember coming to the House as a mayor to look at and t o watch proceedings around
the local government amendment bill that went through at the time.
I do remember the now Minister Nicky Wagner being on that committee. I do
remember Maggie Barry being on that committee. I do remember Nick Smith being on
that committee. I know there are others and I apologise; I cannot remember who they all
were right now. But this committee is a very good committee. It might seem a little
unusual for an Opposition MP to stand up and to compliment Government MPs, but this
is a v ery good committee. It is very well chaired by Scott Simpson —and I see in the
future a very strong Cabinet Minister—along with Todd Muller as the deputy chair.
I think it is the way in which people manage committees —the collegiality that you
enjoy—that actually helps people break through some things that might actually appear
as political barriers for the sake of politics or barriers where people do not want to move
across because they do not see value, they do not share the view, and they do not share
the philosophy. So I do want to pay my respects to Scott Simpson, and Matt Doocey —a
good Rangiora man. He is looking after my previous home town very well, and my
family who live down there—Matt, good on you.
There is Paul Foster -Bell, who enjoys something i n common with me in that he has
been to Oman and I am enjoying having that time with him on the committee. Julie
Anne Genter is on the committee, and Joanne Hayes. Joanne is a Wairarapa girl, so of
course we would hear a lot of common sense and good contri butions out of Joanne,
would we not. Tu Korako—well, he is whanaunga down there, so likewise I always
expected good, sound logic, good reasoning and collegiality, and good performance
from Tu, as we have seen. There are Eugenie Sage and Su’a William Sio —people who
are very experienced in local government, and that is what makes bills like local
government bills easy to move through at times.
We are blessed in this committee with having a good number of people on the
committee who have strong local governme nt experience and can see straight to the
core of legislation such as this, beyond what appears on the paper. They are able to
understand the background and the depth and the effect it has on the communities
because they have served those communities in a local government capacity. Of course,
there is Dr Megan Woods, who continues to impress me each time I go into that
committee.
So, having shared some compliments across there, I think we also need to recognise
the former board who, like Eugenie Sage from the Green Party has said, did a sterling
job—unlike some other people we could probably talk about in Christchurch who
maybe did not insure their facilities in the same way that this trust did. It is from that
platform that the board is now, with the new t rust, able to proceed forward and do the
work that has to be completed. I want to congratulate this board, particularly Jen
Crawford on the way in which she chairs it.
I also want to reiterate the importance of the clause that deals with trust vacancies
and how people are appointed. I think it has been a very good decision to change the
way those appointments are made so it can focus on skill sets. I do think that the
amendment adding new clause 5A, which deals with conflicts of interest, is absolutely
essential. So often, when you change the way in which a board is selected and you bring
on board the governance skills and the executive skills that you need to run what is
going to be a $300 million project affecting 23 category 1 heritage buildings, and people
like that are appointed, they are appointed for a range of skill sets. Very often they have
a strong business background and very often you, unfortunately, have to deal with the
issues of perceptions where those business people are seen to have vested interests in
some way or another because of their business background. They might be property
developers in their private life, or they might be real estate agents —I do not know—but
4286 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3 Jun 2015
having strong clauses around dealing with conflicts of interest is very im portant and I
think this bill has done that.
As a former mayor, I want to also talk about why this bill is important and about the
deeper meaning. This bill is important to New Zealand First for a number of reasons.
One is through having lived in Canterbury myself for 30 -odd years on and off and
having family who still reside there. I went down in 1974 and one of the first things that
struck me about Christchurch was that it was different to the Wairarapa —really
different. It was almost English. The cultur e, the architecture, the way in which people
socialised, and even the way in which they spoke in some parts of Christchurch in 1974
was very English. In fact, the first question I got asked when I went down there was not
where I was from but what school I went to. I found that quite unique, because when I
said it was Tararua College, people did not have a donkey’s idea as to where the hell
Tararua College was. And I think that situation still exists today.
But it is a very English city built on the back of those pioneers and those settlers who
came in the first four ships, and the idea and the notion that every cultural and every
heritage building—particularly in a precinct where you have 23 category 1 buildings —
would not be rebuilt and would not be restored would be devastating to the community
and the people of Christchurch. It is bad enough that the cathedral is in the state that it is
in and is most likely not going to be rebuilt. The other buildings that you can see —
churches throughout Christchurch—that will not be rebuilt and that are going to be
replaced have all taken with them something of the character of Christchurch. So it is
that important. It is so good to hear that legislation like this is going through and that we
will see these buildings fully restored.
There is also the wider issue of community, and the great thing about the Arts Centre
is the way in which it provides for the culture, the community of the people of
Christchurch, and the people who wish to visit and enjoy its precincts. That a bility to
socialise, to display art, to display culture, to display those things that are so
Christchurch is something that would be difficult to replicate in a modern building built
to modern designs and modern specifications. Being a mayor, I understand, and, in fact,
it is probably one of the reasons why I railed against the National Government’s
changes to the Local Government Act 2002, when it removed the four well -beings.
Having been a mayor, I understand completely the importance of community and the
importance of having a centre like this for a town and its people. It is a place where they
can go, where they can communicate, and where they can display and show their arts,
and show everything that is positive about them and different about them.
That is probably the one area where we will have conversations and discussions
going forward. They will be the debates around why it is so important that the Local
Government Act has to have the four well -beings reinstated in it. I actually think that
this piece of legislation is, in a quiet sort of way, a message and an affirmation from
Parliament that culture, the council’s involvement, and the Government’s involvement
in providing cultural and social facilities and amenities is important, should be
supported, and should be maintained. I just think maybe we should reflect on that as we
get into a debate where we will take different sides in this House, going forward from
here. Thank you.

items.speaker: PAUL FOST ER-BELL
items.text: Before I begin my contribution on the Arts
Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill in this third reading debate I would like to make a
couple of acknowledgments that I think do bear some pertinence to the matter at hand.
Firstly, this is the first opportunity I have had, when speaking in this House, to
acknowledge the passing of respected New Zealander Ērima Hēnare. I was fortunate
enough to have had Ērima as my third form social studies teacher at Whangarei Boys
High School in 1990. He was someone who, in his lessons and in the way he conducted
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4287
himself in the classroom, encouraged a love of arts, history, and culture through his
social studies lessons, which carried me forward and encouraged me to take on courses
in history, classics, archaeol ogy, and art history whilst at university. So I would like to
acknowledge the passing of Ērima. It is a great loss, not only to his whānau but to us as
a country.
Secondly, as chair of the New Zealand -  Scotland Parliamentary Friendship Group, I
would like to acknowledge the unexpected and shocking death of Charles Kennedy,
former leader of the Liberal Democrats, at the young age of 55. He was the youngest
MP when admitted to the House of Commons in the United Kingdom. I think this news
comes as a shock to all of us who follow British politics.
But, getting on to the bill, I do want to acknowledge the Minister and member for
Christchurch Central, the Hon Nicky Wagne r, who has sponsored this bill. Nicky
Wagner is a very impressive member of this House. This is the first of two bills that she
brings before us today to advance issues in her local area. She is a very assiduous and
hard-working member, and there are many of us who follow what she does with great
interest because we think there is much we can learn from such a successful and hard -
working member. It is a pleasure to speak on such a bill that enjoys cross -party
support—in fact, unanimous support on all sides of the House. I do want to thank the
speaker who just resumed his seat, Major Ron Mark, for his comments acknowledging
the excellent chairman of the Local Government and Environment Committee, Scott
Simpson, who does work very hard to conduct the committee  in a very non- partisan,
cross-party, and, I think, cooperative way to make sure that we deliberate carefully on
all such issues that we address.
In the particular case of this bill, I did enjoy the opportunity to go down to
Christchurch where we heard about another matter, which we will come to later in the
day, but also we did have the opportunity to tour the Arts Centre, guided by the staff. I
particularly want to single out the chair of the board, Jen Crawford, and the chief
executive officer, André Lovatt, who have made an enormous contribution to ensuring
that this precious asset, this cultural asset—which not only is important to Christchurch
but is actually significant to all New Zealanders and is world heritage—has the
opportunity to be restored and to be saved from the almost certain destruction that the
earthquakes threatened upon it.
As a student of history I would like to touch on a couple of particular parts of the
story of the Arts Centre because I think they are perhaps not as well -known as t hey
could be among New Zealanders. The first is the fact that Lord Ernest Rutherford, Lord
Rutherford of Nelson, did his undergraduate studies at the University of Canterbury, or,
as it was then, Canterbury College of the University of New Zealand. He did
groundbreaking work, which he later continued when he went to McGill University in
Canada. He later went to Cambridge University, where he became director of the
Cavendish Laboratory. Of course, he is famous for having split the atom—I think that is
how we might describe it, in common parlance. But Lord Rutherford, in his early days,
did groundbreaking research including on differentiating alpha and beta rays. It is the
sort of science upon which much of our modern learning and knowledge in the area of
physics is founded. The fact that we now have preserved the rooms in which Lord
Rutherford did some of his seminal work is very important. We have to, I think, take
heed of the fact that Lord Rutherford was not only the first New Zealander but, actually,
the f irst antipodean—the first person from our part of the world more generally —to
receive the Nobel Prize before he actually split the atom. So a lot of that early
groundbreaking work that Lord Rutherford did was conducted in the Arts Centre, and it
is a wonderful thing that that laboratory is going to be preserved.
4288 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3 Jun 2015
Another factor that I think is very important is that the Arts Centre represents one of
the very, very few—it may even be unique—coherent and cohesive neo-Gothic collegial
precincts that exist not only in New Zealand but in the world. We can go to the places
where this sort of architecture originated and it is clear that the college buildings were
designed to replicate the colleges of universities such as Cambridge University, Oxford
University, Edinburgh University, and Glasgow University in the United Kingdom. This
is the sort of architecture that I was quite accustomed to at the University of Otago,
where you have a slightly different Scots baronial neo- Gothic architecture in the
original buildings of the university. But this is a unique site because you have not only
the college buildings but what is now the Canterbury Museum buildings, where work is
under way to make sure that they can reopen to their full potential. A lot of the galleries
are already open and they are available to visit. I would encourage not only Cantabrians
but visitors from overseas to make the trip down and pay a visit to the Canterbury
Museum because it is well worth a look. But you have Christ’s College and, sadly of
course, with the destruction of the cathedral, one end of that streetscape precinct has,
unfortunately, been affected. But we have had some positive news in recent days and
weeks around the potential for the Catholic cathedral to be restored. There are modern
means that allow even heavily damaged buildings to be economically brought back to
something approaching their original status to preserve some of those heritage values,
and I think that is a very positive thing.
This bill has been improved upon by the Loca l Government and Environment
Committee in hearing submissions from, obviously, those intimately involved with the
current governance and administration of the Arts Centre. We have reported back and
made a few changes, including some small technical details  such as the removal of
clause 8, which, if it had been allowed in as originally proposed, would have provided
for the transfer of trust property back to the Crown in the event of the winding up of the
trust. As laudable as that goal in itself may sound, i t carried the unfortunate
consequence of a debt incurred by the trust also falling to the Crown. There has been
some reorganisation, and new clause 5(2) has been added, requiring that all income,
benefit, or advantage received by or accruing to the trust be used to advance its
charitable purposes and objects. I think this sets the trust up well. It was originally
founded some 40 years ago, and, of course, after 40 years, it is time for a bit of a spruce-
up. But I think we are going to leave the trust in a very strong position in which it will
be able to conduct its affairs, including some commercial activities, provided that the
profits and proceeds from those activities go back to deliver on those objects of what is,
quite rightly, a charitable and non-commercial trust. This could include, for instance, the
leasing out of premises to act as cafes. Those of us who visited the Arts Centre pre the
earthquakes will remember what vibrant cafes and restaurants it had.
Those of us who visited pre the earthquakes w ill also remember the theatre that
served up some wonderful productions. My personal favourite, of course, was David
McPhail starring as Muldoon in the eponymously entitled play. He has moved on. I do
not know whether other members have seen David McPhail’ s more recent
interpretations, but he has moved on from the comical caricature of one of our great
Prime Ministers into, I think, a very sensitive and highly dramatic portrayal of Muldoon
the man. That was done in a theatre that has been acknowledged by pe ople who, I think,
are experts in the world of theatre and stagecraft. People such as Sir Ian McKellen and
other great performers have singled out the Court Theatre as one of the pre -eminent
venues that should be rightfully restored. It should be preserved, and it should be put
back into a use whereby the proceeds from ticket sales and hiring it out can actually go
to further making it a sustainable project on an ongoing basis and assist with
renovations.
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4289
Other members have touched on the artistry and artis anship and craftsmanship that
are going into the stonework. I do not think it is necessary for me to go on at great
length about that, other than to say that these are wonderful skills not only to have in the
Arts Centre itself but to be deployed more wide ly throughout New Zealand and, in fact,
even perhaps commercially exported, including to such places, as Mr Mark mentioned,
as the Sultanate of Oman where His Majesty Sultan Qaboos has an enormous aesthetic
and an unlimited budget for doing such works. I w ould like to see that move forward in
the future. I commend this bill to the House. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I call Jan Logie—a 5-minute call.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I rise to take a short call on this Arts Centre of Christchurch
Trust Bill in its third reading, which has unanimous support in this House, including
from the Green Party. I would also just like to acknowledge the Hon Nicky Wagner,
who is the National Party member for Christchurch Central, for bringing this bill to the
House.
It is a bill that was originated by the trust board itself, from a proposal that it took to
the member, and that was a result of a quite comprehensive review and consultation.
The development and the drafting of this bill were also done in collaboration with key
stakeholders, Crown Law, and the Ministry for Culture and Heritage. So it is lovely for
the House to have the opportunity to consider bills that have come from the community ,
in concept and in design, and it is wonderful to be able to offer our support for that —to
have the opportunity for this House to consider and help progress the needs as identified
and developed by the community itself —particularly in Christchurch at this  time. It is
sad that this is in such sharp contrast to some of the design plans that have been coming
out of the council and through the Government and that do not meet the needs of that
community.
Some of the key parts of this bill and what it does is to  shift the structure of the
governance board from a representative structure to a skills -based structure, and to limit
the terms of membership on that committee from 9 years down to 6, which will help
keep freshness on that committee, which, I guess, is the hope of that. It will ensure that
all the members of the committee have the skills to be able to best meet the needs of the
Arts Centre—that very precious national resource that I am sure anyone who has been
to Christchurch absolutely adores and appreciates and that we recognise has been part of
what has defined the heart of Christchurch and has drawn so many people from all
around the world to Christchurch.
The Arts Centre, which consists of 24 heritage buildings, with the first one dating
back to 1876, was built progressively over time, right through to 1923. The buildings
are just so distinctive and so beautiful, those stone buildings that mark the heart of
Christchurch. So we are very, very pleased to be supporting this bill, and the
governance and the protection of the restoration of that. It has been noted in the House
already that the restoration project is apparently the largest heritage rebuild project in
the world at the moment—$290 million going into it over a 7-year period. It is due to be
completed in 2019. It is right that this House provides the best possible governance
structure for the oversight of that rebuild and the future of this taonga.
I know it seems a little bit mean-spirited of me to bring it up, but this is in contrast to
the lack of protection for some of the other heritage buildings in the centre of
Christchurch, where we have lost 200 other significant heritage buildings alongside
Cranmer Court and the Majestic Theatre, and buildings that sat alongside the Arts
Centre and created this soul to the centre of the city, at least in the colonial centre of the
city of Christchurch. So we are, finally, just so pleased to have the opportunity to
provide protection for at least one small part of that city and for the heritage nature of
4290 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3 Jun 2015
the city. It is a shame we were not able to do it and provide it for the rest of the city.
Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I call Jacinda Ardern—a 5-minute call.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: There have certainly been members on the other
side of the House who have not let a second go by, in terms of an opportunity to speak
in great length on this bill. I instead think that this bill has been pretty well canvassed in
this House now, and the good people working on the Arts Centre probably just want us
to pass it at this point in time. So I will not talk about any great sultans; instead, I will
use my short address to acknowledge the commitment and the real sense of purpose tha t
is driving the people who are working on this project, and I thank them for their work. I
have been lucky enough, a little while ago now, to take a tour of the Arts Centre. It is
indeed a great treasure for the people of Canterbury but also of New Zealand. It is a
huge burden of work that the people on the ground working on this centre have taken
on, but they have done so with such passion.
Although this bill provides a legal foundation for the trust board and for the
governance structure, one that is more fit for purpose, none of that can capture all of the
additional layers of work and passion and love and commitment that go into a project
like this—23 heritage category 1 buildings dating from 1876 to 1923. Of course, despite
the terminology in the bill, we in this House have not forgotten the importance, and I
am sure the trust will not forget the importance as well, of the student union building. I
know that those who have advocated for that building will look forward to an ongoing
working relationship with the trust around ensuring that that too is well looked after, but
this is a $290 million project, and even then that figure does not capture all of the
human spirit that will go on behind the scenes to ensure that this project is a success.
My final  word is to acknowledge that as of February 2015 there have been 1,240
demolitions in Christchurch. We absolutely acknowledge —absolutely acknowledge —
that for safety reasons some of those demolitions were absolutely legitimate, but 20
percent of those demolitions were heritage buildings. For a long time Labour advocated
that the powers that sat within section 38 of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act
were being used beyond their necessary term of life and that it was becoming
overzealous and we should revert back to our normal decision- making process. That
was the argument that Labour has made for a long period of time, and that is because,
ultimately, we do believe that heritage often captures all of the flak when it comes to
safety concerns in earthquake -prone cities, and we need to make sure that when
balancing those safety concerns we do not lose some heritage buildings that can
absolutely be saved and used safely by a city and its people. So I wanted to make those
closing remarks.
I endorse what Eugen ie Sage said as well about ensuring that while decisions are
being made around the Christchurch Cathedral, we do not allow the continued rot of
that building because that then makes a decision inevitable and that would be unfair to
the city. With those clo sing remarks, I wish those working on the Arts Centre well.
Thank you for your work. I look forward to visiting the buildings in the future.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: It is an honour to rise and speak to
the third reading of the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill. I am very proud to stand
and speak to this bill, as a very proud born and bred Cantabrian. As Ron Mark
indicated, and was first asked when he was in Christchurch, I ha ve heard they ask in

items.speaker: Christchurch
items.text: “What school did you go to?”. In Wellington they ask where you live as
the first question, and in Auckland it is what job do you have. So I am a proud person
from Christchurch who went to a very good school, St Bede’s Col lege, which until
recent boundary changes was in my electorate, and, interestingly enough, currently six
MPs in the House are former students.
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4291
This is a great day for New Zealand, it is a great day for the South Island, and it is a
great day for Christchurch, thanks to this legislation. In fact, just before speaking I took
a call from my wife, who was feeding my 14 -month-old daughter. Like anyone in this
House, we all make commitments and sacrifices for our families. For me, part of this
job is to ensure t hat New Zealand is moving forward, and also the regions, such as
Canterbury, and cities such as Christchurch. When I think of my daughter, who is now
14 months old, I think to myself: “What sort of country and what sort of city will she
inherit in 10, 12, and 15 years’ time?”. It gives me great heart that because of this
legislation, the Christchurch Arts Centre will be a part of Christchurch and very much a
part of her growing up, and a part of the memories that she will have over the next
decade and further on.
As a proud born and bred Cantabrian I too have great, fond memories of the Arts
Centre. Like most people who grew up in Christchurch, we have very fond memories of
a fantastic city. I go back to thinking about the early 1980s, when, really, there w as not
a rugby team in New Zealand that could beat our Canterbury rugby team, the
undefeated Canterbury rugby team, through the 1980s Ranfurly Shield era. I vividly
remember sitting, as a young fellow, on the embankment and watching Larry the Lamb
running around before the game. And who could forget Larry the Lamb? Those were
the days of Andy Earl, and Bruce and Robbie Deans. Before the game there was a
parade. Those were the days when you could go out on to the field and everyone had
their own banners, whi ch they had graffiti on. It was a time when Christchurch got
together.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Come back to the bill.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: And I will just—yes, Mr Deputy Speaker. So there are memories
like that, as well. The Arts Centre —I have great memories when growing up, and
probably more as a young adult, of spending time in the Dux de Lux. It was not one of
the stone buildings, obviously, that are part of the Arts Centre, but a key part of it and
very well frequented. Thursday nights you would go along to listen to a good
Christchurch band. In the 1980s, and now, Christchurch had very good local music.
Any good Cantabrian will remembe r a great New Year’s Eve spent out in the
courtyard, having a few local craft beers. It is very much like sitting in Cathedral
Square, listening to the Wizard and watching the Birdman. Who will forget Radio Ron?
I saw Radio Ron the other day and, interesti ngly enough, he does not seem to have
aged, unlike myself. He is still going strong. So there are great memories of the Arts
Centre, Lancaster Park, Cathedral Square, going for a hot dog in the Dog House, and
frequenting places like Cashel Mall. But really , for other people, they might remember
the Court Theatre in the Arts Centre. They might remember going to the markets and
the art studios.
It is great, because Canterbury and Christchurch and the South Island are very much
tourist meccas for this country . I have never met one tourist who has not said: “If I had
known how beautiful the South Island was, I would have stayed there longer”. That is
what everyone says. They come down to Christchurch— I mean, it is the gateway to the
whole of the South Island—an d they spend time in Christchurch. The Arts Centre is a
key part of that. It is fantastic that this legislation will keep the Arts Centre at the heart
of the tourism industry in Christchurch, whether that be going for a ride on the tram, or
punting down the Avon River.
I just want to take some time to acknowledge the very hard- working Minister Nicky
Wagner, who has brought this local bill to the House. I think, as a Canterbury MP, what
a role model, what a mentor. But we are a great team of Canterbury Nati onal MPs. And
Canterbury—obviously, at the last election, National won the party vote in every
electorate in Canterbury. I think the Hon Gerry Brownlee had a lot to do with that, in
4292 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 3 Jun 2015
respect of the earthquake recovery. Could I also acknowledge our very hard- working
chair of the Local Government and Environment Committee, Scott Simpson. If I could
name just a couple of bills, it gives you the breadth of the work of this select
committee—from the earthquake-prone building legislation—

items.speaker: Mr DEP UTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! A whakataukī in respect of a kumara and how
sweet it is, is coming to mind. I suggest the member stick to the bill rather than refer to
any others that may be on his mind at the moment.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Deputy Speaker. So the Arts Centre is
very much a beacon of the Canterbury recovery. We have very much got a mixed
economy in this recovery. It is about central government and local government
investment, and it is about private investment. That is why it was so fantastic to hear in
the Budget that the earthquake recovery will get an extra $1 billion. But it is interesting
when we look at the Arts Centre restoration, which at around $240 million to $290
million is currently the world’s largest restoration project. It must be acknowledged that
a lot of that is to do with funding that has not come from the Government. It is people
getting out there, raising the funds, and investing in something that is very much the
fabric of Christchurch.
I think, too, of w hen we went down to Christchurch, as a select committee. We held
the select committee meeting at The George hotel, and then walked down to the Arts
Centre—and thank you to chief executive officer, André Lovatt, and trust chair, Jen
Crawford, for showing us around. What a fantastic story. There will be plenty of people
who will have a go at the pace of the recovery and what is happening with the recovery,
but if you do not take stock and have a look at what is happening, you will miss and
forget great stories like the Arts Centre. That is why legislation like this is much needed,
because the Arts Centre is, like I say, currently the world’s largest heritage restoration
project.
On that tour around the Arts Centre it was fantastic to see the flags from all ar ound
the world that were in the room. They represented every different nationality of the
stonemasons. Most of them had off their own bat engaged with the Arts Centre, to come
to New Zealand and to come down to Christchurch to be part of this amazing story . It
was quite pertinent that one of the noticeboards still had posters from 2010 and 2011 of
events at the Arts Centre before the earthquakes struck.
The Arts Centre very much has a pivotal role in Christchurch. As we know, we are
called the most English  city outside England, and it is no surprise, with an Arts Centre
that is modelled on parts of Cambridge University. And we have our archaic, one -way
street system and, of course, the Avon River and the cathedral. So it is quite right that
we have got legi slation that will support the Arts Centre and very much make it
continue to be at the heart of what is a fantastic city.
Another key part of this legislation is the board moving from a representation model
to one of a skills -based model. I would encourage  all people from Christchurch—and,
of course, Canterbury; even from out my way in the Waimakariri electorate in North
Canterbury, whether it be Kaiapoi or Rangiora —who think they have the skills to put
their hands up, because it is not always about the Sta te. It is about big communities.
What we want to do is support big communities to support things like the Arts Centre of
Christchurch Trust. I commend this bill to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise to take a
call on this bill. I just want to acknowledge the previous speaker, Matt Doocey, and his
ramblings through Canterbury. It was a little bit like a tourist brochure for Canterbury,
so I am—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: He’s no Chaucer.
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4293

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Yes. I am going to confine my comments to the bill at hand.
Firstly, I do want to acknowledge Minister Wagner for her stewardship of this bill
through the House, and the Local Government and Environment Committee for the fine
work that it has done shepherding this bill through its various stages to the third reading
today. I acknowledge that we have the representatives of the Arts Centre of
Christchurch Trust Board here in the gallery. They have been here for every reading,
and through the Committee stage. I know that, because, as a relatively new MP, this is
the first bill that I have had the pleasure of speaking on at every stage through the House
and the Committe e, and they have been here watching the debates and contributing to
the development of this bill, and I acknowledge and congratulate them on this great day.
While we have been traversing this bill as it has gone through the House, everyone
has had the opportunity to reminisce about the importance of the Arts Centre, its various
buildings, and the make-up of the Arts Centre. They have all had an opportunity to talk
about how important those experiences have been to them. Everyone has had that
opportunity. My  colleague Dr Megan Woods talked about her days as a university
student and about many of the fun activities that she encountered, particularly at the
Dux de Lux and other venues. Of course, Eugenie Sage talked about her time actually
working in the buildi ngs, and it is has become a very personal piece of work for many
people in this House because of the love that they have for the Arts Centre, the
buildings, and the complex. I even have my own reminiscences of when my daughter,
who is now 23, was a very young girl. We were visiting a family in Christchurch at that
time and we had a beautiful afternoon there. We had some lovely food and we were able
actually to watch the craftsmen at work in the Arts Centre, and at the time, I thought it
was an extraordinary  thing to be able to watch artisan craftsmen diligently completing
their tasks under the gaze of tourists like me. It is no surprise that we have employed the
best craftsmen to come and restore this beautiful set of buildings. It will be a real
pleasure to watch them throughout its restoration.
The bill itself —what does it do? Well, it offers protection. It offers protection to
enshrine those important objects of the trust so that they cannot be diminished,
tampered with, or changed in any way other than by an Act of Parliament. I think that is
really important because it speaks to how important heritage is in this particular set of
buildings—because heritage is important. Many of my colleagues have talked about
how saddened they have been by the loss of her itage in our city. I know that this bill
actually goes towards restoring some of our faith that a beautiful set of buildings can be
restored. It is going to cost an awful lot of money to do so, and it is going to take the top
craftsmen from around the worl d to do so, but the trust board got it right in terms of
ensuring that they have the insurance cover right and ensuring that they have the vision
right. I, for one, am very supportive of this piece of legislation to ensure that we give
the trust board the support that it needs to be able to find those people and that skill set,
so that it can continue to do fine work into the future.
I do not really want to stand between my speech and the final passing of this bill,
other than to say that there have been a couple of examples in recent times where we
know that heritage buildings will be saved, and there is one final call to go out for one
of the most significant buildings in our city. It is not too late to do what the fine people
from the Arts Centre of Chris tchurch Trust Board have done to ensure that they retain
and restore those fabulous buildings. It is not too late to make a call for our cathedral.
We know that the Catholic cathedral is going to be restored, and I, for one, am really
supportive of doing e verything we can to ensure that we retain as many of those
beautiful old buildings that speak to our history as well as hold the thread into the
future. So on that note, I commend this bill to the House. Thank you very much.

items.text: Tēnā koe e te Mana Whakawā, ā, huri noa i te Whare e

It is indeed my pleasure to take this final call and to talk about the Arts Centre of

As I said in a previous speech concerning this bill, to Ngāi Tahu Māori, the

There have been some wonderful and very appropriate acknowledgments, and like

The interesting thing about taking a walk down memory lane —my esteemed

culture. I want to acknowledge the w ork of the Local Government and Environment
Committee under our chair, Scott Simpson, and also, again, the work of André Lovatt
and the Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust. What they have actually exercised here in

This is because when we look at the make -up of the trust itself, it does represent all
of the major stakeholders that will be responsible for the processes that this trust will
run under the legislation: t he University of Canterbury, the Christchurch City Council,
Heritage New Zealand, the Christchurch Civic Trust, and the Ministry for Culture and
Heritage. The great thing there about the second to last one is that it has also included
3 Jun 2015 Arts Centre of Christchurch Trust Bill 4295
other local businesses and community organisations with interests in the Arts Centre. So
what that does is it encompasses a collective of stakeholders that we probably do not
think about often, but at least it is about kotahitaka, or inclusiveness.
The last part that I want to come to is the fact that Papatipu Rūnanga of Canterbury
are also involved and are part of this trust. This is something that I think reflects the

There was a question because in the original bill, it was actually about the tangata
whenua of Canterbury. But from the work that was done, the questions that were asked,

Just to acknowledge this, when we look at that, it is also an understanding that Ngāi

In conclusion, the Arts Centre is a very important par t of Christchurch’s heritage. It

beyond. I want to commend again all of those people, and to reiterate that for those who

CHRISTCHURCH CITY COUNCIL (RATES VALIDATION) BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I move, That the
Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill be now read a third time . I am
delighted to be here today to present this Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation)
Bill at its third reading. There has been quite a lot of controversy around this bill, but
basically it is very simple, it is very straightforward, it is very short, and it is very
focused. What this bill does is set out to validate rates irregularities that came to light to
the Christchurch City Council just last year.
Let us give you a little bit of context. Each June, the Christchurch City Council —
and, in actual fact, councils across the country —resolve to set their rates for the next
financial year, and since 2004, the wording for that rates resolution has been the same or
similar. But in 2013 the Department of Internal Affairs informed the Christchurch City
Council that the resolution did not meet the requirements of the Local Government
(Rating Act) of 2002. So let me get that straight—for 9 years it had been using the same
resolution and for 9 years, unbeknown to everybody, that rates resolution had been
faulty.
4296 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3 Jun 2015
The problem all began back in 2004, when the council deliberately set out to simplify
and to use everyday language in setting its rates resolution. But, inadvertently, it left out
important bits of information —important requirements —which meant that that
resolution was invalid. Under section 24 of the Local Government (Rating) Act, it
requires that a rating resolution must include the date on which the rate must be paid,
and if that rate is to be paid in instalments, it must include the amount and the date of
each instalment. Section 57, which authorises additional penalties, requires that the
resolution also states when the rates must be paid and the due date, and the resolution
must also state how the penalties are calculated and the date on which those penalties
must be paid. In this case, the Christchurch City Council’s resolution did none of that,
but let me make it clear: all the required information was available. It was all available
in the council’s rating policy and in the funding impact statement. It was discussed at
the council table. It was aired in the local newspaper. It just was not in the resolution.
So the attempt to simplify had, basically, backfired, and although nobody had noticed
and it had gone on for 9 years, finally, in 2013, it had to be repaired.
I must give credit to the temporary chief executive officer of the Christchurch City
Council at that time, Jane Parfitt, because immediately the council was able to correct
the 2013- 14 rates resolution, and then it went back to review all it s other past
resolutions. They managed to identify a number of other technical irregularities. They
found errors in the setting of seven targeted rates and also in the setting of the uniform
annual general charge. It was the same problem. Although the back ground information
was readily available, it was not in that resolution, so all those resolutions were
irregular. As I have said, they were able to fix those resolutions going forward, but there
was no ability for them to fix the resolutions going back, hence this bill.
I would like to thank the Local Government and Environment Committee members
again, who thoroughly canvassed the background to this bill and worked their way
through their process. I would particularly like to thank the leadership of Scott Simpson
as the chair. The debate has gone on because nobody in Parliament ever likes to pass
retrospective legislation. We have done it several times in the last few years, and it is
unfortunate that this bill has had to come to the House. Fortunately, thi s bill is very
much about technical errors. Nobody has lost anything. There has been no fraud and no
suspicious behaviour—just the problem with the simplification of the language where
the council thought it was doing a good thing, which has backfired. I c ommend this bill
to the House.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: I am pleased to take a short call on the
final reading of this local bill. I would like to acknowledge the work of the member who
has just taken her seat, the Hon Nicky Wagner, in bringing this local bill to the House.
As she said in the remarks that she made on this bill, this is retrospective legislation —a
way for us to fix a problem with the way rates have been struck over a per iod of time in
Christchurch City. I share the sentiment that no one likes doing this, that this really is
not what Parliament envisions for itself in terms of what it wants to have as its function
in our great democracy —fix up what has been an error in the  way that rates were
struck—but it is something that needs to be done, and I would like to acknowledge that.
We have had at previous readings of this bill a fair amount of criticism that has come
on the councillors and on the council in terms of making thi s error. In fact, we have had
Government members being incredibly critical of the institution throughout the readings
of this bill. I would just like to make the point that, several times, we in the Opposition
have felt a certain amount of frustration about coming back into this House to play
patch-up on legislation where we have pointed out those very errors at the select
committee or, indeed, in this debating chamber. So I think that we can see that errors,
referred to across the House, occur in this place too.
3 Jun 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 4297
What is fundamentally important about this piece of legislation, what is important for
us on this side of the House as Labour, is valuing that relationship between central and
local government. It is critical that we have strong and productive relat ionships between
Parliament, our territorial local authorities, and our district councils —that local
government is just that. It is where we reach our communities and where a lot of very
good work is done. So I would not like to see any comments made in th is House that
denigrate that relationship. Labour will be supporting this bill, and I am happy to
commend it to the House.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: As the chairman of the Local
Government and Environment Committee I am going to support the Christchurch City
Council (Rates Validation) Bill. I do so reluctantly. The previous speaker, Dr Megan
Woods, made mention of the criticism that had been levelled at Christchurch City
Council in previous debates as this bill has progressed through this House. I want to just
acknowledge that the criticism that was levelled at council members was in terms of
their lack of ability, as highly paid professionals, to get it right. The road to hell is paved
with good intentions, and on this occasion the intention was actually to make the
passing of rates motions by the council easy, more simple, and to use so- called simple
English. The net result of the change, however, was that the motions that were passed
for 9 consecutive years at the council were, in fact, invalid, not correct, and wrong. The
problem with that, the net impact, is that although in this particular instance no
malfeasance, no fraud, no wrongdoing, no maliciousness, and no actual —more by good
luck than good management—financial liability to council or ratepayers occurred, had a
ratepayer decided to challenge the validity of the rates for any one of those 9 years, then
the council would have had not a single leg to stand on in terms of e nforcing those rates
payments.
That is not a situation that is professionally acceptable in one of the nation’s largest
councils, so I do not resile at all from my criticism, particularly in my second reading
speech on this bill, of the lack of professionalism by the council. When we visited
Christchurch as a select committee, we were stuck by the manner and tone of the single
submission that we received on this bill from the Christchurch City Council itself. I
guess that some members of the committee found that it was the tone and the manner of
the submission that was of most concern. It was not the error in itself, but it was that
there seemed to be no sense of proportion, no sense of contrition, no sense of
culpability, and no sense of understanding that , in fact, what had occurred was
something that should not have occurred—simply, that Parliament would put it right by
merely passing a piece of validating legislation. As the previous speaker indicated, this
Parliament does not like passing retrospective validating legislation. When it does have
to, from time to time, usually it is introduced by some local member —and in this case it
was my colleague the member for Christchurch Central, the very good and hard-
working Nicky Wagner, who has had to bring this bill to the House as sponsor, a bill
promoted by the council. She has had to convince her colleagues in caucus, and then
manage and steer it through the House in a way that I do not think a local member
would ever really want to do.
So what of this bill itself? Well, this bill seeks to validate specified rates between the
financial years 2004-05 through to 2012-13. The legislation itself has no impact at all on
ratepayers. There is no change to the amount of rates or penalties due from any
ratepayer as a r esult of the wrong and error -filled wording of the council -passed
motions in each of those 9 years. The errors were entirely restricted to the Christchurch
City Council’s rates resolutions on each one of those years, and the rates assessment
notices and invoices contained the right information. This is the sort of slightly odd
thing about this. The information that went to ratepayers and the actual amounts of rates
4298 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3 Jun 2015
that were levied were correct, but it was just the legal niceties —it was the fine print, the
dotting of the i’s and the crossing of the t’s, that did not occur. The errors were spotted
by the audit process and then, giving full credit to the council, it did seek to remedy the
situation as promptly and as quickly as it could. However, it did not change the fact that
retrospective legislation was still required to validate and legalise the motions that had
been passed for each of those 9 years. So what Christchurch City Council did was it
corrected the situation by issuing a revised resolution and re setting its rates as soon as it
was aware of it, but the historic errors for earlier years from 2003- 04 to 2012-13 could
be corrected only via a validating piece of legislation, and that is this bill.
What this bill does is it validates those payments for  historic rates back over those 9
years. It validates the penalties that were added to unpaid rates for those years, which of
themselves were not legal in terms of the motions that were passed by the council. What
it also does is it validates the basis for  certain targeted rates during those various years
and the penalties that were subsequently added to those rates as a result of non, or slow,
payment. What this bill also does is it confirms that all rates money collected by
Christchurch City Council during those 9 years is, in fact, lawful. What I guess we need
to consider as a Parliament is what lessons have been learnt through this process and not
only how we might ensure that a situation like this at Christchurch City Council never
arises again at any t ime in the future but how other councils, district councils, regional
councils, and other territorial authorities might be protected from a situation of this sort
occurring in the future. The good news is that lessons have been learnt.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Whare. Kia ora mai tātou, tēnā tātou katoa.
The House has resumed. When we reached the dinner break we were discussing the
Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill, and Scott Simpson has 4 minutes 20
