items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker. I do wish to avail myself of
that opportunity to spend a further 4½ minutes speaking t o the very good bill that has
been presented and sponsored by my colleague and very hard- working MP for
Christchurch Central, the Hon Nicky Wagner. In saying that I support the bill, I do so
rather grumpily, and that is because prior to the dinner break I was speaking about how
this House resists and does not really like having the need to bring retrospective
validation legislation before the Parliament. This was a matter that related to incorrect
rates motions being passed by the Christchurch City Council during the years 2004 -05
through to 2012- 13. For those 9 consecutive years, although no ratepayers were
financially impacted in any negative way, nor indeed was the council impacted in any
negative financial way, more by good luck than good management, none the less, had a
ratepayer chosen to challenge the validity of the rates for any one of those 9 years, then
the council would have been found legally liable and negligent.
One of the problems with retrospective legislation is that it is something that
validates something that would otherwise not have been legal. That is exactly the case
here. In August 2013 the Department of Internal Affairs alerted the Christchurch City
Council. This is not some small territorial authority in a remote part of the country ; this
is one of our largest municipalities and the internal affairs audit team alerted the council
to the fact that there was a problem. To the council’s credit it did attempt to remedy the
situation for the future, but it was not able to put right the er rors of the preceding 9
years. That is why Nicky Wagner, the Christchurch Central MP, has had to sponsor this
local bill on behalf of the council and bring it to the House so that we can put right the
dotting of the i’s and the crossing of the t’s that did not occur for those 9 years. This is
an example of a situation where I hope other territorial authorities will learn from the
3 Jun 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 4299
mistakes that have been made in Christchurch City, and that in future more care and
diligence will be shown in the wording and dr afting of motions before the council,
particularly as they relate to rating issues.
I reluctantly commend this bill to the House, but I thank Nicky Wagner and
congratulate her on her efforts in stewarding it through the House.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour —Māngere): I am happy to take a short call on this
and join with my parliamentary colleagues on this side of the House, particularly from
the Christchurch region, who will be contributing to this particular debate. I will just
begin by cautioning members of the House to just control the emotion that they may
feel towards the Christchurch City Council in passing this piece of legislation.
The first point I would make is that this relates to tec hnical issues that took place
from 2003 to 2013. It is not necessarily the fault of the present mayor or the present
councillors. The second point I would make is that we are talking about technical issues.
Essentially, the council had been doing the right thing, except it did not cross the t’s and
dot the i’s as expected by legislation. The third point I would make in just cautioning
members of Parliament, and particularly that side of the House, is that I am somewhat
sympathetic to the local government se ctor in our country, particularly because when
members of this House become scathing of the work that local government does on
behalf of its constituents, it seems like we are seeing them as an extension of the public
sector or a Government department, and that is just not the case. I think what we have
got to recognise and give due respect to is the fact that local government representatives
are elected by the people, by their communities, to serve and provide the necessary
services that the local communities might ask of their local council.
Fourthly, I agree that retrospective legislation, rates validation, is something that
many in this House are rather reluctant to agree with, but in this case precedents have
been set. I would also say that when the bi ll was opened up for public submissions, the
only organisation that made submissions to this was Christchurch City Council itself.
The committee, in looking at this piece of legislation, made not one recommendation
whatsoever to change or amend the piece o f legislation. I have to say that to all intents
and purposes, as far as I can see for my own eyes, the council has done the right thing
by bringing this piece of legislation to the House to cross the t’s and dot the i’s so that it
is within the laws as ar e required. That also raises another question: often I have heard
members of the House ridicule or condemn the local government sector, and I am
referring mainly to the Government members, and I would just ask them to be cautious
and be careful with that a ttitude. Remember that these are people elected by the local
community to represent them. It is part of our democracy. These are local governments,
not a Government department. I am happy to add my voice, along with my colleagues,
in supporting this bill in the House tonight. Thank you.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: Might I say that it is a pleasure to speak on the
Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill under the Speakership of such a
distinguished and illustrious member of this House. I am taking this call in this debate
on the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill because, as previous
colleagues have rehearsed the argument several times, I think it is necessary, given
some of the comments made by members opposite, just to repeat them one more time.

items.speaker: This is something that we do reluctantly
items.text: passing retrospective legislation in this House.
I think it was in the second reading debate that I expressed my personal reluctance to
consider retrospective legislation unless there is a very good reason to do so. If I may
once again refer to the pre -eminent legal theoretician Professor Dicey, the former
Vinerian Professor of Law at Oxford, who talked about retrospective legislation, he—
Simon O’Connor: Who, sorry?
4300 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3 Jun 2015

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER -BELL
items.text: Professor Dicey, Mr O’Connor. He was a very highly
respected Oxford legal theoretician of the 19 th century—a Vinerian Professor of Law.
He made the point that retrospective legislation can either be very, very bad or it can be
something that is necessary and tolerable. Of the examples of monstrous retrospective
legislation that he used to cite, one of the key examples of evil retrospective legislation
was the Habeas Corpus S uspension Act of 1794, which was a very unworthy piece of
legislation and was most unjust. However, he did also believe that it was possible to
have curative retrospective legislation to set right something that was done wrong. I
genuinely believe that this bill falls into the curative category. It does amend a technical
deficiency, and, as my learned colleague Scott Simpson, the chairman of the Local
Government and Environment Committee, referred to previously, in his own
contribution on this debate, there  are no people who will be required to pay additional
rates or levies because of this curative piece of retrospective rates validation. In fact, the
technical deficiency was simply in the wording of the ratings motions, which were
passed by successive city councils in Christchurch over a period of as many as 10 years.
I think it is very important that we do set this wrong right, and this bill does so. And
to other critics of retrospective legislation, I would also refer to recent research that has
demonstrated that in the Commonwealth of Australia —a very comparable jurisdiction
to our own, I suppose —up to 20 percent of legislation carries some form of
retrospectivity in it. So this bill is not entirely unusual. We have been here before, but
one of my main c oncerns when sitting on the Local Government and Environment
Committee was to ensure that we do not end up here again, having to validate rates
retrospectively for another council in New Zealand. Although we were not able to
receive an ironclad, watertight guarantee from officials that such an issue could not crop
up again in the future, I think that we can have some confidence, our being a competent
and very efficient Government on this side of the House —as opposed to the members
opposite—that this is one of the last rates validation bills that this House will, hopefully,
have to address, particularly in terms of dealing with such an issue in the manner that
we are today.
There have also been comments made about the competence of the officials who
tendered advice to the council over the course of the 10- year period during which the
rates were incorrectly set. I am actually prepared to stand by the comments of my
colleagues on this side of the House and by the criticisms and concerns that they have.
Firstly, when the Christchurch City Council appeared before us at the select committee,
there was a complete lack of contrition. We did not have from the highly paid officials
any sense of regret or any sort of apology to the ratepayers of Christchurch or to the
taxpayers of New Zealand, who are faced with a bill that is probably many hundreds of
thousands, if not millions, of dollars in order to pass this piece of legislation. There was
no real apology for the incompetence that has led us to this position. That was , in my
view, regrettable. I do appreciate the arguments advanced by some that the people
whom we saw at the select committee, the people who were advocating —the only
submitters, in fact, whom we heard on this bill —were not those responsible for the
initial error. They were the officials who are the current incumbents, and they made the
point that the councillors and officials involved with the initial incorrect settings and
incorrect motions, including the chief executive at the time, were no longer employ ed
by the council or no longer served on the council. That is a point that is not entirely lost
on me.
We do have a situation where taxpayers and ratepayers have been put to some
considerable expense and inconvenience in order to remedy the situation, so I  think that
we do need to send a very strong message to officials and councils up and down New
Zealand that it is paramount that they understand what is required in the law. It is not,
3 Jun 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 4301
actually, a huge piece of legislation that they have to come to grips w ith, in terms of
understanding the framework within which we set local government ratings in New
Zealand. It is very important that they understand it, that they understand the technical
detail, and that they apply it correctly so that we do not end up, once again, in a
situation where we are expending significant amounts of ratepayer and taxpayer money
to remedy retrospectively a situation like we have here.
There was a question that came up in the second reading debate, and I put the
question to the Minis ter, and we actually had a very clear answer from the Minister.
That question was about what is actually covered by this retrospective validation bill.
Not only does it cover the incorrectly levied rates, which were levied over a 10- year
period from 2003- 04 to 2012- 13 inclusive, but it also covers a number of subsidiary
rates and charges that were levied incorrectly as well. These were the Church Bay sewer
loan rate, the Church Bay water loan rate, the restricted water targeted rate, the waste
minimisation rate, and the water fire service connection rate for those financial years;
the same as for the uniform annual general charge, which was incorrectly levied. I think
that the Minister did give us a full explanation and description of that. There is
something in the order of $600,000 worth of unpaid back rates that should have been
paid. The citizens and ratepayers in question did not behave properly in not paying the
$600,000 worth of back rates, which does require this retrospective validation to be
enacted in order for the council to be able legally to collect that $600,000 worth of back
rates. That is another reason why this validation bill is required. I come back to the
point that the bill does not prejudice the interests of otherwise law -abiding Christchurch
residents who have paid their rates over those years, thinking that they had been
correctly levied, when, as we have now discovered, they had not.
Just to make things really clear, I do want to reiterate some details of the original
failure. It was a breach of section 24 of the Local Government (Rating) Act 2002, which
is the principal Act that determines how local government ratings are levied in New
Zealand. The Act talks about how rates are levied and the fact that they are available to
be paid in instalments, and it sets the payment dates for those instalments. I think that it
is a credit to the people of Christchurch and to New Zealanders in general that there are
so few uncollected rates. There is only $600,000 worth in a great city the size of
Christchurch, which is home to many hundreds of thousands of souls and is arguably
the second city of New Zealand after Auckland —and, obviously, the capital,
Wellington. But I think it is a credit to the taxpayers and the ratepayers in Christchurch
that such a small portion has not been paid, and there will always be cases, I suppose,
where some people do not feel that they are obliged to meet their full obligations and
make their contribution to the running of their city and the infrastructure and services
that the council provides.
The failure we need to resolve was a breach of section 57 of the Act, and was around
how penalties are added and calculated to those unpaid rates that were incorrectly levied
in the first place. Those two errors are being remedie d in this piece of legislation. It is a
necessary thing. It is something that we are doing reluctantly. We need to send a strong
message to councils that they must get it right, to prevent such a waste of parliamentary
time in the future. I just make the f inal point that the retrospective element, although
best avoided, is something that in this case is necessary and curative. For all those
reasons, I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: I am pleased to take a short call on the Christchurch
City Council (Rates Validation) Bill, and it will be short given that it costs over $21,000
an hour for the running of Parliament and that there is wide support across the House
for this technical bill. Yes, it is retrospective, but I would agree with Mr Foster-Bell that
it is curative and tolerable while retrospective. The Green Party is supporting this bill
4302 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3 Jun 2015
because the mistakes that the Christchurch City Council made in its rates -setting
resolutions we re not deliberate. They were simply in the wording of the resolutions.
They did not affect the amount of rates that Christchurch folk had to pay, nor the
penalties that ratepayers were liable to pay for delayed payment or non-payment.
I think we should be very careful in this House not to throw stones. It is a wooden
House, rather than glass House, but tomorrow we will be debating legislation that
corrects a mistake made in the exclusive economic zone legislation. So this Parliament
often has to reconsider legislation that was not fully considered during select committee
consideration and during the House debates, so it is not unknown for errors to be made.
The mistakes that the Christchurch City Council made in its resolutions were in
relation to the payme nt dates for rates and the authority to impose penalties on unpaid
rates. That raised issues with the validity of collecting the rates and the penalties for
non-payment. So the bill validates the payment dates and it validates any penalties that
have been added to the rates. It ensures that all the money the council has received in
respect of the rates is lawful and always has been lawful. As Mr Foster -Bell noted, it
relates to some of the uniform annual charges and some of the targeted rates and loans
for Church Bay and Governors Bay for wastewater and water supply schemes.
One of the issues this bill did not go through is that there is a $683,000 hole in the
council’s revenue stream. If the bill was not passed, the council would be liable to legal
challenge and it would not be able to chase up the 38 ratepayers, who have not paid
their rates and who are liable for penalties, without the risk of a legal challenge. That
would impose quite significant extra costs on the council, which has already got funding
problems, so we have no substantive issue with supporting the bill because the mistakes
were not deliberate—they were procedural —and we are resolving an issue that should
be resolved and that the council has brought to the attention of the public and of
Parliament at the first opportunity after those mistakes were discovered.
But although the council has been able to come to Parliament to get those issues
resolved, it will not be able to come to Parliament as easily if it proceeds with its very
short-sighted decision to sell off major council assets like the port company, the airport,
and Orion, which have been major contributors through the dividends that those
companies provide to keeping the council’s rates low. The $43 million in dividends that
are coming to the council in the 2015-16 year means that rates are 13 percent lower than
they would otherwise be. The Green Party considers that it is incredibly short -sighted to
be pushed—as the city council is being pushed, by the National Government’s failure t o
renegotiate the cost-sharing agreement, to meet the $400 million shortfall in the costs of
preparing the horizontal infrastructure —to consider selling these revenue- generating
assets in order to fund a potential white elephant like the stadium, which is likely to lose
revenue. So we support the bill but we oppose the proposals in the city council’s long -
term plan to sell vital revenue-generating assets. Thank you.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: What more can be said about this bill? It is a very short
bill—a couple of pages, but it certainly has generated some—[Interruption] Sorry?
Simon O’Connor: You can do 10 minutes.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: You think I can? We will give it a lash, shall we? It is a very short bill
and its intent is very clear. For those who might have missed it, and going straight to the
core, which really is at the guts of this bill, what this bill does is pretty much cont ained
in Part 2. Clause 5, as has previously been said, validates the payment dates for the
rates. Clause 6 validates penalties added to those rates. Clause 7 declares all money
received by the council in payment of the rates and any penalties paid in respect of those
rates to be and to always have been lawfully paid to, and received by, the council. Those
are the interesting words to me —“to be and to always have been lawfully paid”—
because they were not, were they? They were not lawfully paid, and that is really what
3 Jun 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 4303
the nub of this bill is and why we have spent so much time in the House, why people
went down to Christchurch and put a lot of time and effort into drafting, hearing and
taking submissions, and moving this bill through three stages in the House.
The words “to be and to always have been” almost sounds a little bit Shakespearean,
does it not? “Lawfully paid”—“lawfully paid”. Would it not be nice if some of us could
actually pop along to the supermarket and say: “Well, you know I came in the other
week and I picked up some groceries. I’d just like you to consider that they have been,
and always had been, paid for.” It is a little bizarre, maybe a little bit Shakespearean.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: It’s like amalgamation of Carterton’s.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: It is like amalgamation —something that boggles the mind as to how
people could actually come up with these things or how people could make simple
mistakes. I guess. I do take on board some of the cautionary comments by my colleague
on my right Su’a William Sio. It is tempting for someone like me who has come from a
small council, Carterton District Council, which is a council about which certain people
out there on the hustings and some people in this House have advocated the view that it
is too sm all to run itself, it could not possibly manage its assets, and it could not
possibly comply with all the intricacies of the Local Government (Rating) Act.
Therefore, on those and numerous other spurious arguments, they say that it needs to,
deserves to, and should be swallowed up into and run by a larger council.
Well, we have never done this. We have never made mistakes like this. Masterton
District Council has never made this mistake. If people really want to get their heads
around what is happening out there in rural and provincial areas with small councils and
how well they are managed and how they do not end up in situations where money you
have sort of paid is deemed to be and always has been lawfully paid, they should really
pull out the latest Bell report and have a quick read. The Bell report is really quite
staggering in its revelations that some of the top -performing councils in this country are
actually some of the smaller ones. Small rural and provincial councils are being run well
and do not r equire the time of this House to retrospectively pass legislation to correct
their mistakes.

items.speaker: I will acknowledge this
items.text: the current Mayor of Christchurch was not the Mayor of
Christchurch when this happened. The current chief executive officer was not the c hief
executive officer, or was not one of the chief executive officers, who was in charge of
the Christchurch City Council at the time that these mistakes were made. The credit for
that lies with other people. But I have to make the point that people who a re elected into
council, whether they be councillors, community board members, mayors, or deputy
mayors, do not, at the time of their election and appointment —and for some of them,
even a few years after that —actually come to grips totally and 100 percent with all the
procedural requirements that go with the job, particularly at the time of the annual
planning and consultation phase, particularly when you are taking submissions on an
annual plan, setting rates —sewerage rates, targeted rates, uniform rates. They are not
100 percent au fait with that procedure, and it is up to the chief executive officer and his
senior managers to guide and steer those councillors, the mayor, and the deputy mayor
in the procedures and the protocols that they must follow to com ply completely, 100
percent, with the Act.

items.speaker: I will say that again
items.text: it is up to the chief executive officer, the chief financial officer,
and the other entourage of senior managers, who get paid hugely well, particularly in
Christchurch. I remember well the  controversy over that particular chief executive
officer who gave himself a pay rise because he thought he was doing so jolly well. Here
we are in the House, with all parties in the House putting all of their time into correcting
something that the chief executive officer of the Christchurch City Council should not
have allowed to happen. On top of that, I remember the visits by the Audit Office and
4304 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3 Jun 2015
how my council would ramp itself up and get ready for that visiting team of auditors.
We would have a prelim inary interview with the chief auditor —the mayor, the chief
executive officer, the deputy mayor, and the chair of the Audit and Risk Committee. We
are talking about little Carterton here; we are not talking about New York. We would do
that, and we would ge t a clear picture from the chief auditor of that team, which might
comprise a team coming in —and you know, we are talking about a council of 8,500
people—that might be three, four, or even five strong.
That team would outline what it was that they were go ing to go through and what
they would be looking for. Well, clearly, the audit team that went through
Christchurch—for year after year after year —did not check the procedures by which
Christchurch was implementing its rates charges. It did not audit those procedures. I
know, from talking to the Audit Office, and we have had hearings and discussions at the
select committee, that people have got a different focus now. I know that in any one
particular year, the Audit Office will come in with a theme. It will come in and say:
“These are the things we are going to be looking at.” But for this to have gone on year
after year after year and to be left undetected, and for us in 2015 to be sitting here in the
House this evening, past my bedtime—I am joking—passing this legislation through the
House is unbelievable, really, particularly with a council that size that employs that
many people in senor manager appointments, and pays them, what, $400,000 or
$300,000? And it pays an audit office—what—what was that last bill? Well, it certainly
was not $90,000, which is what Carterton pays. It was $200,000 in one year for the
audit to be completed and for the council to still miss this mistake. So here we sit.
Like many of the other parties in the House and the other speake rs before me, New
Zealand First has to put on record that it really struggles with retrospective legislation.
We do not think that it is really ideal. I thank Paul Foster -Bell for his comment that 20
percent of the legislation that goes through this House—good homework there, Paul—is
retrospective. We do not like it. We particularly do not like it when highly paid senior
managers of a council are not doing their job and are not advising their mayor, their
deputy mayor, their chair of the Audit and Risk Comm ittee, and their council as
appropriate, and we end up in this situation.
I would say—what can I say to finish off?

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: It wouldn’t have happened when you were Mayor of Carterton.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: It would not have happened if I had been Mayor of Christchurch. I
would say, please, when we are having this conversation and debate about bigger is
better and bigger councils get things right and small councils struggle —when we are
having this argument and this debate about economies of  scale—I would like the House
to remember this: the reason some small councils do not make mistakes like this is that
the very small budgets that they have for them makes them very sensitive to expenditure
and very sensitive to error, particularly errors t hat cost money. The rule of thumb we
used in Carterton was this: for every $80,000 you spend over and above what was
budgeted last year, that will result in a 1 percent increase on your ratepayers. Can you
honestly justify that 1 percent increase? When you are dealing with big councils like the
one in Auckland’s super -city, $80,000 is postage money for 1 day. It does not mean
anything. It does not make councillors blink, it does not make their eyes water, and,
therefore, they can —I guess, understandably —lose sight of the detail, lose sight of the
protocols and procedures they should be following, and they can make mistakes. Let us
hope it does not happen again.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: I rise to take a call on the Christchurch City Council
(Rates Validation) Bill. I must say, after listening to that kōrero from our colleague
across the way over there, Ron Mark, that I agree with him. I agree with him. The
mistake that was made was not made by the current mayor, it was not made by the
3 Jun 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 4305
current chief executive officer; it was made by all of those who went before her. But the
thing is, once you take on those positions and those posts, you do inherit, unfortunately,
all the rubbish that had happened prior to you coming in there. I think that when we
elect our mayors and our councillors, those are some of the things that may come up. I
am not a fan of passing retrospective legislation through this House, either. However,
that is the position we are in with this Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill,
and we need to keep going with it and get it through the House.
I think that with a lot of what you said, Mr Mark, you hit the nail on the head when it
comes to past histories of that par ticular council and the accountability of its chief
executive officers. At times it looks like the bigger councils get, the more complicated it
is to manage, and messages stop getting moved around. I think that for Christchurch
City that is basically what happened —messages were not getting to the people. Was it
incompetency? What was it? We will not know. All we need to know is that we are
going to move this one forward.
I guess that is why this Government has been doing a lot of work around establishing
prudent benchmarks that require councils to produce 30- year plans and strategies.
Councils now have to provide information to their ratepayers about everything that they
are doing, so that the ratepayers can actually judge the council’s performance. That is
really key. I am not a ratepayer of Christchurch City —yet. I am a ratepayer of another,
smaller district council, and these are some of the things that I ask my councillors who
represent our area: “OK, we voted for you, so what are you doing? What type of job are
you doing? What kind of job are you doing for us as ratepayers, and how are you
measuring it?”.
There is a lot to be said around performance measures of councillors and their
workers, and how councillors get around the table to do performance manag ement of
their chief executive officer. I had no idea about that type of work, but it is one of those
things that I learnt. I come from a small NGO, and we had to do that. As Māori NGOs
we had to do that with all of our staff, and our boards had to do that  with managers like
me. I guess there are a lot of lessons to be learnt from the small groups —that is, if they
have good performance management systems, then maybe the big ones could actually
learn from the small ones.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Would we do this for a small NGO or a small council? No, we wouldn’t,
would we?

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: No, but the point is we are dealing with that legislation now for
Christchurch City

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: The point is the National Government’s shutti ng down all those
small NGOs anyway.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Oh, no, no, no, no, no! We are talking about this council, and
that is where we are going to stay.
We are reducing red tape for councils. That is what our role is, and I can tell you
right now that one of our key projects happening within the local government area has
been our Rules Reduction Taskforce. It is an amazing task force that is going around all
the local government areas seeking input from ratepayers, and from people who are
interested who may not be ratepayers but are still affected by some of the things that are
happening in their cities or their towns —especially around the regulations, rules, and
laws that that particular council has. So the task force is asking for feedback.
Recently I hosted one of those Rules Reduction Taskforce meetings in the
Christchurch East electorate. It was very interesting to hear about some of the red tape
issues that some of these developers, and some of the people who were redeveloping
their homes, were actually going through—the really minute things. The task force was
led by Jacqui Dean and sponsored by Paula Bennett, and was looking to actually help
4306 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3 Jun 2015
ratepayers. We are actually there to help ratepayers into the future, to make sure that
their cities and their towns are actually working for them, and that is what it is all about.
So when we start to look at the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill, we
start to ask what it is. What are the sections? What are the sections that require the rates
to be set—the resolutions of the council? The resolutions must specify the financial year
to which the rates apply —I am repeating this, I understand that. I understand that I am
repeating this, but I do so because it is really key. I am hoping that other councils,
which may or may not be perhaps heading down towards the same situation, can
actually look at some of the things that they are doing and the way they set their rates,
and are making sure they are using this as a tick box to make sure that they do not end
up in the same situation. So we are looking at the financial year to which the rates
apply, the date on which the rates must be paid and/or, if payable by instalments, the
payment dates for each instalment, the penalties to be added to the ra tes not paid by the
due date, and how these penalties have to be calculated.
Some of the irregularities made by the Christchurch City Council under the Local
Government (Rating) Act 2002 include a failure to state in the rates resolution that the
rates wou ld be payable in instalments by certain dates. These rates resolutions also
failed to state the penalties that would be added to the rates if they were not paid on the
due date, and the rates that were to be assessed in the previous year that remained
unpaid. So the dates that the penalties were to be added to the unpaid rates, and the
amounts of the penalties that would be added— all of these things were actually missing
from within the rates resolution.
In addition to the irregularities, we also had areas that included the failure —and my
colleagues here have already stated it, but I am going to state it again —to state the
Church Bay sewer and water loan rates system. All of these were provided within the
Christchurch City Council’s funding impact statement—everything that I talk about
from here on is provided in the Christchurch City Council’s funding impact statement.
It failed to state the Governors Bay sewer and water loan rates as a fixed amount, and it
failed to state that the liability for the restricted water target rates was calculated on the
level of service through a restricted water supply system. It failed to state that the water
minimisation rate was set as a fixed amount per rating unit, as provided—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: It was very serious.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Yes, it was very serious. I carry on. It failed to state that the
water minimisation rate was calculated on the number of separately used or inhabited
parts of the rating unit, and it also failed to state the water fire service c onnection rate.
Finally, it failed to state the uniform annual general charge, which was to be calculated
on the number of separately used inhabited parts of the rating unit.
So, again, in order to address those procedural irregularities, this bill validat es the
payment rates for the rates set and assessed by the Christchurch City Council between
2003 and 2013, and validates all the penalties added to any validated unpaid rates
between 2003 and 2013. It validates the basis on which certain specified or targ eted
rates were calculated for the rates in the years that were set out, as I have just stated. It
also declares all moneys for the Christchurch City Council in relation to validated rates
and penalties to be lawful, because prior to that they were not. Fi nally, it provides that
any unpaid rates or penalties in relation to any of this would be made lawful and would
be recovered by the Christchurch City Council.
We have all learnt something tonight, have we not? We have all learnt something
tonight. I just w ant to take this time to take a bow, because that is what you have all
heard from this side of the House.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: They’re just touchy.
3 Jun 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 4307

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: They are just touchy. And we need to keep on reiterating that,
because we do not want retrospective bills from councils coming through this House
again, as my colleague Paul Foster-Bell outlined in his wonderful speech before.
Let us carry on, because I know you are getting very engaged in what I am saying. I

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I call Rino Tirikatene.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Move an extension of time.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: As much as I would like to move
an extension of time, I think that member deserves a drink. We all do—absolutely.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: We’ll all need one by the end of this.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Well, we will wait and see. I am pleased to speak in support
of the third reading. I looked back at my earlier contributions on this bill, and I was
quite critical of the Christchurch City Council and the officials in the 9 successive years
where they ba sically broke the law and did not comply with the Local Government
(Rating) Act. But I think I have said my piece. I know that the Christchurch City
Council has got the message loud and clear. Can I acknowledge the council, though, for
fronting up to Parli ament, acknowledging its mistakes, and going through this process
to correct the errors and the illegality of its actions.
I want to make just a short contribution, and rather than being critical of the
Christchurch City Council I will just say that the e rrors that were made are there for
everyone to see. The council has come to Parliament to correct them, and, through
retrospective legislation, we are doing so. But I would hope that this piece of legislation
is a message, I guess, to all local government in New Zealand, the 78 local authorities
that we have up and down the length and breadth of our great country —the regional
councils, the territorial authorities, and all the different types of councils that we have,
such as district councils, city councils , and unitary councils. Hopefully, this is a lesson
for all of them —please make sure you comply with the law. It is not hard. When you
are setting your rates, just follow the requirements in the legislation and make sure that
you are doing everything by the book. When you are passing your resolutions, make
sure you are actually including everything that is required to be put in the resolution. It
is not hard.
I know that this is an area where Local Government New Zealand is wanting to
improve the performance of local authorities around the country. This is one area where
they can definitely improve on their performance. I ask them to please take the time. I
ask them to do what Mr Ron Mark did when he was the Mayor of Carterton—they
made sure they complied w ith the law, they passed their resolutions, and they included
all of the correct information to ensure that it was compliant with the law. That is really
4308 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3 Jun 2015
my message to local authorities around the country. Please make sure you follow the
requirements, the compliance checklists. It is not hard. Make sure that you put
everything in the resolutions, because otherwise we may be forced to sit through more
contributions like we have had tonight.
We have heard about Shakespeare, we have heard about neoclassical architecture, we
have heard about all sorts of stuff in this debate. Unless the good people of New
Zealand want to sit through more corrective, patch- up legislation, please, local
government across New Zealand, make sure you follow the law, pass your resolutions,
make sure they are all complete, cross the t’s and dot the i’s, and then we will not be
wasting our Parliament’s time on putting through unnecessary legislation to correct
something that should not have happened in the first place. Regrettably, ther e are times
when Parliament has to step in.
Let us hope there is not a concerned citizen or ratepayer going through their local
government official information, wanting to get copies of all the resolutions that were
passed, and trying to marry them up. We know that some people out there might do that.
Certain ratepayers are quite pedantic. Let us hope that more of these errors do not come
to light, because if it has happened with one of our major councils, the Christchurch
City Council, let us hope that the 78 other local authorities around the country have all
been compliant in passing their resolutions. Thank you.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: It is a great honour to rise for the
first time to speak on this bill, the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill, in
its third reading. I must admit that I feel like I have been on the highs of the Arts Centre
of Christchurch Trust Bill and the lows of this rates validation bill. It i s legislation that
is very important to me as the electorate MP for Waimakariri. A lot of people think that
the electorate actually mirrors the “Waimak” district borders, but, in fact, my electorate
covers part of northern Christchurch, Northcote, Redwood, Belfast, and Northwood, and
about a quarter of the population of my electorate live in the Christchurch City Council
zone. So it is a very important issue for my constituents, and it is a very important issue
for me.
I must join with the rest of the memb ers of the House in acknowledging the work of
the Hon Nicky Wagner who has brought this local bill to the House tonight. She is a
very hard -working Minister, who has shepherded what could have been a very
controversial bill through the legislative process.  You very much see why that Minister
has turned a red seat blue. Can I also acknowledge the chair of the Local Government
and Environment Committee equally for shepherding the bill through a process that
could have been very controversial.
I do acknowledg e the sentiments from the other side of the House about respect for
local government. My late grandfather was on the Christchurch City Council for over
30 years in the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s, and he spent several of them as Deputy Mayor
of the Christchurc h City Council. Probably that is where my political ambitions hark
back to. I very much respect the people of his ilk—that it was about civic service and
civic duty. So we must be mindful of that when we do critique local government
performance.
But in sa ying that, we should not reward poor performance. If you do not challenge
something, then you are complicit in it. So I think it was very well summarised by the
Minister when she introduced the third reading and she said that the bill, although
controversial, was simple, straightforward, short, and very focused. I mean, at first I did
not know whether she was talking about me or Ron Mark, but she is quite right. It is a
controversial bill. It is simple, straightforward, short, and very focused, but it could
have caused a lot of issues for the Christchurch people. I must say that that is the last
thing Christchurch people need at the moment. I do not need to rehash the last few
3 Jun 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 4309
years, but we all know it has been a very difficult time for people in Christchurc h and,
of course, in the “Waimak” and Selwyn as well. So it is quite right that we take a very
diligent and thoughtful approach with this legislation.
What we do know, if we look at it in some detail, is that every June the council
resolves to set its rates for the next financial year. We know with this rates resolution
that it did not meet the requirements. And the Minister referred to this —the issue th at
arose from trying to put things in simple language. I actually have some sympathy for
this. In my previous career in mental health, I managed a drug treatment service in
London for the London Borough of Barnet, a local authority in northern London. It had
a policy of having simple English to make it accessible for people to engage with
information and literature. But, of course, when you are talking about technical
information, sometimes if it is simplified you do lose a lot in translation. So I can
understand how this may have happened, but, at the end of the day, like I say, we cannot
reward poor performance, and if we do not challenge something, we are complicit in it.
So we do know that all the required information was available in policy and
newspapers, but just not in the set resolutions, and there were other technical issues
around targeted rates. We have heard a lot tonight about the issues around retrospective
legislation.
So overall, I think that with the issues at hand for both the leadership of the
Christchurch City Council and, of course, the Waimakariri District Council and the
Selwyn District Council as they lead through the recovery, we just need to be mindful
that we do need positive relationships in central and local governments. I want t o thank
our chair, Scott Simpson, for holding the select committee hearing down in
Christchurch for the day. Not only did we get the opportunity to go to the Christchurch
Arts Centre, which was a valuable trip, but we also got to hear the submissions around
this bill. There was only one submission, as people have spoken previously about, and
the councillor who did turn up was Glenn Livingstone. I know there have been some
comments about his performance in that submission, but I would like to say that in my
dealings with that councillor, he is someone who is very humble and very hard- working
in his region, which is primarily in eastern Christchurch. We know they were hard hit
by the earthquakes, and councillor Livingstone and councillor East are doing a fanta stic
job out there. But it was good to see that overall there were no ratepayers who were
affected by this, and what we are doing is just validating the resolutions retrospectively
for about the last 9 years—2003-04 to 2012-13.
It is a tough job for the C hristchurch City Council. I was on Chris Lynch’s radio
show on Monday morning with my colleague Clayton Cosgrove, talking about the
political issues in Canterbury. Quite often we are asked to comment on local
government performance and on mayors, but I mus t say that it is not really our place to
give a running commentary, too much, on their performance. But it was a great
opportunity to take the select committee down to Christchurch and see what is
happening down there. There is a lot of hope —there is a lot  of hope—and I must say
that, at the end of the day, we are delivering in Christchurch. The previous speaker from
the Green Party, Eugenie Sage, mentioned the white elephant of the rugby stadium,
which I thought I had to pick up on, because, at the end of the day, Canterbury is the
best rugby region in the world and we need a stadium to reflect that, like the Hagley
Oval—[Interruption] Thank you very much. Can I just say, just to summarise, really,
that we are one region, one Canterbury, and I am very happy  to be one -eyed. Thank
you.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: I have to make just one quick
comment before I get into the substance of my speech today, and that is to say tha t the
contributions from the last two National Party members have been really, really
4310 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3 Jun 2015
dreadful. I also have to say that those last two National Party members who contributed
were also the two people who stood in the last two elections in Christchurch East and
lost—to me. So I just wanted to remind you, with that little lesson.
This bill is about people who are elected, who have to be accountable for things that
they may not have been responsible for. This is what this bill is about. All of us who are
elected to public office know that at some point we may have to be accountable for the
actions of those who have preceded us. That is exactly what this bill is about.
I know that some of the members of the Local Government and Environment
Committee have been a  little harsh in their comments about the officials from the
council who presented to the select committee. They were expecting them to be really
overwrought in their desire to get this bill passed, and really be grovelling, I think is the
term I want to u se. Well, actually, what they have done is a really sensible thing, at a
time when their council is under some pressure. Let us face it: it is probably one of the
most difficult jobs going at the moment—being a councillor on the Christchurch City
Council—and it has been for the last 4 or 5 years. So for the select committee to be
scathing of the attitude of the officials who presented is, I think, a little bit rich.
While I am on that note, I do want to send my greetings to the Christchurch- elected
representatives, to the hard- working councillors, and to the community board members
who might be listening tonight to this bill finally being passed so that they can get on
with their jobs. They are going through a particularly busy time. They are hearing
submissions on the long-term plan. I want to acknowledge the work that the hundreds of
submitters from the Christchurch East electorate have done into that long -term plan,
with many of them wanting to ensure that the New Brighton community becomes, once
again, the jewel in the crown of Christchurch City. I want to acknowledge all the hard
work that they do, that they have been doing, and all of the hard work that the
Christchurch city councillors and community boards have done.

items.speaker: Let us face it
items.text: it has been a diff icult time, but in the midst of all of this difficult time,
the acting chief executive, Jane Parfitt, found a problem. Back in 2002-03, in an attempt
to have a plain- language solution to the ratings language, the council made a bit of a
mistake, and it did  not actually include, as my colleague Su’a William Sio says, all the
dotting of the i’s and the crossing of the t’s. But it took a very busy acting chief
executive officer, at an extraordinarily busy time —a very busy chief executive officer,
at a very busy time—to find the error and to ask for our help to put it right. And it is our
job to do what we need to do to ensure we can validate those rates so that the council
can be sure that it can use those rate payments that were collected, in the manner that i t
should. But not only that, the council also needs to ensure that it can provide for the
collection of rates that were not collected during that period. From those, I think 38 or
so ratepayers owe in the vicinity of $600,000.
So that is what this bill do es. I am not going to speak too much further on it. I think
what we should do is get this bill passed so that we can get on with the job in
Christchurch. I thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker, for permitting my contribution. Thank
you.

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: E mihi atu ki a koe e te Mana Whakawā. Huri noa e te

items.speaker: Pita Paraone
items.text: Tēnā koe.

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: Kia ora. It is again my pleasure to stand to take the final call on
the Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill. I am not going to relitigate a lot
of the topics around the speeches that have been done over the process of this bill. But I
do want to acknowledge, on both sides of the House here this evening, the real quality
of the speeches, and particularly listening to a former mayor, listening to a very active
Auckland MP, Mr William Sio, and also from this side of the House, as well. I would
3 Jun 2015 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 4311
like to acknowledge, as the final speaker, the sponsor and the driver for this bill, the
Hon Nikki Wagner, the National Party MP for Christchurch Central, and also the
chairman of the Local Government and Environment Committee, Scott Simpson, and all
of our colleagues, actually, who sit on this committee.
I do not believe, in listening to the last speaker, Poto Williams, that the select
committee has been ungracious. I do not believe a lot of the descriptions, in some way,
about how we have handled this bill. I think it has been professional and it has also been
a bill that we all understand. I mean, listening tonight, listening over the last two times
the bill has come to the House for the first and second readings—it is that the words that
we are hearing have commonality. Reluctance, retrospective legislat ion, regretful,
emotive, blame, and blasé are the terms used for councillors. But at the end of the day, I
certainly feel that we have the commonality to agree with the fact that this is what
happened, and we are here to address it. The city council, which was the only submitter,
has put up its hand and has said yes —and past councillors. It is our responsibility and it
is our duty to put this right. On that basis, I think that we have a clear direction on how
we are actually going to vote for this bill.
I think it is important, too, to remember that after the situation was first identified —
and this was according to three or four mayors whom I spoke to—almost every council
across New Zealand actually then suddenly stopped and looked back at its processes
around rating processes. That was a catalyst that this situation created, so that everyone
could ensure for themselves the fact that their processes were correct, so that they could
give their constituents, their ratepayers, the confidence that they deserve. That is very
much an overview of the bill itself, but I think that we need to also look at the council
itself. I remember Glen, when he came to submit on behalf of the council. When you
understand—and particularly those who do not come from Christchurch, w ho are not
actually there day in and day out, who actually have not lived through the last 4 or 5
years of the incredible upheaval, the disruption, and all of that that is going on in this
city—that it is our council, and they do a tremendous job.
I want to just spend one part of this speech to say that yesterday was a very
significant day. Yesterday: “Leri era Italia Giornata Nazionale”. What that means is that
yesterday was Italian National Day. I am bringing this up, il Capo, because of the fact
that—if you read an article in the Christchurch Press on the weekend —it was the
former chief executive officer of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority who
had actually visited the city of L’Aquila. In that city, in 2009, they had over 300 people
who actually lost their lives, and 65,000 people were homeless. If you compare what
they have done in Italy with Christchurch, well, then you will see how hard this city
council is working. But, also, one of the things is that the recovery is in partnership with
the Crown, central government, the regional council, and also the Christchurch City
Council, iwi, and all the major stakeholders. When you compare us with what is going
on in Italy, all the usual suspects —corruption, hold- ups, all of this, you know,
leadership problems—are things that we do not actually experience here.
Finally, just to highlight in this bill the incredible assistance that this Government has
given to the city of Christchurch, it is reflected in the fact that in the 2015 Budget
another $100 million was given to the Christchurch rebuild, which brings it to $16.5
billion of taxpayers’ and ratepayers’ money. That says a lot. That is almost 40 percent
of the total estimated cost of the Christchurch rebuild, which is in excess of $40 billion.
In t ying all of that together, our council, the Crown, the Government, the regional
council, and all the major stakeholders are really a shining light, another beacon to the
world on how we actually work together. This is a reflection— I am looking at both
sides of the House —that we support this bill in its third reading. On that note, just to
4312 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3 Jun 2015
finish off, is the fact that I would like to, again, acknowledge all of the contributions
here this evening and to commend this bill, il Capo, to the House. Kia ora.
Bill read a third time.
SOCIAL SECURITY (CLOTHING ALLOWANCES FOR ORPHANS AND
UNSUPPORTED CHILDREN) AMENDMENT BILL
Third Reading
Debate resumed from 6 May.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I am very pleased to resume my call on the Social Security
(Clothing Allowances for Orphans and Unsupported Children) Amendment Bill, which
was unable to pass on the last members’ day because, for some reason, the Government
members felt compelled to waste the time of this House on what seemed like endless,
meaningless, repetitious speeches on bills that no one disagreed with. That is not
uncommon, given the behaviour we have seen again this evening. I was disappointed
that the children and their families who are following the progress of this bill so closely
were again left hanging. That, to my mind, was disrespectful.
I would now like to acknowledge Tracey Martin from New Zealand First for
bringing this bill to the House, and for  shepherding it through the select committee so
effectively to get it to this point. Tracey Martin has had to swallow, I would say, some
dead rats in the process, but she prioritised the needs of children and getting a result
over the intent that she origi nally came to the House with. I think that deserves to be
acknowledged.
The Green Party supported this bill at its first reading and supports it now, but we are
greatly disappointed by the Government’s warped priorities and meanness, which has
reduced this  bill down to making children wait until 2018 to get the intent of the
original bill for only an amount of money that is less than the flag referenda in practice.
What this bill is about is fairness. It is about addressing a small but important inequity
in the funding that goes to support some of the most vulnerable children in Aotearoa
New Zealand, those who through death or family breakdown have lost the support of
their parents and are now in the care of other family members. Although the quantum of
the funding discrepancy around this issue of the clothing allowance may seem small to
us sitting here in the House —and it really does seem small to me, I have got to say, in
the scope of all the things that this House considers —it means a lot and it counts for  a
lot for those families who are struggling to get by, and are wanting to provide the very
best for the children in their care.
Basically, to recap again what the heart of this bill is about, it is that children who are
in foster care in New Zealand becau se of family breakdown or death are entitled to a
clothing allowance of just over $1,100 a year, to be able to buy whatever clothes they
need. Usually, they will be new clothes, and that is really, really important for kids —
what you wear at school; I am sure we remember that. It counted when I was a kid way
back when, and it seems to count even more now. That $1,100—plus a little bit—
allowance is not available to children who are being cared for by their family members.
Those family members, many of whom ar e grandparents, who are getting by on fixed
incomes, have no ability to provide for just that extra for those children to enable them
to have those new clothes —they are not able to do it. They are looking at these other
children and feeling that they are l etting down the kids in their care. They are giving up
so much of their life to care for these children, and they feel as if, somehow, they are
letting them down because they are not able to provide for them in the same way as
children in foster care. There is just something so perverse about that to me.
3 Jun 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 4313
In some cases, these grandparents, or people in our community, are so wonderful that
they are caring for their own children and family and they are caring for foster children.
Their foster children are enti tled to this money, and so there they are in this one
household buying new clothes for these children, and not able to buy those same clothes
for their own kin, in the same house, at the same time. That is a perverse, perverse
thing, and should be rectifie d by this House, and I thank the member Tracey Martin for
bringing this bill to the House to enable us to fix that injustice and inequity and to
enable parity between children in foster care and those being cared for by kin carers.
It is just a very, very sad thing that the Government has said that it will not do it until
2018, despite getting entreaties from those children. I am sure members of the
Government have been getting, as we have, letters with the picture of those children
asking us not to make them wait until 2018.
I do just, before I close, want to touch on some of the process around this and what I
saw happen in this House. I had a Supplementary Order Paper in the Committee stage
of this bill to bring that time forward so that it would be able to happen this year for
those families. I had support from the Labour Party and support, I think, from other
parties within this House. There was the intent for New Zealand First members, Tracey
Martin and her party, also to be able to support that Suppleme ntary Order Paper,
because that was the initial intent of this bill. They wanted to be able to vote for that
Supplementary Order Paper, and while we had that in front of the House, the Minister
came down and sat beside the member and told her that the Gove rnment would
withdraw support for the bill entirely unless they voted against that Supplementary
Order Paper. That degree of pettiness and politics disgusts me, to be honest. To prevent
a member from being able to deliver —or even vote symbolically for the intent of the
bill to show that, actually, this is what she wanted for children and she wanted to be able
to deliver it to them now, as they are requesting —and to be able to bully a party into
voting against their own intent and desire, to me, is a misuse of power, and one that
speaks to the heart of this Government, and it is not a pretty sight.
But I will finish on the positive note that this bill, at least, will deliver parity in 2018,
and it has the hearts and the well -being of children at its centre, and it is at least a great
thing that the House gets the opportunity to put children first at any time in this House,
because it does not happen very often. Sadly, it is still not happening with this
Government, but at least it is in there in the intent of  this bill, and the Green Party is
very happy to support it and recommend it to the House.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: It gives me great pleasure to stand in
support of the third and final reading of the Social Security (Clothing Allowances for
Orphans and Unsupported Children) Amendment Bill. Can I first make a comment on
the previous speaker, Jan Logie. I find it quite extraordinary that every time the
Opposition gets up and bemoans the fact that the Government side is taking due
consideration in terms of its responses to these bills in taking our full calls, only to then
spend the next 10 minutes stepping through, in fa irly woeful tones, the various reasons
why, ultimately, they think they may support the bill, whereas, if perhaps they were
going to stand by their intent, they would sit down after 10 seconds. That would have
certainly pleased some of us on this side and, perhaps, the wider Chamber.
But I will, of course, take my full call because this deserves to have an appropriate
consideration. As I say, it is great to be able to stand here for the third and final time and
speak in support of this bill. It does feel, actually, like I have spoken more than three
times on this bill. There are certain bills that when you speak to them, they sort of go
through—bang, bang, bang—and you feel like you have spoken a couple of times and it
is done, but this is a bill that I fee l like I have spoken more than three times on. Perhaps
4314 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3 Jun 2015
that is true, or perhaps it is just one of those bills that have got through to me and sort of
impacted on me.
It is a fair bill. Kin carers are entitled to assistance to help with the costs of raisin g
orphaned or unsupported children. In 2009, as most of the House would know, National
ensured kin carers got the same weekly amount as foster carers and, of course, now with
this bill, we will match this with the closing of the clothing allowance inequity.
Can I first acknowledge those who do provide care to our most vulnerable. A few
months ago, I spent a little bit of time up in a lovely place called Dargaville. When I
was out there, I met—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Talk about the bill, Todd Muller.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: I will. I met some foster parents, actually, from Dargaville. The
foster parents in Dargaville, although not kin carers, gave me, for perhaps the first time,
a very close understanding of the commitment that it takes to open your family to those
whom you know need help and are vulnerable —and so I think this is something that
perhaps you would like to listen to, on the other side. When you open your heart and
your family to people who are in need of help, and when you actually sit and speak with
this family—I am talking about a husband and wife, who live a number of miles out of
Dargaville. They are involved in a dairy farm. They have got three kids of their own but
they have got two whom they have brought into their family and are providing with
support.
Obviously, I got the opportunity to be able to see firsthand the stress, the impact, the
joy, and the love that that environment does create, particularly for those who are
coming in and having that support, but it also did gi ve me an insight into some of the
challenges that those families are under. Of course, they shared with me about some of
the allowances and support that they received as foster carers, and it did— I will be
honest—give me a sharper and more acute understand ing of those who are involved in
this caring, and the support that is available for them. It also showed the importance of
ensuring that this bill is supported and that the clothing allowance can be provided to
kin carers, because clearly it is currently an omission.
There are a number of kin carers in the community whom I represent in Te Puna. It is
a strongly Māori community. I have had a number of engagements with many, many
families from that area. Often, as is the Māori tradition, there are a number wh o are
providing support for those of their wider whānau who, for various reasons, do not
necessarily have the support of mum or dad, or both. I have seen that in action, and I
have seen the power of it, particularly when it is provided by an uncle or aunti e, or, in
some cases, by grandparents. I am in awe of people who make this commitment for
their whānau and family, and of the impact that they provide on those children’s lives,
and I do want to acknowledge them here tonight.
Of course, we are talking big numbers of New Zealand children who are looked after
by their wider New Zealand family —12,000 New Zealand children. There are 8,600
carers, and half of those carers are grandparents. I want to particularly acknowledge
tonight the grandparents who are looki ng after their grandchildren in this context. As I
have mentioned before in this House as we have traversed this bill’s various readings,
when you are a grandparent you are at a particular stage in life when, arguably, you can
perhaps finally focus on your  own needs, and yet there are many, many families and
grandparents in this country who actually give up their retirement and their needs to be
able to provide support and love and care for their wider whānau.
Look, this is a huge personal sacrifice. You know, I have never met a grandparent
who would not put their hand up for babysitting, but it takes a different type of person
and a different type of commitment to be able to step in and take the role of a parent in a
kin carer context, particularly when you are older in years. Many would want to flop on
3 Jun 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 4315
to the sofa and say: “See you later.” to the grandkids after the visit, but this is a
particular cohort who stay engaged and provide that love and support full -time for their
whānau. The Government acknowledges this effort and, of course, through this bill it is
providing additional support. Through this bill we have heard about and discussed the
Extraordinary Care Fund that is available, which is assisting more than 300 children and
young people, who have benefited. That equates to about $2,000 a child, on average.
What is this money spent on? Extra tuition for kids struggling in school, orthodontic
work that has not been funded by the Ministry of Health, or maybe it is covering costs
for the kids to be able t o attend regional sports tournaments. These are examples of
what this funding has actually been able to support in terms of the family environment.
Maybe it is spent on music lessons for the children who are progressing ahead of their
peers. These are all examples of the Extraordinary Care Fund in action. We are
providing this extra support so that children in this environment can obviously have the
opportunity—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I ask the member to
address the bill for a while now, thank you.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: So—[Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can the member take
his seat. I do not expect to have negative comments about my rulings or positive
comments about my rulings. I think that the member knows that she should not
comment on Speakers’ rulings, and I do not want to hear it again.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. A s discussed through the
select committee process, grandparents, in particular, who are kin carers have the
opportunity to get access to Work and Income support in terms of having a case
manager helping them to navigate their role as kin carers. I think tha t does need to be
acknowledged. There is a particular course that has been put in place to enable kin
carers, particularly grandparents who are now having the opportunity to be able to step
forward and provide this support and who perhaps have not been ful l-time parents for
quite a while, to receive support. This programme costs $600,000 per year and is
facilitated by the parenting course, and I think that is very positive.
In conclusion, I do want to acknowledge Tracey Martin. This is a good bill. It has
wide support across the House, and I think it is important to acknowledge that when
good policy arrives, wherever it comes from, it should be acknowledged and supported.
Clearly, this Government has seen the merits in this bill and is now supporting it, whi ch
is acknowledgment of Tracy Martin’s tenacity and acknowledgment of her particular
passion for this community within our wider country. So she does deserve that
acknowledgment. She has been a fierce advocate for these children and for families that
are i n this position. Although we may not always agree on all aspects of the policy
response and the priorities of that and the sequencing of it, it is important to
acknowledge courage when you see it, good policy when you see it, and good effort
when you see i t. So I acknowledge you, Tracey Martin, and put my support to this bill.
Thank you.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: It is really difficult to even
contemplate not supporting a bill with a title like this bill, the Social Security (Clothing
Allowances for Orphans and Unsupported Children) Amendment Bill. I want to
commend Tracey Martin for putting this bill forward. We will get to the point tonight
where we will allow for another member’s ballot tomorrow and, hopefully, another bill
will be pulled out of the ballot that will be a compassionate bill like this one, where
everyone in the House is forced to—whether they like it or not—support the bill.
The previous speaker, Todd Muller, spoke a bout woeful contributions. I just want to
say that it is disturbing that that member would spend 10 minutes talking about this only
4316 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3 Jun 2015
so that we could avoid having a member’s ballot tomorrow, because of National
members’ fear that we might pull another bill like this one out of the ballot. Let us be
honest, that is where it is at. I am not going to speak for long because it is important that
we get to that process tomorrow, and Tracey Martin and other speakers in the House
have done this bill justice in terms of what they had to say about it.
The only two things I want to touch on are two areas about which I am personally
disappointed—and, I know, the rest of the Labour caucus and, I think, the rest of the
House are also disappointed—in the Government members. They are in respect of,
firstly, the fact that those members voted down Jacinda Ardern’s Supplementary Order
Paper 72, which would have included weekly pocket money and annual birthday and
Christmas allowances, to align all of the allowances for unsupport ed children and
orphans with those provided to foster children under the Children, Young Persons, and
Their Families Act 1989. How mean -spirited of the National members not to support
that Supplementary Order Paper.
The second thing I want to point out is that the Government members also voted
down Jan Logie’s Supplementary Order Paper 70, which would have changed the
commencement date of this bill, bringing it forward from 1 July 2018 to 3 months after
the date on which it receives the Royal assent. Childr en in respect of whom an orphans
benefit or unsupported child’s benefit is paid should not have to wait until 2018 to
potentially benefit from this bill. Again, can I just point out how mean- spirited it is of
the National members not to support that Supplementary Order Paper.
So although it is good that we agree in general on this bill, and that we will all be
supporting this bill in the House, I do need to just point out those two things. How
mean-spirited of the Government members not to support Jacinda A rdern’s
Supplementary Order Paper and Jan Logie’s Supplementary Order Paper. I commend
this bill to the House, and I thank Tracey Martin for putting it forward.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: I find it somewhat ironic that we have just had a
Budget that for the first time in 43 years increases the benefit payments for families that
have children in them, and yet the member opposite, Carmel Sepuloni, calls the
members on this side mean -spirited—I see some irony there that I just could not let
pass—mean-spirited people who would want to put up benefits for people who have got
children! It is bizarre.
I want to talk about this bill, though, because this is an important bill. In doing so, I
particularly want to start off by acknowledging the important role that kin carers play
within New Zealand society. In almost every circumstance, I think it would be fair to
say, when somebody finds themselves being a kin carer, when they are looking after
children who are not their own, they do not do so out of choice. They do so often in
situations where there has been a high level of stress, where there has been perhaps a
death in the family, where there has been for some reason —through abuse or neglect or
otherwise—parents not being available to care for their own children. So these kin
carers, many of them grandparents, find themselves at a stage of life, when they were
planning on doing something completely different from caring for children, having to
once again care for young children. I can only imagine how challenging that would be.
I am fortunate enough now that my youngest child is 17, but on the weekend I had
the privilege of looking after some friends’ younger children. We had a nice afternoon.
It was OK. We went down to the park. We played and kicked a ball around and all that
kind of stuff, but the thought, I have to say, even at my stage of life, in my late 40s, not
necessarily in my 70s or 80s as some of these people find themselves—

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: You’re holding up very well.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: Thank you very much. I—

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: You’re looking well for a man of your age.
