items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: Well, there you go.
I think that at a certain stage of life it is going to be a stressful situation that these
people find themselves in, having to return to looking after small children. So this bill,
in fact, actually seeks to lessen that stress. It seeks to lessen that burden. I want to just,
as I said,  acknowledge those people for the work that they are doing. There are over
6,000 children being raised in New Zealand by their grandparents, and that is pretty
significant. There are another 6,000 - plus children who are being raised by other family
members. It is a pretty difficult situation, as I said.
You see, when the State has custody of a child, everything is taken care of. There are
board payments that are made. There are all sorts of other payments that are made for
the upkeep of those children. But  when there is a payment made under the orphans
benefit or the unsupported child’s benefit, the payment is less.
In a previous part of my life I had a very short stint as a Child, Youth and Family
social worker. It was part of our job to actually assess the position that foster carers
were in, and whether or not it would be appropriate for the State to take a step back in
order for them to take on additional guardianship. What was a little bit disturbing at the
time was that I had a manager who, before he w ould sign off on other payments for
shoes and uniforms and stuff, used to ask us: “Have you asked them this question about
additional guardianship?”, and he used to put a little bit of pressure on us to reduce the
number of children in care because I think it meant that there was less coming off his
budget. But that is by the by. One of the key questions that we needed to address before
a child was moved from being under the full care and custody of the State, and perhaps
then went into an additional guardi an situation, was the type of bond that they had with
the family, whether or not there was any need for additional social work input.
One of the challenging things that I used to find as a social worker in going to those
caregivers and asking them whether or not they would be prepared for the State to take a
step back, and whether they would be prepared to take on additional guardianship of
this child —because on the surface of it it seemed like a very good idea because the
bonds were there, and it seemed l ike it would be the most stable thing for a child, going
forward—was saying to them: “Oh, and, by the way, you won’t be getting as much
money anymore.” It was a challenging thing to actually have to say to someone:
“Thanks. You’ve done a great job. We real ly appreciate the fact that you’ve been
looking after this child. We really appreciate the great investment that you have made in
this child, and we see that you have made such a great bond with this child that you
could now take care of them on your own, but we’re going to pay you less money.” I
have got to say that I used to find that pretty challenging.
This bill actually seeks to bring a level of redress to that, because at the end of the
day the last thing we want is for young people to remain in the c ustody of the State any
longer than they need to. It is important that, as much as possible, young people who
have suffered the trauma of either having their parents sort of taken from them through
death, or who perhaps have had to leave their parents’ car e through abuse or neglect,
can somehow establish as normal a life as possible, to establish the kind of life that I
guess most children in our country get to have. So it is really critical that we do
everything that we can to ensure that these kin carer p lacements stay in place, provide
stability for these young people, and do not begin to fall over through financial hardship
or otherwise. So, as I said, this is exactly what we are trying to do. It is an incredibly
challenging thing for someone to take thi s on, particularly if it is smaller children or
sometimes, I guess, teenagers, depending on where you are at that stage of life. They
each provide their own challenge, of course.
Just in going through this bill and preparing to come and speak tonight, I thought it
was appropriate to go back and have a look at the submissions that were made to the
4318 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3 Jun 2015
Social Services Committee. I obviously was not around when this bill went through the
select committee, so I wanted to just get a bit of a feel for some of the things that
submitters had said. In particular, there was a very substantial submission from the
Grandparents Raising Grandchildren Trust. I just want to commend it because it does
fantastic work in supporting these grandparents who are raising their grandchi ldren. It
does incredible work in terms of providing networks for people in order to provide
support, and I think it is well worth listening to.
If you will bear with me, I just want to read a couple of the things that the trust said.
There were about 9 pa ges of submission, and I am not going to read the whole lot, you
will be pleased to hear, although it would be probably just about as riveting as Mr
Faafoi’s reading out of the entire list of National MPs the other night, but—

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Don’t make me do it again.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: Oh, it would be so much fun if we could just hear that over and
over again! In fact, the thing I liked about that so much, actually, was that if we had
returned the favour to the Labour Party, it would have taken only half as long.
But, anyway, here is what the Grandparents Raising Grandchildren Trust had to say.

items.speaker: It said
items.text: “A number of anomalies exist in our child welfare and social security system
creating inequities between kin/whanau carers and foster ca rers. It is important to
acknowledge these anomalies in the context of discussing this Bill because they
highlight the substantial disparity that exists in the level of financial support available to
the two types of caregivers who undertake the same role as principal caregiver to a child
who cannot be cared for by his or her parents.” I think the trust made a very good point
there.
Also, one of its last points was this: “We challenge the committee” —and I guess,
challenge this House—“to consider this Bill in the light of the anomalies in our system
and consider the question: is it fair in our society for a child being raised by its
grandparent to be denied access to the services and financial support it needs and would
receive if it were in foster care, only because it is being raised by a grandparent?”.
There were a couple of other submitters, and I will not name them, but they made
some really good points too. Briefly, someone said: “My husband and I have been
raising our twin grandchildren since they were  7 weeks old and they are now 9 years
old. We feel that a clothing allowance would be an amazing help as it is a struggle to
keep up with everything.” I will not go into the other one, but I think it is a really
important thing that we are doing here.
Finally, I just want to remind the House that this is in the context of a wider
framework. This is in the context of a Government that is supporting this —it is
obviously a member’s bill, but we are supporting it —in the context of the extra $10
million that has  been set aside through the White Paper for Vulnerable Children, the
extra $10 million set aside to help with kin carers. It is in the context of us wanting to
work harder to address the needs of our vulnerable children in New Zealand. So it is
with great pleasure that we support this bill, because we think it will help those very
children—not for the reasons referred to by the previous speaker. Thank you.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: I rise to take a short call on this bill because I, like
many others on this side of the House, would like to see this bill passed tonight, rather
than waiting for another long drawn- out process to ensue before carers and kin carers
can actually get a little bit of assistance. We support this bill.
I want to pay tribute to Tracey Martin for bringing this bill to the House. It is an
example of an MP who has seen a need from constituents, and where she has actually
decided to address that need. This House i s actually working towards doing something
good for kin carers after all —it is not often it happens —and so, Tracey Martin, I do
appreciate the fact that you have worked really hard to get it here.
3 Jun 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 4319
The reason we support this bill is that we too agree that t he carers of children who
are not their own, orphans, or family members who are not in foster care but are being
cared for by their kin have been discriminated against. This bill will make the difference
of over $1,000 a year. We do have to wonder whether, in the context of the benefit
increases that the Government is trumpeting loud and wide, these people are actually
going to be any better off than what they would have been if they had been able to
access that $25 a week increase. What I do have some conc erns about, and I am still not
clear on, is whether the $25 increase in the benefit allowances that the Government has
introduced in the last Budget will actually go to those people who are caring for these
children—kin carers who are on unsupported child benefits. I am not sure that that is the
case. If these carers are not getting that benefit, this addition of just over a thousand
dollars a year—and it will not be introduced for a couple of years —they will be falling
behind, and they basically will be even with this in place.
I have read through the submissions, and I do have to congratulate the Grandparents
Raising Grandchildren Trust, which certainly raised its voice about it. When I read
through the submissions, some of them were incredibly moving. They talked about the
discrimination and the loss of income that they faced when they moved from being a
foster carer of their grandchild, potentially, or other children, to being a kin carer. As
one person put it, Mr Hunt, “I support the bill because as a  Grandfather raising a
Grandson, he has the same needs and level of support whether he is under CYFS control
or WINZ control … In fact had I been fully aware of the huge inequity in financial
support for my Grandson (from CYFS to WINZ) I would have ‘fought ’ to stay under
CYFS control. I strongly believe my Grandson is better off in ‘family care’ than foster
… yet we are penalised because we are a caring, loving family wanting to look after
their own!”.
If we accept that in the State support sector it is better for children to be raised by
whānau, family, and grandparents than it is to be wards of the State and raised by
strangers or in institutions, God forbid, if we accept that it is better for them to be
looked after by their own kin, then we should be acknowledging that, and not exploiting
those family members because we can. We have seen this time and time again in this
House. We have seen it with the way this Government has treated family carers of adult
children with disabilities, and the enormous lengt hs this Government has gone to to
prevent those family carers of adults with disabilities from getting any type of top -up in
their support, any type of equity.
Although this is a very small improvement, and it is an improvement that does not
kick in for 2 years—and we acknowledge that that was a deal that Tracey Martin had to
do to get this into place—we will be supporting this bill. We think it is a good thing that
she has brought to the House, and we commend it.

items.speaker: JENNY SALESA
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call on
this bill. This bill is really close to my heart because I see so many of these families in
my electorate office. Can you imagine four children who grow up in a  loving family
with both parents? The father is the only breadwinner in the house. This father passes
away suddenly. These kids are all under the age of 5. Their mother, unfortunately, also
passes away, due to a car accident. However, this bill is a great bill because what it will
do is it will address the parity issue that these four children currently face. These four
children who are looked after by whānau right now cannot have access to the clothing
allowance that other foster children have access to. This is just not fair.
Here in New Zealand there are so many grandparents who raise their grandchildren.
A lot of these grandparents go to court to fight for the right to look after these
grandchildren. Some of these grandchildren suffer abuse and trauma, which is one of
the reasons why these grandparents go to court to fight to look after them. What these
4320 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3 Jun 2015
grandparents are actually asking for, all that these grandparents are asking for, is parity
with foster parents. These grandparents just want to be treat ed in the same fair way as
foster parents.
What this legislation will do—and I would like to commend and thank Tracey Martin
for bringing this bill to the House —is ease the financial burden that these families face
in raising these unsupported and orphane d children. What would have been a really
good and caring thing for this Government to do is implement this bill this year, in
2015, instead of in 3 years’ time in July 2018. Instead of, say, wasting Government
taxes of $26 million on a flag referendum, this would have been a better and more
caring way of supporting our children, our really vulnerable children. The Labour Party
strongly supports this bill, and thank you so much.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: It is a pleasure to speak on the Social
Security (Clothing Allowances for Orphans and Unsupported Children) Amendment
Bill. Often I think members read out the name of the bill, the longer the better, to take
up a bit of time, but I am not doing that tonight. It is a pleasure and I would like to pay
due homage to Tracey Martin for bringing this bill forward. I note in the speech that she
led off the third reading by saying that it was not her bill, it was Diane Vivian’s bill, and
she paid a lot of credit to her.
I take on board what she was saying and I know the point that she was trying to
make, but one of the responsibilities that comes with being a member of Parliament is
passing legislation, and this is the only way that it can be done. So I know what you are
saying, but actually it is your bill. It is your name that is going to be on it, Tracey, and it
is quite an achievement to get it this far. As has been alluded to, you had to do a deal,
but that is politics. Politics is the art of the possible, so well done for doing that.
I also think there is quite a bit of irony tonight as it was only last week in the Budget
debate we were given a hard time for not speaking for long enough; now we are being
given a hard time for speaking for too long. I think it is a bit of an odd thing, but that is
politics. I guess being in Opposition is about opposing, so that is fair enough, I guess.
I was not on the Social Services Committee, which considered this bill, because,
obviously, the bill was considered prior to the election, but it seems like a pretty good
result that has come through from this committee. I think, as has been said by Jenny
Salesa, the previous speaker, that it is a pretty tough sort of a thing to have to deal with.
I know that those families in that situation have got enough to deal with without having
to worry about money, but this is what this bill seeks to address.
Under section 363 of the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act 1989, the
chief executive is responsible for the administration and has the discretion to determine
rates of payment for foster children. At present that discretion has been used to
determine a rate for clothing allowances for which orphans and unsupported children
are not eligible, so this bill seeks to address that. This bill seeks to insert new section
29B into the Social Security Act 1964 to establish a clothing allowance for children
whose caregivers receive an orphans benefit or an unsupported child’s benefit, and that
will allow this mecha nism to work. In the interim the Government, as part of the
Children’s Action Plan, has committed an extra $10 million to provide further support
for kin carers, and a ministerial reference group was set up to organise the funding and
how that might be applied.
An unsupported child’s benefit is available only when a family breaks down, as was
mentioned in other cases, but the orphans benefit applies when the children’s parents
have died or cannot be found. Either of those situations is very traumatic for the fami ly
as a whole, certainly for the children, and when kin carers step in to deal with this, they
have enough to deal with without having to deal with the knowledge that they are not
3 Jun 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 4321
actually getting the same amount of money that they would if they were looki ng after a
child who was not related to them. As I said, this bill seeks to address that.
I think one of the major things we need to realise is that under the current rules there
is no income test or asset test for the people receiving these benefits. The y can receive
another benefit at the same time, which obviously makes sense —they are going to have
extra costs. The child automatically qualifies for a community services card, which is a
great financial benefit for them. We have to recognise, as one of my  colleagues said
earlier, that there are more than 12,000 children in New Zealand who are being looked
after by kin carers. That is a heck of a lot of children when you think about it.
It must be pretty traumatic for those families, but it is not that man y generations ago
that families were involved as a matter of course with the wider family in bringing up
children. I know that in the Pacific Island community, in particular, in my electorate this
is quite common today. It is not, generally, in the Pākehā community, but if we go back
only a few generations that was the case. I think we have lost something today when we
no longer have that close connection with grandparents in that way, because there is so
much you can learn from previous generations. Lots of things were passed down
through the families, as in fact is the way with Māori and Pasifika. That is in fact how
their whakapapa was passed down. I think that is an interesting thing, and I hope it
keeps up, as it is going through a renaissance at the moment.
Of course, for grandparents who are bringing up children today, the gap between the
age of a grandparent and a grandchild is much greater than it was all those generations
ago when families were involved. Couples are now choosing to have their famil ies later
in life than they were before—whereas they would quite often be in their early 20s, they
are now in their mid -30s, often, and late-30s. So that gap, for the grandparents, is much
greater. In addition to that, of course, technology has come into play today, and a whole
lot of things have moved on. I am sure most people and members in the House are
involved with social media in one form or another, as I certainly am —and I see that my
colleagues are busy indulging in it at the moment. I have teenage children and they are
light years ahead of me in the way they utilise social media.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: That’s not—it’s rubbish.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: Yes, but it is true.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Can the member at least
attempt to relate that to the bill.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: I am, Mr Assistant Speaker. There is a refresher course offered
to grandparents and kin carers who are returning to the front line of parenting, and it is
absolutely a part of that. It is a very important part, I believe.
More than 300 children have benefited from the first round of the Extraordinary Care
Fund grants that were put up, and this is going back to the select committee decision,
which I will come to in a moment. The grants were available for up to $2,000 per child.
That covers extra tutoring for kids struggling at school, orthodontic work that is not
funded by the Ministry of Health, the costs of attending national and regional sports
tournaments, and music lessons where a child is progressing ahead of their peers. I think
when a child is in a situation where they are being brought up by their grandparent or
kin carer and they have a talent or they need some extra help with their tutoring or with
orthodontic work, it is only right that they should have the funding to cover that. I think
that is fantastic.
There has been a lot of talk about the 2018 implementation date, but I note that the
select committee decided that the existing measures  that are in place, which I have just
spoken about, along with changes proposed to the bill, which have been accepted,
would sufficiently address the issue of parity. The school and year start -up payment for
4322 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3 Jun 2015
carers is a new policy initiative and its fundin g is expected to fall back within baseline
levels by 2018.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! For the last minute I
am going to challenge the member to not just read out the select committee repor t.
Thank you.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: I am not reading out the report.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Word for word.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: OK. The select committee made a decision to put the
implementation date out to 2018, and I think that if we do not do that, we are going to
fix one inequity by creating another. I think it makes perfect sense to delay the start
until 2018. They will not be any worse off, although it will be under a different payment
format. Therefore, it is with great pleasure that I commend the bill to the House. Thank
you.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Firstly, I would like to
acknowledge the work that Tracey Martin has done on behalf of grandparents
everywhere and other kin carers. Thank you very much for that work. I am not going to
take too long, because I do not want to stand between you and the passing of this bill.
I do want to acknowledge another person who spoke during the first reading of this
bill, Dr Rajen Prasad, a colleague of mine who is not in the House any longer. He is a
social worker extraordinaire, a man who knew about the care of chi ldren, and someone
who was very passionate about this bill. He would be very happy to know that it is
passing this evening.
This bill is about the equitability of access to allowances for kin carers of children, to
bring them in line with the allowances f or foster children. We traversed the complexity
of family issues over the course of this bill, but before we had Whānau Ora we had
Puao-te-Ata-tu, which really was the genesis of the work that went to support the
original idea of kin carers, some 20 -odd ye ars ago —perhaps more than that. I was
talking with a colleague today; we were trying to figure out when that happened, but it
was some 20 years ago. It has become, really, what we would know as Whānau Ora
today. Puao-te-Ata-tu talked about developing processes for families to take the primary
role of care of their children when the parents were unable to do so, when it became
impossible for parents to continue with that care. Today what we are going to do is pass
this legislation, which will allow for those  kin carers to have the same rights to
allowances that other foster carers have.
The only small but important blight on this is the commencement date. It is a shame
that these children will not have access to these allowances before 2018. It has been
well traversed throughout the House. It is the only thing wrong; it is otherwise a really
fantastic bill. On that note, my commendations to Tracey Martin; I commend the bill to
the House.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Mana Whakawā. Just to advise
you, Mr Assistant Speaker, that this is a split call with my colleague, and may I request
a bell at 4 minutes?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: You will have a bell at 4
minutes.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Assistant Speaker. That is very
kind of you. I am not on the Social Services Committee at Parliament, but I specifically
asked whether I might take a call on this bill, and our very gracious whip granted me
that privilege, because of a personal interest that I have in this particular subject. I want
to begin, before getting on to that, by congratulating the member Tracey Martin. She is
a member whom I hav e enormous respect for, and she has brought a matter before the
House that is of great significance to the 12,000 or so families who have a situation of
3 Jun 2015 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 4323
kin carers caring for family members. We have heard from colleagues that 6,000 or so
of those particular families are grandparents caring for their own grandchildren, and my
family fits into that particular situation. My parents, relatively late in their lives, when
they thought they had got beyond caring for children, once we had grown up and left
home, found themselves in a situation where my little brother ended up having an
accidental pregnancy situation with his girlfriend, and they stepped up and took
responsibility for that when my brother was not able to.
So I have got a beautiful niece, who is now nearly an adult herself, who has
succeeded in life and had the best possible opportunities because she was fortunate
enough to have had grandparents who could step in when her parents were not able to
take the sort of responsibility that is needed for a child. So can I congratulate the
member Tracey Martin on bringing this measure forward, because it is something that
we on this side of the House do agree with. We agree with the intent, and I am very
grateful to the member for the constructive way she has w orked with Government
Ministers to actually enable this bill to be implemented.
In terms of the implementation date, we have heard some rather spurious arguments
from some that we are somehow trying to hold this up. Whether this bill is passed
today, tomorrow, in a week, or in a month, it actually takes effect on 1 July 2018, and
that is to ensure parity and alignment with other measures, including school and year
start-up payments that may no longer be available at that stage. So well done, Tracey
Martin, for taking the initiative and bringing this before us. In relation to the $10 million
capped fund that we introduced via the White Paper for Vulnerable Children measures,
we believe that these changes are able to be made within a fiscally responsible cap. That
is on top of all the other support that this Government is providing to vulnerable
children, including the $790 million extra benefit payments to those children who are
the very most vulnerable.
But something of particular relevance to grandparents that I would point to is the
significant increases in superannuation that have been available to them over this term
of the Government. In fact, since 2008 we have had more than a 30 percent increase in
the rate of national superannuation, and just this we ek there will be an $11 per week
increase in national superannuation for married couples and a $7.59 increase for
individuals. There has been, over the course of this Government, a 30 percent increase,
which is way in advance of the 15 percent increase in the cost of living over the same
time.
This bill is one measure that actually adds to some of those other measures that we
on this side of the House have been working on. It brings parity for kin carers, in
particular grandparents—I am delighted about tha t—and it does address some of those
issues that children face when they already have the stigma attached of being an orphan.
I, and many members of this House, I am sure, do not attach a stigma to being an
orphan. It is something beyond the control of any child, whether their parents have
passed away or have been imprisoned or simply have not been able to take the
responsibility to care for their children as the vast majority of parents in New Zealand
do. There are additional stigmas that can be attached: f or instance, if they have been
brought up by grandparents who do not have the financial means to give them the
fashionable clothes or the treats in their lunchbox that the other kids have at school, or
to allow them to go on the music or sports trips, and to play the part that we want all
young New Zealanders to play —to grow up to be strong, productive, and contributing
citizens to our great country. For these reasons, I think this is an excellent bill. Tracey
Martin is to be congratulated once again, and I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: BRETT HUDSON
items.text: It is a delight to stand and speak in this third reading
of the bill. As a first- term MP, I would just like to note that I am beginning to
4324 Social Security (Clothing Allowances etc.) Amdt Bill 3 Jun 2015
experience some of the interesting and almost labyrinthine -type parts of the legislative
process, but, within that, also seeing the opportunity that affords itself through that
process for parties that might start off with differing positions to find some common
ground and some means to meet through a consultative process and through
compromise. I would just like to congratulate Tracey Martin, as colleagues across the
House have done, on her deep commitment to people in need and particularly to the
children whose needs this bill will address. I also congratulate her on her perseverance
in working constructively to find some common ground that can be built upon to lead to
a solution that will see a very, very practical bill come into effect soon, one that will
bring real assistance to those kin caring environments that are dealing with children in
need, and one that has leveraged the ability that the select committee process
particularly affords to make some headway and reach some common ground.
In reviewing the Social Services Committee’s recommendations, and hearing
colleagues talk about that process, what I saw was an ability to reach across a divide and
reach convergence. We on the Government side looked at the $10 million that had been
earmarked through the W hite Paper for Vulnerable Children and looked at how we
could apply that to the very real and positive changes that Mrs Martin was looking to
achieve with her member’s bill. Instead of taking a position of complete confrontation
or opposition, we were both able to come together and say: “Well, how about we take
the fund that we have earmarked and set it to the purpose that you have set out? In
doing that, as we work through that, we will work together at an even more targeted and
more effective regime, but we will be able to put into effect the intent, at least, Mrs
Martin, of what it is that you had in mind.”
So we reach this point. We have this bill —this bill that will see the discretionary
ability of the chief executive to make a ruling on clothing allowa nces for orphans and
unsupported children extend to that situation we are talking about of kin carers, and one
common example of that, as we have heard from both sides of the House, is
grandparents. So it is with great pleasure that I rise in support of the third reading of this
bill.
One of the members on this side raised a point about the assistance that the
Government had brought in through the Extraordinary Care Fund. I do note that it is
true that that fund was helping in making the job of grandparent s and extended family
members who were raising children easier. It was working in the areas of tutoring,
orthodontics, and in music lessons, but it is very true, as Mrs Martin pointed out with
her member’s bill, that it was, in fact, missing some areas. Ch ildren in situations other
than being cared for by kin carers were, in fact, receiving some assistance through the
State in the area of clothing allowances, in a discretionary move that the chief executive
had made. And although we had this Extraordinary Care Fund in place, and it was doing
a lot of good, it still was not necessarily covering every situation of assistance that other
children in need were receiving. So it is an extraordinarily positive move to ensure that
there is a real parity across the different sorts of caring arrangements.
I would note that in the election campaign this Government did make the point that
we wanted to open discussions around the whole range of caring for children and the
different models of care, for instance in parental  care for young children and in paid
parental care for young children in environments where it may not be either of the
biological parents who could be caring for that child—those parents could be back at
work. This reaching of consensus and agreement in t his area is, in fact, an example of
taking that thinking and putting it into implementation. So I am absolutely delighted
that I can stand as a first-term MP in an example of a situation where we have been able
to reach across the House and reach a point of agreement, and I commend this bill to the
House.
Bill read a third time.
3 Jun 2015 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 4325
First Reading
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour —West Coast -  Tasman): I move, That the
Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Transport
and Industrial Relations C ommittee to consider the bill. Like so many members’ bills,
this one has been some time in gestation. It was a bill I introduced after the Royal
Commission on the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy, which had recommended that an
“effective regulatory framework f or underground coal mining should be established
urgently.” The royal commission identified through its hearings the fact that
Queensland and New South Wales have, arguably, the best practice in this area.
Effectively, what I did was take those Queensland mine regulations, and what this bill
will do is implement them immediately into New Zealand to protect the lives of miners
working underground.
I am sure that we will hear from the Government the excuse that much has happened
in that time, and I acknowledge that, and that there is no need for this bill. If I can take
us back through a pathway, in 1994 I was given a lecture on underground mining by
Bill Brazil, who was a former mines inspector. He told me that the change in the
legislation in 1992 by the Na tional Government would be rued by this country, and that
we would be shamed by the consequences of deregulation of mining regulations that
had been established through over a century of experience. How right he was.
It took some time. In fact, it was in the early 2000s before we started to see some
major faults in the practice of underground mining. The theory had been that the
Occupational Safety and Health Service would deal with the safety and the challenges
and the risks of underground mining, and tha t, in fact, a code of practice would be
established and would be passed and would protect miners. That code of practice was
never, ever properly implemented and, indeed, the question is whether it has been
implemented today—but I will come back to that iss ue. The inevitable catastrophe and
loss of life because of an unregulated mining environment cost the lives of 29 men at
Pike River, and some others before. In fact, I wrote a letter to the Minister of Labour
just some months before Pike River, raising issues that had been brought to my attention
about lax practices in underground mining, but I was given by the Minister —who had
got it from her officials, no doubt—a reassurance that all was well.
This bill is my best attempt to try to protect the lives of u nderground miners. It was
the best thing I could do, because we had let our experience and that of international
miners drift into the naivety of deregulation and market forces to protect the miners at
work. This bill takes Queensland regulations, which ar e not perfect —in fact, of Pike
River some have said that Australians designed the mine, Australians ran the mine, and
Australians were, in part, a big, major cause of its disaster—but Queensland regulations,
not implemented in New Zealand, would have protected those men.
The Government did move forward and pass legislation. In fact, the original bill it
brought in was split into three parts. One was to set up WorkSafe, which has happened.
The second was, of course, to ensure that Mines Rescue had the right  authority to do its
job properly. And the third was the Health and Safety in Employment Amendment Act,
“Pike River” having been dropped from the title. That was passed in 2013, and a key
component in amended section 20A of the Health and Safety in Employm ent Act is
subsection (1), which states: “A code of practice, an amendment to a code of practice, or
a revocation of a code of practice has no force or effect until it has been approved by the
Minister.” I rang today to see whether that code of practice has been implemented, and
no one could give me reassurance that it has.
4326 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 3 Jun 2015
We have had the establishment of a High Hazards Unit. We have had progress. In
fact, we have had mines shut down until we could be sure that a safer regime was being
carried out. Although people point the finger at Pike River, the reality is that Solid
Energy, the Government’s own miner, had such lax practices that for 6 months its mine
was closed down post Pike River. Not one tonne of coal came out, because it, too, was
overseeing a dangerous mining situation. We cannot take anything for granted.
What I ask of the Government is that it supports this legislation going to the select
committee. It may say it has done all it can. What I say is that I want to check, and this
Parliament must check, that the legislation is being implemented as intended, that the
codes of practice as identified have been implemented and are up to standard, and that
everything we can possibly do to make underground mining safe has been done. So I
ask of the Government: can it support this bill and send it to the select committee, where
a group of MPs from all parties can come along and we can hear submissions from
people who are responsible in the mining area, to give us that reassurance?
We need to know that the  High Hazards Unit set up by the Government has the
proper resourcing to do the job. The reality, and one of the contributing factors to the
Pike River mine disaster, was that the Department of Labour was under -resourced. We
need an assurance that Mines Rescue, through the passage of this legislation, has the
right authority to act in the best way, should we ever have to face such a terrible
situation again.
The legislation passed by the Government oversees safety in quarries. This year,
within a 1-month period, we had two deaths in quarries in this country. That says to us
that we still do not have things right. We need to know that the people in positions of
authority and the people with responsibility have not only the qualifications but the
experience to oversee proper and safe workplace practices.
There are unresolved issues. Twenty -nine men still lie in the bowels of the Pike
River mine. Their families have been asked to move —some say, to move on. I would
never ask them to move on. If you look through history, if you look at all cultures, one
of the things we are most committed to, most passionate about, is trying to identify our
loved ones whenever they are lost to us in any way. That is the driver for those 29
families, and I would never ask them to move on. No one has been held to account. Last
week in the High Court two family members were asking the court to review the
decision by the Government agency that it would not proceed with the prosecution
against the mine manager. Indeed, the royal commis sion report, and all the reports,
identify clear faults in decision making at that mine. It is not for me to judge, but it is
for me to say that those families have a right to ask the questions in a court of law. Mr
Dave Feickert, a staunch advocate for mi ne safety, made a submission to the royal
commission. The family of Mr Feickert, who, unfortunately, has now passed away,
wants his submission to be made public. That has been blocked.
Those are but three unresolved issues that I think need to be resolved. I ask the
Government to support this bill going to the select committee to allow Parliament to
review the progress or otherwise that it has made, to question whether there is still a
need for more improvement in the area of mine safety and work safety in this country,
and to ensure that everything that we can do as parliamentarians to prevent another mine
disaster in this country has been done. We do not want one unnecessary death in mining
or in quarrying or, indeed, in any workplace in New Zealand. We s hould not rest until
we are assured that, through legislation, through the oversight of regulation, and through
our commitment to the parliamentary process, we have done everything we can to
ensure that men and women, when they go to work, can return home to their loved ones
and to their families. This is what the families want most from that terrible disaster: to
ensure that others do not have to suffer as they still suffer. I ask the Government to
3 Jun 2015 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 4327
support this legislation going through to the select commi ttee so that we can review the
progress or otherwise that we have made in this House since the Pike River mine
disaster.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I just want to acknowledge the
member from West Coast -  Tasman, Damien O’Connor, and the support that he has
offered his community during this very difficult time over this last number of years.
Acknowledging the tragic loss and the gaps in the health and safety regime has be en
something that this Government and, I am sure, all New Zealanders have done with
utter sincerity, in respect of those who lost their lives and also in respect of those
families, of course, who lost their loved ones. Mr O’Connor said in his opening remar ks
that in the early 2000s “they” —I assume he means the Government, or the industry, no
doubt—began to see the failings in the health and safety regime in underground mining.
I guess our response to that statement is that at that particular point in time his party was
in Government. We would look not for retrospective criticism but for proactive action
when people see those issues. Also, one other point is that legislation is not necessarily
the process to do the checks. I understand what the member is sayi ng. The annual
review of, perhaps, WorkSafe New Zealand —maybe he can sub on next time that
happens—is the time, I think, when accounts can be asked for regarding the
implementation of legislation that is being put in place to make our workplaces safer.
We understand, of course, that on that tragic day, 19 November 2010, 31 miners and
contractors were present in the mine. Two miners managed to walk from the mine and
went to hospital with moderate injuries. They were released from Grey Base Hospital in
Greymouth the next day. But the remaining 16 miners and 13 contractors, sadly, lost
their lives. Immediately following that event, days later in November 2010, the Prime
Minister ordered a royal commission of inquiry led by Justice Graham Panckhurst.
While Ju stice Panckhurst was performing this royal commission of inquiry, the
Government also commissioned a review of health and safety practices in New Zealand.
From that we have this report, The Report of the Independent Taskforce on Workplace

items.speaker: Health and Safety
items.text: He Korowai Whakaruruhau, which I have no doubt you are familiar
with. That group was chaired by Rob Jager, chairman of the Shell company here in New
Zealand. It is an industry that is very, very familiar with hazardous situations. Shell is a
company that prides itself on having international best practice in that particular field,
and he was the right man for the job.
Though initially the royal commission report was due to come back in March 2012,
obviously we know it was a very extensive commission of i nquiry, and it finally came
back on 3 October 2012, when Justice Panckhurst reported to the Attorney -General, the
Hon Chris Finlayson. Not long after that, that report was made public —people
obviously scrutinised it, and on 5 November it was made public. T he royal commission,
as the honourable member has said, came up with 16 recommendations, the second of
which was this —it is in the bill that the member has presented to the House —“An
effective regulatory framework for underground coal mining should be esta blished
urgently.”
The commission did refer to Queensland and New South Wales framework examples
as demonstrating international best practice. One of the commissioners on the royal
commission was Stewart Bell, who was the Queensland state Commissioner for  Mine
Safety and Health. And so it was important to bring that expertise over to New Zealand
at that time, as we underwent this commission of inquiry to look at the factors that led
up to this tragedy that happened at Pike River.
On 12 December 2012 the Government released its plan to implement all 16 of those
recommendations, and, as I said before, on April 2013, 4 months later, this report, The
Report of the Independent Taskforce on Workplace Health and Safety: He Korowai
4328 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 3 Jun 2015
Whakaruruhau, came out. One of t he things, I think, that this report states is that New
Zealand’s culture in workplace health and safety was very lacking. If we look at
international figures—for example, for 100,000 of population—in the United Kingdom,
one worker per 100,000 a year would lose their lives in the workplace. Here in New
Zealand, for that same 100,000 population, we would lose four in the workplace. So,
obviously, we know there is something that is happening in New Zealand that needs
addressing, and it is attitudes, it is culture, and it is practices and behaviour. I believe
that as we in this House, in due course, look at the Health and Safety Reform Bill, we
will be able to address some of those issues, which will make New Zealand a safer place
for people to work in and, cer tainly, to come home from their day of work and enjoy
their families and their homes in.
After this report, which came out in April 2013, and also after the royal commission
and the Government’s response to that came out, a month later in May 2013 we saw two
significant reports. They came from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment. One is this report I am holding—it is Safe mines: safe workers . It is the
discussion document summary. Its subtitle is Implementing recommendations of the
Royal Commission on the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy . Some of the sections are:
“Have your say”—not your say, Mr Assistant Speaker, but the people’s say —“We’re
seeking your feedback”, “A new regulatory approach”, “Training and qualifications”,
“Worker participation”, and “Emergency management”. So we see from the Pike River
royal commission, from the independent task force, that some very, I guess, forensic
work has been done into workplace activities and behaviours.
Then 4 months later came the response to the submissions —this document from the
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment that I am  holding, Safe mines: safe
workers—Response to Submissions . It reported that the ministry “received 113
submissions by the 1 July 2013 deadline”: “55 from quarry operators … 21 from mine
operators … seven from individual mine workers, six from mining contr actors, two
from unions, four from employer or industry organisations, five from mining
associations, two from quarrying associations, and two from tunnelling associations,
and nine from other industries, interested parties, and the public.” So we see that  the
Government has canvassed broadly and widely and has had some significant response
in terms of what we should do regarding health and safety, particularly for mining.
The member’s bill was presented to the House 1 month later: the Underground Coal
Mining Safety Bill, under the name of Damien O’Connor. As he said, for some time, no
doubt, the bill had been in the ballot waiting to be drawn. We do understand his intent
and his response to what happened in his part of the country, and so we do just
acknowledge that.
I am sorry, Mr Assistant Speaker, if you think I am looking at notes, but I am just
reading out a chronology here that I think is important for the record. Then in December
2013 the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment released a further
document. Here it is—I am holding it here. It is Safe mines: safe workers—New laws on
mining health and safety: A quick guide for mine operators . But what the ministry says
in this is not to just rely on the guide but to go and read the legislation. I think what it is
addressing is the fact that people do not delve deeply enough into the issues around
health and safety. What it states here in the introduction—it says: “The Government has
recently made changes to the laws concerning health and safety i n the mining industry.
This is in response”, obviously, “to the … Royal Commission” and the tragedy that
obviously happened in Pike River and to the families there. It says: “The new legal
requirements have been developed with help from an expert reference  group of mining,
health and safety and regulatory experts from New Zealand and abroad. The
Government has also worked closely with people in the industry”.
3 Jun 2015 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 4329
As I conclude, what I want to say is that the Government does care, immensely,
about the safety of  miners and workers and contractors, and we have demonstrated that
by passing sound legislation—

India—Minister of State and Goodwill Delegation to New Zealand 
Mr SPEAKER: I am sure that members would wish to welcome Mr Rajiv Pratap 
Rudy of the Lok Sabha, Minister of State in the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, and 
members of the In dian goodwill delegation to New Zealand, who are present in the 
gallery. [Applause] 
ORAL QUESTIONS 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Free-trade Agreements—Saudi Arabia Negotiations and Al-Khalaf Group 
1. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: When 
he said that part of the reason for paying $4 million of taxpayer money to a Saudi 
business was “wanting to resolve the issues that were holding back the Gulf States free -
trade agreement”; what were those issues and why did he think paying Hamood Al Ali 
Al Khalaf’s company $4 million would help resolve them? 
Mr SPEAKER: In calling the Prime Minister, my office has been advised that the 
answer will be longer than normal. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): I stand by my full statement, which was that 
there was a range of different issues, including the potential exposure to a legal claim, 
wanting to resolve the issues that were holding back the Gulf Stat es free -trade 
agreement, the fact that we thought we could promote New Zealand in an international 
environment, and that we thought it was the right thing to do. In respect of what the 
issues were, it has been well canvassed in this House that New Zealand’ s relationship 
with Saudi Arabia had been damaged by the events relating to Mr Al Khalaf’s business. 
Minister McCully took steps to resolve that issue, and those steps included a contract 
for service between the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade and Mr  Al Khalaf’s 
company. The $4 million relate to costs associated with shifting operations that were 
previously based in New Zealand to a new hub in Saudi Arabia. The Cabinet was 
satisfied that the full partnership outlined in the Cabinet paper resolved full y the 
prospect of any litigation.  
Andrew Little: Given his answer yesterday that part of the $4 million payment was 
to settle a potential legal claim, why did he admit on Breakfast  TV today that the threat 
of legal action was withdrawn a year before the Cabinet paper was ever written? Is it his 
Cabinet’s normal practice to settle legal claims that have already been withdrawn? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I think the point that I was making this morning—it is not new 
information—is that people do set aside, on the basis of negotiation, legal claims that 
they might want to take. The second point I would make is that these issues are issues 
that have actually been dealt with by successive Governments. I would take this 
opportunity to encourage the member to speak to Annette King and Phil Goff about the 
warnings that they received on these issues when they were in Government and about 
the actions that they were looking to take. He might be amazingly surprised to hear the 
answers.  
Andrew Little: Is he aware that on 14 May Murray McCully stated that he was 
unaware of any threatened domestic legal action by Mr Al Khalaf? 
4246 Oral Questions 3 Jun 2015

question to the Minister for Primary Industries regarding the number of possums that

poison. It turns out that over the last 9 years or so, TBfree has autopsied something like 
124,213 possums and of those 54 were found to have TB. So that is 54 possums out of 
more than 124,000, which works out at a touch over 0.04 percent.  
David Bennett: Ha, ha! What’s the percentage?  
RICHARD PROSSER: Four one-hundredths of 1 percent of the possum population. 
David Bennett: Oh, good on you. 
RICHARD PROSSER: Mr Bennett, be quiet, the adults are talking. From that 
number we are invited to believe that the humble possum is putting our dairy and deer 
industries in some kind of deadly peril.  
So I got to wondering whether in fact any of the other justifications that are given for 
the continued use of 1080 poison are actually capable of holding water —and holding 
water is a very valid argument, because next month Auckland Council is planning to 
drop 1080 poison, 50,000 kilograms of it, about 50 tonnes of 1080 poison baits, over the 
Hunua Ranges, in what is explained as an attempt to target possums and rats not for the 
purpose of eradicating TB but because the rats and possums are blamed, according to 
Auckland Council’s website, for harming native plants and animal life and their 
habitats. Maybe they are. Possums eat plants —this we know. Possums live in the bush 
and they eat the bush, and one could be forgiven for asking how after 150 years of 
possums eating the bush we still have bush. The Hunua Ranges are covered in lots of 
nice green lush bush and that is the way we want them to stay. The possums do eat the 
bush, so we kill the possums, and that is the way everybody likes it.  
But how much of this is actually based on reliable data? I ask because if the farming 
sector and TBfree New Zealand and the Animal Health Board can justify carpet 
bombing thousands of hectares of New Zealand with 1080 in order to wipe out a 
problem that is present in just 0.04 percent of possums, how can we be s ure that 
Auckland Council has good data to back up using 1080 over what just happens to be its 
single largest and most important drinking water catchment? It is targeting rats as well, 
of course, and rats do eat native birds, and we need to do something about that. But do 
we need to do it by dropping tonnes and tonnes of deadly poison over the most 
important water catchment of our biggest city?  
We know there are better ways. There are better ways, and we know that because all 
the initial survey work that i s done to ascertain what the pest populations are and what 
the native bird populations are, before a poison drop and after it, are done on the 
ground. It is all groundwork. It is all trapping, which is used to establish what those 
numbers are beforehand and then again afterwards, to see how successful the drop has 
been. So it can be done, and it can be done even in the rough country, in the steep 
country. This is important because quite a lot of the ground in the Hunuas is rough and 
steep. It is just this s ort of country where, if something is going to go wrong it will go 
wrong there. In steep country there is no way of guaranteeing that poison pellets are not 
going to bounce and slide and end up in places where they are not meant to be, like in 
the reservoirs and in the creeks that run into the reservoirs.

Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green) : At question time today, just a moment ago, I 
asked the Acting Attorney -General whether the terms of reference of our intelligence 
review would be amended to reflect the views of other legislatures that are moving to 
protect civil liberties. This included the US Congress, which yesterday passed the USA 
Freedom Act to end the mass collection of metadata. Minister Adams was not especially 
forthcoming in her reply. She stressed the  adequacy of the terms of reference and then 
confessed that she basically lacked the ministerial competence to comment further on 
the question, the question having been passed on to her by the Prime Minister. So let us 
analyse the issues that were passed o ver so lightly by the Acting Attorney -General. The 
terms of reference contained two general tasks. The first is to determine whether the 
legislative frameworks of the intelligence agencies are well placed to protect New 
Zealand’s national security arrangem ents while protecting human rights. The second is 
3 Jun 2015  General Debate 4267 
 
around whether there are sufficient safeguards to ensure the agencies act lawfully and 
maintain public confidence.  
Well, if we are talking about public confidence, it is time that New Zealand emulated 
the United States in restoring the principles of civil liberties laid down by Jefferson and 
cherished in the United States and, presumably, here as well. There is a distinction 
between the general review requirement that is in the statute and the precise terms  of 
reference that the Attorney -General has crafted. The statute foresees a review of any 
matter relevant to the functions of effectiveness and efficiency of the agencies in their 
contribution to national security. But the terms of reference are more focus ed. They are 
on whether the legislative frameworks are well placed to protect national security while 
protecting human rights. It may be a coincidence, and it is good to have human rights 
included, but what we have here is national security as the primary value and central 
framework, with human rights as a secondary value, something to be protected from the 
onslaught.  
A specific task identified in the terms of reference is whether the recent foreign 
terrorist fighters legislation should be extended or modified beyond March 2017. This is 
an issue of some moment. Just last Friday the Security Council adopted its latest 
presidential statement on foreign terrorist fighters. The overriding concern is that 
foreign terrorist fighters have increased in numbers to 25,000 from 100 countries. 
Receiving one back into one’s own country is proving too dyspeptic for Australia, but 
New Zealand, at least, is maintaining for the moment a level head on the matter. The 
Attorney-General’s statement to the council had many good elements—in particular, the 
stress he placed on countering violent extremism through supporting individuals in 
communities in having a positive stake in society. The key, he said, is to be inclusive, 
not exclusive—to integrate, not marginalise. We agree and  commend him for this. But 
that approach needs to be buttressed with legislative reform on mass surveillance. It 
needs to lead with the principle of human rights and make national security compatible 
with the inalienable rights of the individual.  
That Jeffersonian principle has just been rediscovered in the United States in the past 
few days, following the loss of its constitutional compass 14 years ago. Sanity at last is 
being restored. The USA Freedom Act, replacing the notorious Patriot Act, limits the 
Federal Government’s ability to collect phone data. It requires the FBI to formally 
declare a statement of facts showing reasonable grounds to believe that the information 
sought is relevant to a particular investigation, and that the facts give rise to a 
reasonable, articulable suspicion of activities associated with a foreign power or its 
agent. Under the terms of reference here in New Zealand, the review will also have 
regard to any additional matters that arise during the review as agreed by the Attorne y-
General. We therefore recommend that the Attorney -General notify now in writing in 
the New Zealand Gazette  that the modification of intrusive surveillance powers and 
restoration of civil liberties, as legislated in the United States, be taken up as a matter 
that has arisen and that New Zealand consider emulating the US initiative.

CHRISTCHURCH CITY COUNCIL (RATES VALIDATION) BILL 
Third Reading 
Hon NICKY WAGNER (National —Christchurch Central) : I move, That the 
Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill be now read a third time . I am 
delighted to be here today to present this Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) 
Bill at its third reading. There has been quite a lot of controversy around this bill, but 
basically it is very simple, it is very straightforward, it is very short, and it is very 
focused. What this bill does is set out to validate rates irregularities that came to light to 
the Christchurch City Council just last year. 
Let us give you a little bit of context. Each June, the Christchurch City Council —
and, in actual fact, councils across the country —resolve to set their rates for the next 
financial year, and since 2004, the wording for that rates resolution has been the same or 
similar. But in 2013 the Department of Internal Affairs informed the Christchurch City 
Council that the resolution did not meet the requirements of the Local Government 
(Rating Act) of 2002. So let me get that straight—for 9 years it had been using the same 
resolution and for 9 years, unbeknown to everybody, that rates resolution had been 
faulty.  
4296 Christchurch City Council (Rates Validation) Bill 3 Jun 2015 
 
The problem all began back in 2004, when the council deliberately set out to simplify 
and to use everyday language in setting its rates resolution. But, inadvertently, it left out 
important bits of information —important requirements —which meant that that 
resolution was invalid. Under section 24 of the Local Government (Rating) Act, it 
requires that a rating resolution must include the date on which the rate must be paid, 
and if that rate is to be paid in instalments, it must include the amount and the date of 
each instalment. Section 57, which authorises additional penalties, requires that the 
resolution also states when the rates must be paid and the due date, and the resolution 
must also state how the penalties are calculated and the date on which those penalties 
must be paid. In this case, the Christchurch City Council’s resolution did none of that, 
but let me make it clear: all the required information was available. It was all available 
in the council’s rating policy and in the funding impact statement. It was discussed at 
the council table. It was aired in the local newspaper. It just was not in the resolution. 
So the attempt to simplify had, basically, backfired, and although nobody had noticed 
and it had gone on for 9 years, finally, in 2013, it had to be repaired.  
I must give credit to the temporary chief executive officer of the Christchurch City 
Council at that time, Jane Parfitt, because immediately the council was able to correct 
the 2013- 14 rates resolution, and then it went back to review all it s other past 
resolutions. They managed to identify a number of other technical irregularities. They 
found errors in the setting of seven targeted rates and also in the setting of the uniform 
annual general charge. It was the same problem. Although the back ground information 
was readily available, it was not in that resolution, so all those resolutions were 
irregular. As I have said, they were able to fix those resolutions going forward, but there 
was no ability for them to fix the resolutions going back, hence this bill.  
I would like to thank the Local Government and Environment Committee members

UNDERGROUND COAL MINING SAFETY BILL 
First Reading 
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour —West Coast -  Tasman): I move, That the 
Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Transport 
and Industrial Relations C ommittee to consider the bill. Like so many members’ bills, 
this one has been some time in gestation. It was a bill I introduced after the Royal 
Commission on the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy, which had recommended that an 
“effective regulatory framework f or underground coal mining should be established 
urgently.” The royal commission identified through its hearings the fact that 
Queensland and New South Wales have, arguably, the best practice in this area. 
Effectively, what I did was take those Queensland mine regulations, and what this bill 
will do is implement them immediately into New Zealand to protect the lives of miners 
working underground.  
I am sure that we will hear from the Government the excuse that much has happened 
in that time, and I acknowledge that, and that there is no need for this bill. If I can take 
us back through a pathway, in 1994 I was given a lecture on underground mining by 
Bill Brazil, who was a former mines inspector. He told me that the change in the 
legislation in 1992 by the Na tional Government would be rued by this country, and that 
we would be shamed by the consequences of deregulation of mining regulations that 
had been established through over a century of experience. How right he was.  
It took some time. In fact, it was in the early 2000s before we started to see some 
major faults in the practice of underground mining. The theory had been that the 
Occupational Safety and Health Service would deal with the safety and the challenges 
and the risks of underground mining, and tha t, in fact, a code of practice would be 
established and would be passed and would protect miners. That code of practice was 
never, ever properly implemented and, indeed, the question is whether it has been 
implemented today—but I will come back to that iss ue. The inevitable catastrophe and 
loss of life because of an unregulated mining environment cost the lives of 29 men at 
Pike River, and some others before. In fact, I wrote a letter to the Minister of Labour 
just some months before Pike River, raising issues that had been brought to my attention 
about lax practices in underground mining, but I was given by the Minister —who had 
got it from her officials, no doubt—a reassurance that all was well.  
This bill is my best attempt to try to protect the lives of u nderground miners. It was 
the best thing I could do, because we had let our experience and that of international 
miners drift into the naivety of deregulation and market forces to protect the miners at 
work. This bill takes Queensland regulations, which ar e not perfect —in fact, of Pike 
River some have said that Australians designed the mine, Australians ran the mine, and 
Australians were, in part, a big, major cause of its disaster—but Queensland regulations, 
not implemented in New Zealand, would have protected those men.  
The Government did move forward and pass legislation. In fact, the original bill it 
brought in was split into three parts. One was to set up WorkSafe, which has happened. 
The second was, of course, to ensure that Mines Rescue had the right  authority to do its 
job properly. And the third was the Health and Safety in Employment Amendment Act, 
“Pike River” having been dropped from the title. That was passed in 2013, and a key 
component in amended section 20A of the Health and Safety in Employm ent Act is 
subsection (1), which states: “A code of practice, an amendment to a code of practice, or 
a revocation of a code of practice has no force or effect until it has been approved by the 
Minister.” I rang today to see whether that code of practice has been implemented, and 
no one could give me reassurance that it has.

We have had the establishment of a High Hazards Unit. We have had progress. In 
fact, we have had mines shut down until we could be sure that a safer regime was being 
carried out. Although people point the finger at Pike River, the reality is that Solid 
Energy, the Government’s own miner, had such lax practices that for 6 months its mine 
was closed down post Pike River. Not one tonne of coal came out, because it, too, was 
overseeing a dangerous mining situation. We cannot take anything for granted.  
What I ask of the Government is that it supports this legislation going to the select 
committee. It may say it has done all it can. What I say is that I want to check, and this 
Parliament must check, that the legislation is being implemented as intended, that the

ask of the Government: can it support this bill and send it to the select committee, where

We need to know that the  High Hazards Unit set up by the Government has the

The legislation passed by the Government oversees safety in quarries. This year,

There are unresolved issues. Twenty -nine men still lie in the bowels of the Pike 
River mine. Their families have been asked to move —some say, to move on. I would 
never ask them to move on. If you look through history, if you look at all cultures, one

Dave Feickert, a staunch advocate for mi ne safety, made a submission to the royal 
commission. The family of Mr Feickert, who, unfortunately, has now passed away, 
wants his submission to be made public. That has been blocked.  
Those are but three unresolved issues that I think need to be resolved. I ask the 
Government to support this bill going to the select committee to allow Parliament to 
review the progress or otherwise that it has made, to question whether there is still a 
need for more improvement in the area of mine safety and work safety in this country, 
and to ensure that everything that we can do as parliamentarians to prevent another mine 
disaster in this country has been done. We do not want one unnecessary death in mining

ensure that men and women, when they go to work, can return home to their loved ones 
and to their families. This is what the families want most from that terrible disaster: to 
ensure that others do not have to suffer as they still suffer. I ask the Government to

I am sorry, Mr Assistant Speaker, if you think I am looking at notes, but I am just 
reading out a chronology here that I think is important for the record. Then in December 
2013 the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment released a further 
document. Here it is—I am holding it here. It is Safe mines: safe workers—New laws on 
mining health and safety: A quick guide for mine operators . But what the ministry says 
in this is not to just rely on the guide but to go and read the legislation. I think what it is 
addressing is the fact that people do not delve deeply enough into the issues around 
health and safety. What it states here in the introduction—it says: “The Government has 
recently made changes to the laws concerning health and safety i n the mining industry. 
This is in response”, obviously, “to the … Royal Commission” and the tragedy that 
obviously happened in Pike River and to the families there. It says: “The new legal 
requirements have been developed with help from an expert reference  group of mining, 
health and safety and regulatory experts from New Zealand and abroad. The 
Government has also worked closely with people in the industry”.  
3 Jun 2015 Underground Coal Mining Safety Bill 4329 
 
As I conclude, what I want to say is that the Government does care, immensely, 
about the safety of  miners and workers and contractors, and we have demonstrated that 
by passing sound legislation—

debate is interrupted, and set down for further consideration next sitting day.
